comment_text: I love these 'free market' pundits that selectively dish out obvious falsehoods disguised as market theory. As I understand the 'Free Market Theory', scarcity drives up prices and abundance drives them down, no? If what the fast food industry says is true about labour shortages, the wages at these outlets should be outrageously high but strangely they are not. Obviously if Canadians won't accept $10 an hour jobs at Tim's, then Tim's should have to offer better wages to attract employees from McDonalds and vice versa. This is a fundamental 'free market' tenet. It appears that it's the crappy pay that is the problem for these companies, not a lack of people to take the jobs. Why is it that these jobs must be kept at minimum wage at all costs? Is it so that we can pay a buck less for a cheeseburger? Why has the 'invisible hand' of the market not driven wages up? Well it's because the temporary worker policies are designed to ensure that they stay low. This is not a case of an industry not being able to compete in the so called global market, a fast food company competes with the outlet across the street. Funny how even public companies (CBC) justify staggering executive salaries and bonuses by saying that they are necessary to attract the best talent but this 'principle' never seems to apply to ordinary workers. Why does scarcity in a 'profession' lead to fabulous wages but scarcity in unskilled labour results in FTW programs? What we are seeing is a deliberate ongoing program to drive down wages of the working class and maintain a permanent underclass of workers to be exploited at will. Nothing new here. Why do we not import FTWs at near starvation wages to work as policemen, firemen, notaries, engineers, lawyers, radiologists or doctors for that matter, where the savings to public expenditures would really be significant? The obvious result would be a country full of FTWs, very high unemployment and eventually the pay for these jobs would bottom out at the minimum wage (less 15%). Anyone who contends that the FTW program for unskilled labour is necessary or even good for 'the economy' rather than just a plan to keep wages low for blue collar workers is either badly informed or a liar. I don't believe Amanda is badly informed.

comment_text: The problem with this editorial is that is factually incorrect. Banking and cashing out are two different issues. Banking sick days is not uncommon, nor is it an problem. That an employee doesn't use much sick time and winds up with a significant bank to guard against serious illness is a good thing. What isn't a good thing is a cash out provision on retirement/termination for any form of sick leave. That is the benefit that Ottawa (and all employers who have agreed to it in the past) should target. The theory is that by banking sick days for a future cash benefit, sick leave will be reduced. It doesn't work. The evidence is that it causes no long term material impact to sick leave usage. More problematic is that it is an unfunded liability (a sick day earned in 2001 at 2001 dollars will be paid in the future at a future wage rate). My opinion is that unionized employers get the collective agreement they deserve. They bargained an idiotic provision (banking sick days for payout) it is up to them at the table to bargain it out. If they can't, hire better bargainers.

comment_text: The Liberals have come and gone in the public affection before. But I agree with Jeffrey that it is now different. Before, while the public might have accepted or rejected Liberal policies, at least the party had credibility. People might have rejected the Liberals at particular elections, but there was always the thought that they could be gone back to if the new people weren't up to the task. This credibility has now been lost (probably irrevocably) as a result of their numerous squandered chances, bad decisions, lack of policy and commitment, and weak leaders. At one time, we had parties with identifiable differences--the left, the right and the centre. The left and the right made good protest votes (and some would vote for them out of reflex or inability to think things through), but Canadians being what they are, the centre was the best long term bet for a lot of people. But now the centre doesn't hold much appeal. It means nothing and stands for nothing. The country has become polarized between the right and the left, and increasingly people are willing to take a stand rather than voting for the party that offers the least contentious choice. I have been a lifelong Liberal supporter, but cannot see myself ever voting for them again. The choice is between the NDP and the Cons.

comment_text: Interesting cynical take on post-partisanship. Erroneously conflates Trudeau and Obama. Trudeau will not be facing a hostile Congress, the Canadian political system doesn't work that way, and the article is surprisingly simplistic for someone who teaches political science and is a fellow at Massey College. The election of Trudeau should mean we continue to escape the polarization of ideologies that plagues most other Western countries, and with which we flirted briefly when we considered having the Conservative and NDP as our two major parties. While it gives the electorate a clear choice, and clarifies the ideological differences, it is also based on the idea that one side is right and the other wrong. Canadians have always known this is not true, and thus have tended towards electing consensus governments, whether Progressive Conservative or Liberal. If the Tories respond to this defeat by tacking to the centre, we will have reestablished this pattern, in which it could be argued we have been 'post-partisan' for much of our history. In that interpretation, non-partisanship can be a good thing. Partisanship is so in the DNA in the US that the parallel doesn't stand up under any serious analysis.

It is true that some of us, reviewing this case, will come down strongly on one side or the other but the fact remains that no neat formula or process exists in a few cases like this whereby persons of good will can all agree upon the balance between contending rights that is most appropriate. For what it's worth I would argue that both Professor Grayson and York University each addressed the situation they faced with good will and intelligence and that each tried their best to weigh how the respective rights and dignity of all the persons involved could be best respected. Further, the fact that the Human Rights Code does not provide a ready-made answer in this situation does not negate the value of that Code as a framework within which to strive to resolve difficult cases like this. The truth, arguably, illustrated by this story as a whole is that morals, ethics and legal reasoning are processes rather than fixed outcomes. The point is that we must try to do the right thing realizing that discerning what the best outcome should be is sometimes difficult and that other, no better or worse than ourselves, might honestly come to a different conclusion in the circumstances - and also that the very effort to arrive at the best solution (even if 'best' is murky) is a worthy exercise.

Britain experienced phenomenal economic growth in the 17th and 19th centuries. The economy evolved alongside developments in family and government. The early modern late-marriage family, working and living in a household, stimulated the economy because wives closer in age to their husbands acted as partners and joint decision-makers, not as master and servant. 17th century democratic politics grew out of the need to justify a revolution that cost King Charles his life. The trauma inspired brilliant minds such as John Locke, who explained government as an association of people, who all expected benefits and responsibilities. Everybody had a right to protection from the government, not just the rich and the successful. Government's policies needed to meet the needs of the peasants and worker, not only those of the nobility and the capitalists. Contrary to the narrow perspective of today's capitalists, 18th century England provided Josiah Wedgwood, an inventor, manufacturer and social reformer. He took pride in efficient factory organization as well as the jobs her provided for the working class of England. People such as Lang see only the interests of profits for the entrepreneurs. Democracy works well only insofar as government preserves this organic shared existence. Early modern and Enlightenment England, America and continental Europe authored policies and built government for all the people. The notion of all the people expended in the course of the 19th and 20th centuries. Democracy and freedom will erode if governments ignore the interests of the weak trusting Lang's unsubstantiated assumption that eventually the poor will catch up.

comment_text: I find this column to be very strange. Regular readers will know that I am no big cheerleader of the current PM, and that I thought Mulcair was a much stronger and more deserving performer in the debates. But I find this column strange. I find myself actually wanting to defend the Prime Minister. The writer is trying to ascribe some kind of cunning, manipulative intention upon the Prime Minister, as if the PM is some brilliant but diabolical villain who is up to no good, in complex, convoluted ways. Sorry, I do not see it. I may not agree with the PM's timetable or policy, but I think the straightforward analysis is more like accurate: That is, what you see is what you get, a promise made shall be a promise kept. That's it, that is what is going on with the PM and the refugee matter. There is no 'there' there, so to speak - sometimes a cigar is just a cigar. Two other strange things in the column: No, wrong, Canadians do not all see it as 'smooth and banal' and part of the normal 'underlying hum of the country, that it’s barely noticed', having these huge immigration levels we have. Plenty of Canadians actually firmly believe the rates should be cut back. And Europe has troubles with immigration for a reason not mentioned (strangely): Unlike Canada, they do not filter and select for highly intelligent well educated families. That is actually what mainly leads to our success, it is our filtering - it is actually NOT our multicultural-mosaic-kumbaya stuff that makes Canada peaceful and low on violence. It is the smarts of our carefully selected immigrants.

To coin an American standard, the person holding the gun makes the rules; in this case, it's Quebec.

comment_text: THE ARCTIC SEEMS TO BE WARMING UP.Reports from fishermen, seal hunters, and explorers who sail the seas about Spitzbergen and the eastern Arctic, all point to a radical change in climatic conditions and hitherto un-heard-of high temperatures in that part of the earth's surface. In August, 1922, the Norwegian Department of Commerce sent an expedition to Spitzbergen and Bear Island under the leadership of Dr. Adolf Hoel, lecturer on geology at the University of Christiania. In connection with Dr. Hoel's report, it is interest to note the unusually warm summer in Arctic Norway and the observations of Capt. Martin Ingebrigtsen, who has sailed the eastern Arctic for 54 years past. He says that he first noted warmer conditions in 1915, that since that time it has steadily gotten warmer, and that to-day the Arctic of that region is not recognizable as the same region of 1865 to 1917. Many old landmarks are so changed as to be unrecognizable. Where formerly great masses of ice were found, there are now often moraines, accumulations of earth and stones. At many points where glaciers formerly extended far into the sea they have entirely disappeared. The change in temperature, says Captain Ingebrigtsen has also brought about great change in the flora and fauna of the Arctic. This summer he sought for white fish in Spitzbergen waters. Formerly great shoals of them were found there. This year he saw none, although he visited all the old fishing grounds. comment_text: Great column. It is worth remembering in this context that until after WW II the two Federal Parties that have alternated as our Governments since Confederation did not really differ on what we now see as a left-right ideological basis. Rather, they differed over matters such as the British connection vs reciprocity with the US, religious affiliation and ethnic origin, urban vs rural development, etc. Even over the latter issues, each Party tried to maintain some link with the proponents of interests generally favoured by the other. Political affiliation tended to be a matter of family tradition and the religious or ethnic group with which one was associated. Patronage networks tended to perpetuate these linkages. In the wake of WW I these quasi-tribal patterns were tending to weaken, especially west of the Ontario-Québec border, and ideological questions that we today would recognize as such were increasingly debated, but aside from the rise of marginal third Parties, it would be an oversimplification to see the Liberal and Conservative Parties differing fundamentally on these questions during the 1920s and 30s. With the rise in popular support for the CCF (and, briefly, for the Labour Progressive Party as the Communist Party then called itself) during the closing days of WW II, the Liberal Party, more so than the Conservative Party, saw the need to compete for an emerging left of centre oriented voting public, especially in the West, Cape Breton Island and parts of Ontario. However, both the Conservatives and Liberals in general supported the broadening of the welfare state and public sector on both public policy and patronage grounds. What by the 1960s became to be known as the Red Tory phenomena was the Conservative Party response to these post-Depression and post WW II trends and were initially strongest on the Prairies, parts of Ontario and Atlantic Canada, but receded on the Prairies following the end of the Diefenbaker era. Many families had been traditional supporters of the Conservative Party (and staunch opponents of the Liberal Party) for generations (i.e. the quasi-tribal phenomena discussed earlier), but had become attracted to progressive causes in their current circumstances. This arguably is a major root of the Red Tory phenomena. In the 2011 General Election, the NDP had some success, especially in Newfoundland, in getting Red Tories to vote NDP. Thomas Mulcair in his opening speech of the formal 2015 campaign made a focused appeal to the traditional Red Tory voting groups. For the reasons well described in Jeffrey Simpson, we should expect the NDP outreach to be especially focused in Atlantic Canada and parts of Ontario, where the Conservative Party is increasingly seen as abandoning its Red Tory tradition.

comment_text: Someone must have put something very strange into the water cooler in the Globe & Mail's editorial quarters. I can't think of any other explanation for what has to be the most bizarre editorial endorsement in the paper's history, if not in the history of all Canadian media outlets. Normally we look to editorials as a source of clear thinking about difficult issues. But the G&M has produced a muddle-headed, reality-denying mess. But after much twisting and turning, G&M then endorses a choice that doesn't exist! What the hell? The writers admit that 'Canada needs a change.' They gamely argue that if the election had been fought solely on economic issues, the Conservatives would have won easily. And they even admit that it was the Conservatives' decision to run instead on issues that the country rightly perceived as divisive. Only in G&M fantasy land can one vote for Conservatives without also voting to continue Harper in office as prime minister. Yet it is exactly peoples' unhappiness with the non-economic behavior of the Conservatives that threatens the party's hold on power. The editorial shows a stunning lack of understanding of the voters whom the paper purports to inform. If I were the owner of the paper, I would fire everyone involved in producing this shameful embarrassment.

comment_text: This has to be one of the most convoluted, contradictory pieces of opinion in a very long time. I confess, I have been waiting with bated breath to see what stance the Globe would take on this election, hoping against hope 'the subject who is truly loyal to the chief magistrate would neither advise nor submit to arbitrary measures.' In other words, I hoped the Globe would have the guts to step up and say 'throw the rascals out!' But I never suspected our national newspaper would engage in such a ridiculous exercise in self-pretzeling as it has here. Several voices have already pointed out the absurdity of re-electing the problem with the assumption it would then resign. Do you really think, should he in fact win on Monday, that your stern words for Steve will be enough to make him slink out the back door on Tuesday? You also seem to have overlooked the problem of who would then fill his jackboots. Jason Kenny? Pierre Poilièvre? Laureen? Despite your efforts to worm your way around the problem, you are clearly suggesting that we bring back a PM who has devolved into a dictator, liar, suppressor of truth, manipulator, dredger of slimy-bottom, racially driven emotional responses to non-issues, among other attributes. Of course, cavorting with the reviled Fords gives us confidence that he is actually a noble man. Also, to suggest that this guy has given us “sound financial stewardship” is laughable. Are you referring to his ditching of the surplus inherited from the Liberals? To the steady string of deficits he has rung up? The huge waste of money on non-existent fighter jets? On jeopardising of the entire Canadian economy by putting all our eggs in the slippery oil basket while stiffing our manufacturing base? Any of these and many others would serve as arguments to deflate the knee-jerk response that “Conservatives make good money managers” but, as you rightly point out, this is not even the Conservative Party, this is the Harper Conservative Party. At some point we have to stand up to the Chief Magistrate and say: THIS IS YOUR DOING. In this case, I think we also have to admit that both the baby and his very dirty bathwater have to go. Then the tub needs to be scrubbed. The Liberals had to go through a long rebuild after their fiascos; the same now holds true for the Tories. comment_text: Ms. Wente is fundamentally wrong about this, though she makes her case well. But she still misses the most important points. The right of a woman to wear a niqab is protected in Canada by two fundamental rights: the right of freedom of religion and the right of freedom of expression. Those are rights that can only be taken away under the most dire circumstances. This, clearly, is not a case that fits that criteria. But let's think this through. If we are really talking about symbols that oppress women, then we hardly need to start with women wearing niqabs. In Canada and Quebec, the Catholic Church has a far longer and infinitely more influential history in oppressing women. It still does not treat women as equals. Shouldn't the Church and its ubiquitous symbols be sanctioned if what we are talking about is symbolism? If not, why not? And why stop with Catholics? Why not condemn and legally sanction orthodox Jews, Christian fundamentalists, and any other religion that oppresses women? I would argue that the obvious answer is that the Church (and other Western religions) is simply part of the background noise in Canada, whatever it symbolizes, good or ill. But the niqab is strange and different. That is what has made it a lightning rod for protest. In a liberal democratic society, one group of people cannot simply declare illegal the beliefs of others, especially if those others are not harming anyone by practicing their beliefs. Even more, one group of people do not have the right to tell others what they believe. The niqab may symbolize oppression to feminists and progressives in Quebec, but they do not have the right to tell the women wearing it what it should mean to those women. Just because I feel uncomfortable with someone else's dress code does not mean I have the right to impose my discomfort and values on that person. At the end of the day the niqab debate matters because it does indeed, reveal, that there is a powerful strain of bigotry and muddled thinking on the part of most Canadians on this matter. In this case, both Mulcair and Trudeau are to be commended for taking the position that is right rather than the position that is politically convenient and that appeals to the worst, most xenophobic tendencies of Canadians.

comment_text: I believe the reasons Ford Nation remains intact goes far beyond hypocrisy of conservatism. After all, that same hypocrisy is clearly evident on the left. Certainly it is very obvious in the environmental puritanism we observe around us.Over time our society and culture has undergone a massive shift in attitude. Long gone are the days of our fathers and mothers who believed, we as citizens owed our country. Today, Kennedy would be a laughing stock if he said 'Ask not,,,,,,,,,'.We have gone from a common view of honour and duty, to materialism and entitlement. We have become a society of individuals who feel no sense of duty or loyalty to our fellow citizens. It matters not what is in the best interests of our country. All that matters is what is good for ME.Look around. All authority is deemed to be corrupt and malevolent. Every opinion you disagree with is tainted by conflicting interests. Unions are evil incarnate. Science, knowledge and facts are servants to 'the elite'. Indeed, we define the elite by what we are not. Not rich? Those that do are elite? Not well educated? In fact, any others we envy have become 'the elite' to be despised. What was once used to describe the brightest and best has become a pejorative. As do the people we label as such. The politics of this envy is ugly and damaging our society. As a culture of individuals, we are in it for ourselves and we assume all these others are also, thus we detest them. In this culture we care not one iota what a buffoon like Mr. Ford does. We care only for what he delivers (or convinces us he delivers) to us.Is there a cure for this malaise? I am an optimist. I believe there is.We must shrink the size of the lowest socio/economic groups. We must ensure the fruits of our society are better distributed. Trickle down does not work. We must ensure our youth have access to education and/or practical training. Hard work and skill must be rewarded. People like Mr. Ford and so many other unethical politicians must be disqualified from office. NOT by rules but by the action of voters.

Evil's always there. Where you least expect it!

Universal health care didn't happen by itself, it took courage, commitment and a drive to address the common good against a backdrop of constrained resources and the opposition of motivated interest groups. Rob Ford is just the latest, greatest and most *entertaining* of a long line of arguably much more talented and skilled administrators at all levels who lacked vision. There is a line of policitians decades long who've failed to address Toronto's ever increasing, and increasingly complex, needs simply to function in a way that is meaningful to its citizens beyond the gridlock, zoning, much less encourage a dynamic, vibrant and healthy place to live. I have hope that Toronto's registered voters have learned a thing or two from Ford's spectacular blow out, but like Jeffrey Simpson perhaps a sizable chunk of them are addicted to, and actively cultivating, a penchant for what amounts to political porn. Can't keep your eyes off it, as Wente would say...

comment_text: Gibson is in way over his head with this article. The subject matter is above his pay grade. That being said, over the last few years the SCC has made a number of important decisions that might reasonably have been decided the other way, and those decisions may well have important negative implications for Canada. For example, take the recent decisions on the constitutional right to collective bargaining, and the limiting of the ability of the provinces to restrict the right to strike of employees providing essential services. Pay in the public sector is out of control, provincial government deficits are through the roof, hospitals in Ontario are in the red and cancelling elective surgeries, and the burdens on the health care system are only beginning - they will be growing exponentially over the next decade or so. So how will the provinces deal with this given the SCC decisions? Are these decisions in the best interests of Canada? The way many industries in the US overcame otherwise insurmountable labor problems was to outsource. The US auto manufacturers used to manufacture the entire vehicle, everything but the tires, and now they just assemble them from parts supplied by hundreds of contractors, with two or three suppliers for each part. The objective is to minimize the labor from their own employees, who are the most expensive, and to reduce their of strike risk. The labor movement in the US destroyed many industries, and now the SCC has set the stage to allow the labor movement in Canada to destroy the provincial governments. Could these SCC decisions force a fundamental change in Canada's public healthcare system?

comment_text: Thanks for a nice dose of perspective. I live in Saint John NB which has long prided itself as 'the Loyalist City'. At one time Saint John was the 4th largest English speaking city on the continent, but it has long been in decline and now has less population than Moncton. A component of this decline is a culture that right into the 1950's saw itself as uniquely enlightened and dare I say - Anglican. Lesser souls were certainly seen as being lesser. The city is now culturally much more dominated politically by the descendants of Irish Immigrants and I think, speaking as a person of protestant roots, that the changes toward being less presumptuous have been refreshing. I think we now have a far nicer and more open and more welcoming society here than once we were, and that certainly includes the Anglicans too who have much to be proud of in their great heritage. But we also have a lot of poverty now, and for folks in such circumstances it is never easy or nice. Interesting how our poverty is particularly concentrated on the home turf and still the headquarters of one of Canada's greatest industrial families. So much for trickle down!

comment_text: I am not offended by Ms. Wente's column this morning but I do have some concerns with what she has written. Ms. Wente is known of course for having admirable skill in providing effective opinion where there's a vacuum, as she did in labeling Paul Martin 'Mr. Dithers' so many years ago. She is trying to do the same thing today and naturally many have jumped in with appreciative comments. However, there is a hollowness to the column. Objectively, it is quite hard at this stage to criticize the new Liberal government for mistaken judgements or overlooked opportunities; it is too soon and the government is on too much of a good run. Instead, she frames the government's situation, and our country's overall situation, in world terms. Fair enough, but the world is on fire for many big reasons none of which have much to do with the Liberal government. comment_text: A lot of people here seem to want to advance the idea that citizenship is contingent on taxation, that an ex-pat isn't a 'real' citizen if he/she doesn't pay what someone else deems an acceptable level of taxes and therefore shouldn't vote. comment_text: I'm an expatriate. Like most of the other Canadians that I know living overseas (and true for most expats from anywhere that I've known) I did not as much 'leave Canada' as I explored my life and career interests. With the exception of the very few, we all still love the country (and you should see the number of Canadian hockey jerseys during olympic games at bars and restaurants in places like Hanoi, Bangkok and Hong Kong). I pay income tax on my taxable income in Canada (modest investments). I make earnings overseas that are non-taxable and Canada - quite rightly - can't touch it. I take ZERO from any Canadian program, benefit, credit etc....not a single penny. I buy Blue Cross when I come to visit every year. The argument for taking away my right is really just an attempt to stranglehold my sense of being Canadian (which strongly includes, by the way, being allowed to vote) and to basically say that if I don't live there, and I don't earn taxable income there, then I'm not 'Canadian enough' to have a say on the nation's leadership. It's also basically saying that some Canadians who (for various good reasons... none of them related to screwing the government) have an interest or passion or circumstance that leaves them living and working overseas... well, you should have just 'stayed at home' if you want to have any say on the nation....'true' Canadians don't aspire to such nonsense. So call me biased but I can't make any sense out of this.....unless, of course, I consider for a moment the fact that historically expatriates tend to not vote for right wing party as much as they vote for one of the other parties

comment_text: Firefighters HAVE NOT been receiving raises twice as high as other public sector workers or private for that matter. The expected increase in the private sector in 2013 is 3.1 per cent, slightly above the three per cent increase given last year. The average increase for employees in the public sector is expected to be 2.8 per cent in 2013. Owen Sound firefighters actually make a salary closer to $80,000 per year, the 29 firefighters on the Sunshine list making $100,000+ only did so because they received 3 years worth of back pay from the arbitrators rulinga 24 hour shift averages out to a 42 hour work which is longer than the typical Canadian's 40 hour work week. Is there down time? Absolutely, but there is down time within every job. Anyone who claims they work non stop for their entire 40 hours per week is lying to you. I've worked enough jobs to know that two hour lunches, time on the golf course, surfing the net, gossiping, etc fill a great part of the week in many professions. Firefighters are not given a lunch hour or 15 minute breaks, and preparing and eating meals are often interrupted by responding to calls. They don't complain, it's part of the job. Contrary to popular belief there still are MANY fires. They burn hotter than ever before and are more dangerous due to lightweight building construction and synthetics. A city like Toronto will have more than a dozen fires per day, most of which will never make the news because they are small kitchen or electrical fires with no injuries. Pumpers responding to medical calls do not cost a million dollars, $300,000 is a more accurate figure. The pumper and 4 firefighters are already stationed in the firehall regardless, so responding to a medical call in the area is a value added service firefighters can provide 'in their downtime' for the low cost of just a few litres of diesel. comment_text: In the early 1970's I was a guidance counselor at Espanola High School. We had a program whereby a group of 30 or so students from Attiwapiskat and Kashetchewan (pardon my mis-spelling) were voluntarily brought down to this modern composite secondary school for a pilot project to orient them to modern education and our society. They stayed in local homes, and attended a special program for them with the flexibility of integrating into any of the regular secondary school subjects in which they would be interested or capable. Special attention was given to their English language skills and life survival skills in a modern society. This program collapsed at Christmas when the kids were allowed to go back to their reserves for the holidays. Most chose not to return! The program collapsed after a year or two. The kids and their parents obviously did not value education! The school serves two other local reserves and had an Indian Affairs counselor for the native students and integrated the students into the curriculum as best as possible, including several remedial programs. I locked horns with one Indian Affairs native gentleman over my attempts to encourage a bright Grade 13 (at that time) native girl to consider college or university. She lived at home on a reserve south of Espanola, under harsh circumstances, having a major responsibilities for starting the morning fires and meals and other domestic responsibilities that took away from her ability to focus on her school work. I could have arranged at no cost to her or the band a home in town where she could stay from Monday to Thursday nights so she could focus on her education returning home Friday to Sunday nights. I was opposed by the Indian Affairs Counselor, not because she had obligations to her family, but that her role was to ensure the continuance of the culture and her place was on the reserve, not going to college.

comment_text: Yes Canada has a duty to accept its share of refugees. But, as with the other elements of a smart immigration program, we should not accept any softening of our security standards in the process. Beyond the refugee issue there is a fundamental policy question that Canadians expect their government to address. Is it enough that our immigration policy be reactive - accepting all comers and allowing circumstance to dictate who and how many new Canadians we accept? Or should we engage in recruitment policies that target groups on the basis of (1) their potential for a strong contribution to our economic and industrial needs; and (2) their cultural affinity with Canada's core democratic principles and ideals. Should, as one example only, the latter include a predisposition to the acceptance of women as full, equal and independent members of society? The notion of a Canada that embraces diversity, a principle strongly reiterated by the new Trudeau government, should not be seen as an invitation for immigrant groups who seek to isolate themselves from mainstream Canadian society. The question, more bluntly, is whether there are groups whose cultural identities and social proclivities are so distant and alien to our own that they are unlikely to be happy here and whose expectations we will likely find frustrating to accommodate? I think this is a reasonable question - one all Canadians should be given an opportunity to weigh in on. I can accept the answer - whatever it is - provided it is a true consensus of Canada's will.

comment_text: I generally respect Clifford Orwin's ideas, but this column is so deranged that I wonder about his general overall competence as a commentator. I find it utterly remarkable that Mr. Orwin can, apparently, so casually dismiss George Bush's profound responsibility for the disaster in which he left his country. If Bush was 'demonized' before Obama took power it is precisely because his administration was an absolutely unmitigated disaster. I imagine the allusion that Orwin is making is to the financial crisis which, admittedly, had its roots in the deregulation begun by the Clinton administration. But Bush carried on and exacerbated those policies then terribly mismanaged the crisis when it happened, even while driving the US into a financial hole by launching unnecessary wars and cutting taxes. He left an extraordinary mess for Obama to clean up, a task at which Obama has been largely successful. comment_text: For the first time since as long as i can recollect, I agree with Ms. Wente. Mr. Obama has lost a great deal of face and prestige. He has, I think, made himself essentially impotent in foreign affairs by failing to carry the American people with him retreating from tow of the positions he has maintained for the past two years. First, he has stated the U.S. is committed to regime change is Syria. This led to the brief flurry of international diplomatic activity where the West and others recognized the Free Syria Coalition as the legitimate government. Secondly, he has stated that the use of chemical weapons is a red line which Assad could not cross without “consequences”. We are now told by the media that Assad has used chemical weapons some 14 times, the last being in the horrific attack on August 21.The state of Syria has ceased to exist. The Assad writ runs north from Damascus to the Allawite homeland with pockets of rebel controlled areas interspersed. The rebels control the Euphrates Valley. And the Kurds in the north-east are drawing closer to their cousins in northern Iraq. More than 100, 000 killed, two million refugees and now five million internally displaced. And due to the continuing brutality of the Assad regime, more and more Syrians are turning to the militant Islamists as their last hope in fighting Assad. The centrist groups in the Free Syria coalition are losing support. The West does not want to support the el Quaeda affiliated Islamist for fear they gain power. The U.S. is now embroiled in an interminable process of U.N. inspections (in the middle of the war and after the dispersion of his chemical weapons by Assad to many sites to protect the weapons from American missiles) and the impossible task of determining if Assad will tell the truth. A Syrian signature on the U.N. convention against chemical weapons has no more truth that Hitler’s signature on the Munich Pact. Can this become more of a mess? And people continue to flee or die. Someone should take away from Mr. Obama the pen he uses to draw his red lines. It is no longer needed. He has lost all credibility.

comment_text: Tragically, Margaret Wente chooses to parrot jingoistic American conservatives in the most cartoonish fashion instead of appropriately assessing the most important aspect of these efforts at diplomacy – namely, the impact on the Syrian people. In recent years, the United States has employed military force with impunity in many hotspots around the world. It is a relief that instead, high-stakes diplomacy reminiscent of the Cold War era is slowly returning. No amount of wounded pride from an article in an op-ed can compare with the many more victims of war that would result from a Western-led bombing campaign. Their plight is indeed grim. Already, 6 million Syrians are displaced, in and outside of Syria, and over 100, 000 are dead. In spite of this – or rather because of this - they are fairly certain that more bombs being dropped on their heads is a step backwards, not forwards, for peace and stability. For some reason, it seems to be incredibly difficult for Washington’s jingoists – and now, Ms. Wente – to recover from bruised egos long enough to give sober thought to the impact on these already-suffering millions. Other considerations need to be added to the list. Would a fractious and in some cases radicalized Syrian opposition be any better for the Syrian people when it takes the offensive? How do we handle the Shia-Sunni divide that the war is settling along the lines of? Who else do we have to worry about potentially drawing into the conflict, and on which side? What, in the end, are we trying to accomplish by bombing Syria? All of these complex issues have been pushed contemptuously aside by Ms. Wente and the jingoists who would agree with her. Instead, it’s all about whether or not America looks like a weakling.“Like most else,” admits Wente, “I’m confused as hell over Syria.” Informed readers of her article would no doubt concur.

comment_text: Wente is wrong on a number of points. Over any reasonable period of time, government revenues and expenses should balance. To my view, cutting any taxes before the books are balanced is irresponsible. Do we really need to fire 100, 000 of our neighbors and relatives to balance the books 1 year sooner? The reality is that we can shrink government with far less pain. It isn't magic, it isn't rocket science. Simply hold the growth in government spending to the rate of inflation. This ensures that the size of government shrinks relative to the GDP. As the real growth in GDP rises, the proportion of governments' share declines. The growth in revenue will take care of the deficit. This leaves room for true negotiation with government employees and forces government to make choices on how our tax dollars are spent. It avoids the Conservative pain and the Liberal waste.

comment_text: While this is a delightful article to read, and I would love to think it plausible that America might come to its senses on this and start restoring a shred of sense to its gun policies, this piece omits a fairly key point to this discussion: a private right to bear arms existed in British common law before the US Constitution was written. While Saunders is correct that the US Supreme Court did not broadly interpret the Second Amendment until recently, the Court in 1876 wrote, 'The right to bear arms is not granted by the Constitution; neither is it in any manner dependent upon that instrument for its existence.' (United States v Cruickshank). The Court was stating that that particular right predated the Constitution, and the Second Amendment served to prevent the federal government from passing laws that would infringe it. Most common law jurisdictions have jettisoned that right, which apparently originated as far back as the 17th century, because times have changed and we no longer worry too much about being assailed by highwaymen on journeys through the countryside. Perhaps the US would be on the way to getting rid of it also, if not for the influence of people Saunders discusses.

comment_text: I am a full time firefighter in a large municipality and would like to respond to some of the myths/misconceptions stated below in the comments. But first I would like to apologize for the fact that we are seen as 'entitled', 'pigs at the trough' 'self-professed heroes'...insert stereotype here. I accept that there are some of my colleagues who give that impression, but like in any profession, especially public service professions, a few rotten eggs are seemingly used to exemplify the majority. Secondly, the general impression is that firefighters are mostly uneducated, lazy, workshy members of a boys club that is openly raking in taxpayer dollars for their own profit. To put that claim to lie, before I was hired I was a Senior Non-Commissioned Officer in the Canadian Army, with numerous qualifications in technical skills and proven combat leadership. A number of my colleagues have college diplomas, and in fact one person I work with is currently pursuing an MSC. I applied to be a firefighter because I felt it was the best way I could serve the public without the strain put upon my family by spending half my life away from home. Also, a young adulthood spent preparing for, deploying to, and recovering from the longest war in Canadian history did not give me many marketable skills for the private sector. As to the claim that we are underworked, I will tell you this: I am busier now as a firefighter and hazardous materials technician than I ever was as a senior NCO in the Army, between teaching, courses, re-certifications, daily training detailed to us by the battalion chiefs, emergency calls, non-emergency calls, public education, site pre-plans, maintenance and studying. As to the danger of the job, sure, technical advances have made the job safer than before, however only recently has it come to light the long term serious consequences of routine exposure to the by-products of combustion, namely a whole host of carcinogens, which is why the average firefighter is 2-3 times more likely to develop any number of forms of cancer throughout their career. Nevermind the mental health effects of routine exposure to trauma, an problem which is suffered by all 3 emergency services, not just firefighters. comment_text: The entire Earth's atmosphere, from the ground up to space, stores only about as much heat energy as the layer of sea water two meters deep. But the ocean is on the average 4,000 meters deep. Which means everything else is negligible and the ocean is the place to look for climate change. Which is precisely what NOAA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in the US is doing by taking precise measurements of sea temperatures at thousands of locations at different depths. The results are summed up in a graph of oceanic heat content and anyone good with high school science can calculate from it the so-called climate forcing, which is the difference between the Earth's heating and cooling expressed in watts per square meter of the Earth's surface. I suggest that anyone who genuinely wants to know the truth about Earth's heating or cooling or staying the same first finds the graph on the NOAA website, and then picks up a calculator and calculates the average climate forcing for a chosen period, say from 1990 to 2010 (I didn't say 2013 because the results are not in yet).This is science, not politics, and the truth can be found by careful measurement and correct calculation. If you paid attention in science class you should be able to do it!

So, what happens in Ontario if the PCs win but the Liberals and NDP form a coalition government and continue running $10B+ deficits year after year until they collapse?

comment_text: In Thunder Bay, where I lived for a time, sending your kids to Catholic School was essentially a declaration that you didn't want your kids to go to school with Native kids. I had several people advise me to send my kids to Catholic school on that basis. Here in London, where I now live, the local Catholic school actively encourages any kids with learning disabilities to leave the school and enroll in the public school. This both save the Catholic board money and artificially inflates its scores on the province-wide testing, helping to reinforce the perception that the Catholic board is 'better'. The Catholic school system, in short, is awash in money but doesn't want to deal with social problems and/or more challenging (and capital intensive) students. It creates two classes of education in the province and is an anachronism that needs to be done away with.

comment_text: This column tries to score emotional and political points at the expense of careful thought. Canada is a Western democracy, but does not have a history of colonial, imperial, or military interventionist policies. Britain, France, and the US on the other hand have deeply involved themselves militarily in the Middle East for the past century - Britain and France through direct colonial adventures and the US and Britain through oil politics and cynical support for authoritarian governments. Borders were drawn arbitrarily, democratically elected governments overthrown, oil-friendly authoritarian regimes propped up, etc. And then there was the invasion of Iraq, championed by the US and Britain, leaving perhaps 600 000 dead. Having gotten themselves so deeply into a Middle Eastern quagmire, they are now faced with the problem of how to extricate themselves. It's a problem we have sympathy with, but not one we should become militarily involved in at this point. ISIS is a horror, and Islamic fundamentalism (like all religious fundamentalism) is a bad joke on the concept of God. As a democracy based on freedom and individual rights, Canada should oppose those movements. But the phenomenon of ISIS is pretty much a direct result of the invasion of Iraq, a truly ill-conceived intervention which we rightly stayed out of. Does it make sense policy-wise to now reverse ourselves and get involved in 'the sequel', particularly when our military contribution is minimal? We feel outrage and sympathy after these horrendous attacks, but we should draw a clear line between helping to defeat ISIS through non-combative roles versus identifying ourselves militarily with the old 'imperial' Western power club that is so unpopular in the Middle East. We can both help our allies and be true to our principles and history by supporting the local enemies of ISIS through training and supply, and by helping in humanitarian ways. It is entirely legitimate for Canada to present itself as a Western nation but one not tainted by military interventionism, and to craft its longterm foreign policy accordingly. Just as we see our strength as a country augmented by our own diversity, so the strength of Western democracies is increased by a variety of independent approaches united by a common belief in freedom and democracy. Canada has a unique voice and should use it.

comment_text: Load-of-crap. Firstly, the author is incorrect in stating that 'In an election about the economy, the Conservatives might have won, and would have deserved to. But thanks to the Harper government’s own choices, this election has mostly not been fought on the Conservative Party’s strong suit. '. Mr. Harper-apologist, Harper was declining in polls even BEFORE he decided to create wedge issues. He created these wedge issues BECAUSE he thought that he will do better in the polls. And he did for a little while, until Canadians decided that he is playing the politics of division. Secondly, Mr. Harper-apologist, you say that 'the Conservative Party has a solid record' when it comes to the economy. Now, we don't know how the country would have fared under a Liberal or NDP government, but we know that since the recession there has been a net-loss of jobs. In fact, we have lost around 600, 000 jobs since the recession. At the very least, we can't say that the conservatives have a 'solid record'. Thirdly, you write that, 'The key issue of the election should have been the economy and the financial health of Canadians.' Should have been? Why do economic issues trump everything else. Of course, economic issues are extremely important, but other issues are also very important, such as the integrity of the PM, the PMO and his party. Issues of minority rights, environmental protection, accessible elections, free speech are not unimportant issues. Many Canadians have decided that they don't want a xenophobic, racist, fear-mongering PM.Fourthly, you write that, 'pushing marginal income tax rates' will lead to 'promoting brain drain'. SERIOUSLY? This government has muzzled scientists, cut millions from research and has made intelligent discussions and debates a thing of the past. Harper won't even sit down with premiers to have dialogue. Please, Mr. Harper-apologist, don't just make statements without stats and facts. Lastly, for all your praises of the Harper government and their economic acumen, do remember that a half-million less people have jobs today than before the recession. Remember that, the Liberals left the country with billions in surplus, but now we are left with billions in debt. Remember that we had many consecutive surpluses before Harper, and since then we have run 9 consecutive deficits. Remember that the Americans are doing extremely well economically (under a 'liberal' president, might I add, after Bush left the country with TRI-llions in debt), and, so, why aren't we? Finally, I am not suggesting that Canada would have done better under a liberal or NDP rule. All I am saying is that your assumption that the CONs have been great for our economy is simply not supported by evidence. Hence, I can only assume that you are a Mr. Harper-apologist.

comment_text: Years ago, a waggish colleague characterised Simpson's 30% as 'conservatives who have nothing to conserve'. Others, putting it less delicately, might have been inclined to remark upon their failure to own either a urine-receptacle or a window from which its contents might be jettisoned. Regardless of commentators' levels of delicacy and/or earthiness, the point they make is the same; namely, that the 30% represent abject co-opting of the 'mob' by the 21st century Ricardian Whigs and/or Libertarians who seek to eviscerate the state. Of course, if the 'mob' were truly aware of the agenda, and of the potential loss of their cherished benefits, the association/co-optation would end immediately. So, why is the 'mob' so blissfully unaware of the agenda, and why is the 'mob' so resistant to acquiring such awareness? A visit to sites such as http://plato.stanford.edu/entries/epistemology/#EVR would give readers some insight into the epistemological issues of trying to understand why the 30% is so defiantly resistant to such minor inconveniences as facts and analysis. Unfortunately, with the Harper Tories' emasculation of Statistics Canada, the supply and quality of those 'minor inconveniences' will only worsen, thus offering even less opportunity to create some dissonance among the 30%.

comment_text: The comments here are ludicrous. Over the years the Globe and Mail, and many other media outlets have chosen not to publish material that was intended to offend. The G&M takes editorial positions... those positions irritate people who have a different view, but they are not put forward with the idea of provoking and enraging. Our society endorses and provides a limited right to freedom of expression; that's what all liberal democracies provide. Within those bounds, many things can be said that are crass, rude, inflammatory, and offensive. Some consider it their right to exploit such license to make a profit and to have fun at the expense of the sensibilities of others. That's fine. Others want to make profit and take pride in getting news and responsible opinion into the public realm. We tolerate the former and we depend on the latter. My only complaint about the G&M is that it does the 'responsible journalism' job poorly sometimes, NOT that it has chosen to BE responsible. I feel sorry that Charlie Hebdo was attacked and that people were killed. It was obviously completely wrong and I despise the narrow-minded, religious ignorance and hate that led to that. Charlie Hebdo is entitled to be offensive. But I don't lose the fact that much of what it did WAS offensive. I can support Charlie Hebdo's rights without ever wanting to do or consume or support what they called 'journalism'.In a free society, we generally provide for latitude in rights so that we can reach a social stability that reflects what we feel and want in general. Such peace can only be achieved if we let everyone shoot their mouths off so that we get a sense of where opinion stands and how it diverges. THAT is the reason that Charlie Hebdo was allowed to publish, NOT because the things that they would choose to say or show would be right or worthy. Just because someone exercises their right to be offensive doesn't mean that we're all under an obligation to be offensive. Mocking religion--any religion--is not offensive to me. But we know that it offends lots of people. Mocking gay people does offend me because they are singled out for their nature as humans. Charlie Hebdo abused both. Why? Because some people would pay to see the bounds of good taste and responsible discourse ignored. The G&M gets my business BECAUSE it is an institution that is trying to do the job responsibly. They fail frequently but they don't set out to fail. They set out to be credible.

comment_text: Oh, yes, indeed, Ladies and Gentlemen, the Globe and Mail has no real reason to show solidarity and stand up to evil forces that want to put a lid on democratic free speech. This is what men and women want; but the Globe has clandestinely become a corporation, which only got revealed to us now. Think about it. To a corporation, does free speech matter, does democracy and personal integrity matter? Or does to a corporation only the bottom line of financial success matter. Solidarity is such a human thing!! The Globe wants to do nothing with it. It's not anything it recognizes as 'important', or anything it recognizes in the first place. Solidarity in this instance means risk, and the risk, if taken, may negatively impact the bottom line. No corporate entity will willingly undertake such a risk. The soul of the machine realizes that it gets no appropriate return for that risk. So it decides against taking that risk. There is no solidarity in corporatian souls. (No spelling mistake.) There is no long-term foresight, either. Today the free press is threatened. Today the atmosphere is damaged. Today the frogs are dying out, but the pipelines will be built, the jets will be kept in the air, the oil will be burned, because those activities increase the bottom line like crazy, for today. Tomorrow too, and even the day after. Ten years later no, the burning of oil will have a disastrous effect on humans and on corporations in ten years' time, but the corporation has no long-range foresight. The corporation says, 'we must outsource, we must shift production and assembly to China', and they do, and the corporation does not care that the domestic market equilibrium gets damaged beyond repair by doing that. Similarly in the newspaper and news media trade. Human values, such as responding to moral expectations and standing up for humans' rights is virtually a pointless exercise. It helps to do that but only when it generates money for the corporation. Otherwise they are moot, less than moot; morals, solidarity and human values are worth nothing, nothing at all, in fact, it is worth fighting to show to the readers and convince them that being brave is a stupid thing. Bravery, morals, values, they are worth nothing, the GnM wants us to believe and therefore writes articles to convince us of this belief, in one after another of Globe and Mail editorials. The loss of free press, actually, will not affect the Globe as a corporation. The freedom will disappear, but the press will stay on. It will continue to publish articles, and people will continue to buy the paper. What else does a corporation need? It sells its products, makes a profit, and bob's its uncle. The Corporation devoid of human values, that the Globe has shown to us it has become, is doing fine and dandy, without needing to risk, without showing solidarity. Just exactly how the Ancients did not say. 'Ipse quotum ad humani se te lavour distu.' Humans toil, as if it was worth it.

But when a conflict is contained within a nation, and even though their may be loss of life, outside nations must not take part it in short of a catastrophe of Rwanda-like proportions. End of story.

comment_text: Excellent column Ms. Wente. I've attended a few seminars put on by wind power advocates as an observer and was not impressed. Ground source heat pumps, solar panels, small hydro electric dams, and even small windmill installations that assist in taking individual homes or farms off the grid are all great and interest me tremendously. Putting the argument of CO2/anthropomorphic vs. an indeterminate cyclical planetary induced global warming aside, as I think the jury is still out on the cause as there are major flaws on the CO2 side, I still basically believe like most Canadians it's a good idea to ween us off fossil fuels for the basic reason that we will eventually run out of this source of energy. comment_text: I have seen comments about people voting directly for the President of the US in a number of posts, so thought I would repeat a comment here. You don't vote directly for the US President. In the US, you vote for a slate of electors that represent a party/candidate in each state and that elector then casts a vote for the US President. There are some variances on this from state to state but it is mostly a winner-take-all system at the state level. There appears to be is confusion about this and it probably results from watching the media in recent US elections, who know how US Presidents get elected but have decided to report on overall popular vote, which means precisely nothing, but allows for much angst when a 1% difference in popular vote results in a huge difference in the electoral college. That huge amplification of the difference due to the winner take all result in most state's electoral colleges is an intentional design feature of the electoral college, not an unfortunate accident of design. comment_text: Jeffrey Simpson here conflates two quite separate debates: 1. How should the NATO, Russian and other allied outside interveners in the Syrian/Iraq proceed against ISIL (and the Assad regime?)?2. How should Canada contribute to the NATO intervention? Regarding the NATO and related outside intervention, there are clearly limits to the possible success of high altitude air strikes against presumed ISIL targets in the absence of credible domestic ground forces in Syria and Iraq to confront ISIL militarily and politically. While the Assad regime, the Kurds and the Iranian and Hezbollah allies of the Assad regime do manage to hold ISIL somewhat at bay in Syria, serious policy and military confrontations ensue with Turkey and NATO objectives and Sunni Arabs, who constitute about 70% of Syria’s population are increasingly alienated by the actions of that Assad related alliance’s policies and actions. This alienation is mirrored in the Sunni Arab regions of northern Iraq, where incursions by Shi’ite militias nominally supporting the ineffective Shi’ite dominated Iraqi Government (but controlled and augmented by the Iranians) make little headway against ISIL. The Kurds in Iraq are effective in repelling ISIL from Kurdish majority areas and, like their brethren in Syria, are the one generally effective moderate element (although, there are increasing reports that Kurdish fighters are taking harsh reprisals against Arab Sunni residents whenever they retake areas from ISIL), but there is every indication that if and when the forces nominally supporting the Iraqi regime and the Kurdish fighters are able to link up on the ground, they will come into serious conflict. In the context just described, NATO aerial bombing too often is based upon inadequate local intelligence and lacks credible on the ground consolidation by anti ISIL forces. It can disrupt ISIL movements and destroy ISIL supplies and infrastructure and kill ISIL fighters and leadership to some extent, but not fatally to the ISIL cause and only at the cost of (a) further alienation of the Iraqi and Syrian Sunni Arab populations, (b) risk of NATO confrontation with the Russian and Iranian interveners, and (c) propping up the Assad and Iraqi regimes that both are clearly willing and unable to reach out to the domestic Sunni Arab (and, in the case of the Iraqi regime, the Kurdish) elements of their nations. More damningly, the NATO bombing program in the current circumstances can legitimately be characterized as an attempt, in the absence of a viable policy, for western Governments to give the appearance to (a) their own domestic audiences the appearance of ‘doing something’ and reeking vengeance upon ISIL, and (b) other players in the Iraq/Syria arena, that NATO is engaged. In this context, ISIL can goad the NATO nations to ever greater bombing efforts, which is clearly ISIL’s goal. Regarding Canada’s role, our token current air strike involvement does not enhance NATO efforts and for Canada to simply continue that element of our involvement because that will not draw further attention to any reservations Canada may have about the questionable utility of current NATO policy is no favour to our allies. Joining the majority of NATO nations that currently focus their efforts on humanitarian aid and, in some cases, on well designed and executed training and logistic support of credible, moderate domestic opponents on the ground in Iraq and Syria is the way to go, especially now that Canada has already announced this policy shift.

comment_text: Dear Mr. Simpson My name is Ivan, and I am a grade 9 student. I am writing in regards to your article 'Too many first nations people live in a dream palace'. Two examples of these would be the Environmental Assessment Act and the Navigation Protection Act, both of which could cause extreme harm to Canada. I don't think anyone can deny that most Aboriginal people live in horrible conditions, many of their communities fraught with alcoholism, violence, and poverty. Presenting the Aboriginals as an obnoxious community with their many protests and acts is very wrong. Especially when these protests are directed at laws that would greatly impact and harm all of Canada, and would have gone unnoticed. Under the Navigation Protection Act, major pipeline and power line project advocates aren't required to prove the safety and stability of their projects, unless the waters through which the pipeline is going through is on a pre-prepared list made by the transportation minister. Idle No More claims that 99.9% of waterways will now be unprotected. I would have never heard of such a law if it weren't for the Idle No More movement. First off, the First Nations had little or no say in the reserves they would receive, and weren't informed on how 'isolated' they would be. comment_text: I agree with Margaret - this is low priority. I actually like FPTP so bias admitted. It forces political parties to appeal to a wide range of the public on a wide range of issues. If you are a single-issue party, it is going to be very difficult to get into a position of power - and I'm fine with that. Naturally, certain parties will give up and/or merge with other parties as did the Conservatives when the PCs & Reform party realized they would never form a majority government - two to four parties is about right under this system, keeping it fairly simple for the electorate (as politics go), and I don't believe there is any net benefit from having 10 parties share in the governance structure. I also see this naturally leading to more moderate and centrist party views (i.e. you need to appeal to more people to get into power) than you might otherwise have - which, I would argue, is a good thing (perhaps think of Harper's policies without PC moderates). Proportional, to me, leads to an ineffective government. My view: give the majority government a chance by giving them full control over decision making - just like in the business world where each CEO get's his or her shot - the alternative would be an ineffective and inefficient decision-making structure. And the multiple round system/ranked ballot system is definitely biased to the middle party which, shockingly, is the party currently in power proposing to make the change and to do so unilaterally. Back to MW's original argument, all systems will have faults; what we have is simple and effective enough and I don't see a compelling reasons to change it.

comment_text: Reading the article, and articles just like this one that appear to surface annually just to stoke the fires and engage the language debates. Ms. Wente’s views continue to perpetuate a number of myths around the French immersion program. We felt that it would be important to dispel a few of these myths and shed some light on what the research is showing us regarding French immersion in Canada – because it is 2016. This article chose to share that the percentage of Canadians who can speak both official languages has dropped. Perhaps seeing the actual numbers may be enlightening: in 1961, 2.2 million Canadians self identified as being able to speak French and English; by 2011, that number had ballooned to 5.8 million – a 160% increase. This despite the large number of immigrants coming into Canada in the last twenty years who do not speak either French or English. The notion of French immersion being an elitist program may have been true historically, but the program has evolved. Data from the Toronto District School Board shows growth in French immersion enrollment in the city’s most disadvantaged neighborhoods just as in the rest of the city. The argument that the French immersion program filters out a variety of students was primarily due to old administrative policies discouraging – or in some cases even denying – students with learning disabilities from entering French immersion programs. Provincial ministry of education policy and resource documents are continuing to be updated to address equity and inclusive education strategies, stating that FSL is for all students. Immigrant kids (as you call them) are enrolling, in droves, into French immersion programs across Canada. Ironically, studies show immigrant students who learn French as a third language easily adapt to French immersion. Students never regret becoming bilingual, most will offer tout the benefits of how second official language acquisition opened doors for them personally and professionally. In 2016, in Canada, parents want the very best learning opportunities for their children. And what is wrong with that? •Bilinguals earn more than unilingual Canadians when they live outside Quebec. Canadians who speak both languages earn on average 10% more and have a lower unemployment rate than unilinguals. Men who speak both official languages earn an average of 3.8% more, and bilingual women earn an average of 6.6% more than those who speak only English. (Workopolis, 2015) •Bilingual job candidates face much lower competition for jobs. This is especially pronounced in Ontario, providing a strong competitive advantage in markets such as Toronto or Guelph where fewer bilingual candidates are available. Mario Lefebvre, director of the Centre for Municipal Studies at the Conference Board of Canada stated, “In communities with a limited number of French speakers, you are a scarce resource. If you are a limited resource, you will be welcome wherever you go.” (Workopolis, 2015)

comment_text: In terms of fossil fuels and climate change: look at Scotland and Norway. These are two progressive countries and they both have significant and well-developed renewable energy industries. I know that Scotland produces more than 50% of its electricity from renewable energies. However both Scotland and Norway produce and export oil & gas from the North Sea. I also know that Scotland and Norway are not going to shut-down their existing North Sea oil industries based on fallacious and illogical climate change arguments. Nor will they ban new pipelines in the North Sea that can produce oil or gas from newly discovered oil and gas fields. They are not that stupid. In fact both Scotland and Norway are encouraging investment in their oil and gas industries by reducing taxes. So, you can promote renewable energies and fossil fuels at the same time. There is no contradiction about it.Also, if Scotland or Norway shut down the North Sea it only means other oil-producing countries will produce more oil to meet global demand for the product. That means the likes of Saudi Arabia sells more oil to replace production from Scotland or Norway. That also means more money flows into Saudi Arabia for financing terrorism and/or promotion of religious extremism. Demand for oil and gas does not go away when oil and gas supply runs out from one oil or gas field. What happens is that new fields and new supplies are found to meet demand. This is a dynamic situation that's going on all the time all over the world. So, obviously, shutting down the North Sea would do NOTHING to mitigate climate change. North Sea oil production will simply be replaced by production from somewhere else. Exactly the same argument applies re Alberta. We could shut down everything in Alberta tomorrow but the world will still need approx. 100 million bbls/day for electricity, heat, cooking, transportation, chemicals and other manufacturing. Opposing the energy industry (including pipelines) in Alberta only results in an economic/jobs disaster in Alberta and a serious fiscal and economic problem in Canada.

comment_text: “China alone now accounts for a whopping 28 per cent of the world’s C02 emissions – twice as much as the U.S.” (Margaret Wente - The It Girl of climate change doesn’t get it Add to ... The Globe and Mail; Sep. 23 2014). Ms. Wente, like many authors, politicians and journalists, does not hesitate to mention the whopping contribution of China to the world’s emissions of carbon dioxide. True enough, China, as a country, contributes a lot to global CO2 emissions. However, using national emission levels is disingenuous, misleading and perhaps somewhat dishonest. Per capita emissions are more relevant and revealing. According to World Bank, in 2010, the average person in the USA emitted 17.6 tons of the CO2; the average Canadian 14.7 tone, and the average Chinese person 6.2 tons, almost three times more than the Chinese inhabitant and close to two and a half times more than a Canadian. (http://data.worldbank.org/indicator/EN.ATM.CO2E.PC). This begs the question: Why the average Chinese individual would not have the right to produce as much carbon dioxide as the average American or Canadian? No book on climate change should ignore elementary facts such as countries’ contributions to global CO2 emissions. Why does Ms. Wente ignore the elementary fact that USA and Canadian per capita emissions are close to three times those of China? Is that serious journalism? To paraphrase Ms. Wente’s conclusion she, and journalists of her kind should do themselves (and us) the favor of growing up and provide their readers with all relevant facts.

comment_text: Clarity -- FPTP provides a clear-cut choice between two main parties. But has inbuilt disadvantages for third and fragmented minority parties. IOW, it's a thing of the past, when debates were simple, and polarized. Not so good when the number of stakeholders increases. Winner can fully implement its agenda -- Cabinets are not restrained by having to bargain with a coalition partner. Money is spent to implement things. And when the tide turns, money is spent to undo things, and implement the opposite. FPTP is said to exclude extremist parties from representation -- This should encourage parties to be ‘broad churches’, encompassing many elements from different societal groups. Extremists have been excluded. But we have not always seen the broadening really to cover many groups. It produces representatives of geographical areas -- But is not the 'only system' having this advantage. OTOH, it can lead to choosing between people rather than between programs. It is simple to use and understand -- 'Simple things' aren't always 'best'... all 'things' considered. Simple things often look good only from one perspective. On the not so bright side of the Moon, FPTP isn't 'fair': the 1993 federal election had the Conservatives win 16 per cent of the votes but only 0.7 per cent of the seats. The 2011 and 2015 elections are 'mirror images' of one another. It excludes minorities from fair representation -- Parties put up the most broadly acceptable candidate in a district. If voting behaviour does dovetail with ethnic divisions, the exclusion of members of ethnic minority groups can be destabilizing. It has excluded women from the legislature in the past, by the ‘most broadly acceptable candidate’ syndrome -- Trends can be and have been reversed. There can be a boomerang effect: built-in safety is nice to have. It can encourage parties based on regions, dividing the country into separate strongholds, with little incentive to make appeals outside their cultural–political base -- Can you remember having ever seen this in Canada? ;)FPTP favours ‘regional fiefdoms’ where one party wins all the seats in a province, excluding minorities and reinforcing the perception that politics hinges on who you are and where you live -- Can you remember having ever seen this in Canada? ;)It leaves a large number of wasted votes --- With regional fiefdoms, minority party supporters may feel that they have no hope of ever electing a candidate of their choice. It may not respond to changes in public opinion -- Geographically concentrated support means that one party can maintain exclusive control in the face of a substantial drop in overall popular support. FPTP is dependent on electoral boundaries -- There is no technical process to produce a single ‘correct answer’. There may be pressure to manipulate boundaries by gerrymandering or malapportionment. This made the news time and again for 60 years.[http://aceproject.org/ace-en/topics/es/esd/esd01/esd01a/esd01a01]

comment_text: I think for too long we have had this idea that the USA is a melting pot and that Canada is a mosaic. As a consequence of the 'mosaic' concept, official policy has been to encourage immigrants to over emphasize culture of origin over Canadian culture. We talk about Scottish-Canadians, rather than Canadians of Scottish origins. Being Scottish comes before being Canadian. The fact is that melting goes on in both countries, with some group of immigrants - to continue the analogy- melting at a lower temperature than others. I don't think many Canadians expect immigrants to give up their cultural heritage, but maybe we should stop spending money trying the keep them holding onto their cultural past, and spend this money helping them to integrate into their cultural present. If preserving their cultural heritage is important to them, they will see that that happens within their family and communities. They don't need our tax dollars to make it happen. If they are not prepared to put the time and money into preserving the heritage of their cultural origins, maybe it isn't that important to them after all. I think as Canadian we need to acknowledge our history as an immigrant nation, allow people to celebrate and take pride in their cultural heritage(s) but focus our money on cultural integration rather than cultural segregation.

comment_text: About 35 years ago I was in Florence and was sitting on the Church steps enjoying life in the piazza, when suddenly two young men one brandishing a knife threatened to fight each other. They did a lot of swearing and dancing around and they threw a few punches that missed, but the guy with the knife did not lunge at the other, he just waved the knife about in a threatening manner. Some people stopped to watch the show, others bored just walked on by.After about 10 minutes 4 police officers arrived in two squad cars. They immediately sussed out the situation and did virtually nothing. They did not draw their weapons but they did tell the guy with the knife to drop it. He didn't.The cops just stood back and watched as the guys continued yelling at each other for what seemed like 20 minutes until both were totally exhausted. Then the guy with the knife gently hands it over to one of the cops, apologizes and quietly gets into one of the cop cars. They did not even handcuff him. After briefly talking to the other guy the cops let him go free. He crossed the piazza and disappeared down a narrow side street. At the time I was astonished that the cops seemed to do nothing, but they in fact did everything. It was only later as I grew much older and wiser that I realized it was the finest street policing I would ever witness.
