comment_text: Two simple things that can be done to improve this situation. First, put Supreme Court nominees through a U.S. style confirmation process. Their record, credibility and even personal lives of nominees should be held up to the most intense public scrutiny and questioning by anyone who has an opinion. Supreme Court judges have too much power for their appointment process to be any other way. Second, governments should start using the notwithstanding clause each and every time they disagree with a Supreme Court decision. The reason why section 33 is such a boogie man politically is because politicians themselves are too gun shy to use it, concerned about the political reaction. Because it almost never gets used, section 33 becomes this almost mythical barrier, in the minds of Canadians. On the one hand politicians complain that the Supreme Court limits our democracy, but then by not using the notwithstanding clause they are themselves preventing debate from being moved back into the democratic (political) arena. If you think that you are right then put your money where your mouth is and use section 33 and then fight the battle in the political arena, where you think is should be in the first place. The more you use it, the more people will get used to it being used and then let the people decide.

comment_text: 'Even the once famously tolerant Dutch and Danes are increasingly voting for parties that fulminate against the scourge of immigration 'There are all manner of reasons why citizens of any particular nation may desire to see either less immigration or slower immigration, but the choice the professor provides regarding the once famously tolerant Dutch and Danes is interesting. The citizens of Holland , Denmark, and Switzerland as an added example, are not under-educated nor are they technology averse or isolationist from cultural standpoint. They do not fear modernization. They are almost completely bilingual , at least in English along with their native language, travel extensively and are non-belligerent geo-politically.What they are also however is small, patriotic, and confident in their successful approaches to life built upon hundreds of years of refinement. Small, democratic, socially-liberalized and socially-cohesive nations such as these , while sometimes having a codified set of rights such as do the Swiss, rely more on an unwritten long standing cultural affinity for the continuance of what it means to be Danish or Dutch etc... and it is strange that it appears so difficult for many to understand that truth when it comes to attempting to understand potentially growing concern for non-aligned immigration into such nations. Denmark has a population of 5.5 million people. It has no room to grow and a social support network that relies on a historical acceptance of a citizen's commitment to the nation and it's historical context. If the famously tolerant Danes are becoming wary of immigration, perhaps the author would do better by asking the Danes why that is so. Rather than leaving the impression that something hard and sinister is growing within a traditionally tolerant people, perhaps he could have an open and tolerant discussion about what it means for a Dane to be Danish, and whether they have any right to feel that way.

comment_text: I suspected for a long time that Mrs. Wente does not really know (or care) what she is writing about. Now I have the proof. My son was enrolled for four years in the Toronto French School. And yes, it is a private school, and no, we could not afford to live next to it (Bayview and Lawrence). Instead we were driving him to school in the morning and he would take the TTC back home. Later on he would just take the TTC both ways. Surprisingly, this was how many of his classmates were commuting to school. After only four years in TFS our son developed a profound connection to the language, which he still speaks and reads whenever he can. He would have been even more fluent had we enrolled him in grade 1 - despite what Mrs. Wente professes to know - as his accent would have been better. I learned both French and English - French through full immersion - and I can attest to the fact that only full immersion will turn a child (or person for that matter) into a fluent speaker. The quality of teaching at any French school will depend on the quality of the teachers. Having to be find teachers that are fluent in French does narrow the choice significantly, so if the best math teachers available are not fluent in French, well, they will not be hired by a French immersion school. That's the conundrum of any immersion program. My advice to parents who are considering French immersion would be to start early - kindergarten or grade 1, and then switch to a regular English school in grade 9 (we switched in grade 10). Then it is up to the parents to keep French alive (movies, books, magazines on topics of interest to the child). It sounds funny, but when we switched our son to an English high-school, he had a bit of difficulty adjusting to the English names of geometric figures (losange vs. rhomb, ... etc).Do your child a favour and enroll him in French. He will thank you later.

comment_text: One and a half cheers for democracy. It use to be said that among all the various modes of governing, democracy was the most fair and the least dangerous. However, as the world becomes full of superannuated dinosaur-people who do nothing to adapt their abilities to technological change -- not even to bother to become computer-literate -- democracy becomes an extremely precarious mode of governing. In fact, a strong-man has now erupted from the very heart of democracy, bragging, lying, cheating, bullying, groping, threatening, and promising to satisfy (he says) the longings of those who indignantly feel that society has left them behind. When a monstrous event like the election of Trump takes place, it is time to reconsider our notions of democracy -- or to admit that in certain circumstances it doesn't work at all. It worked in its birthplace, the ancient city-states of Greece, notably Athens, because each citizen did his share of the work, including defending the city, and was as industrious and well educated as his fellow citizen. It is this last point that I want to dwell on: in today's democracies it is absurd to believe in the one-person-one vote system because there is now an enormous discrepancy among our fellow-citizens in their abilities and willingness to think, work, and contribute to the good of the social whole. The simple truth is that some people are far less capable of casting an intelligent vote than others: they are just passengers, cruising lazily on the coat-tails of more diligent people. I suggest that if we want to preserve the gratifying fiction of one-person-one-vote, we must first assess the value of each person's vote. Expressed very simply, some people are more intelligent and energetic than others, and their votes should accordingly carry greater weight than their less-fortunate, non-contributing fellow citizens. There are apples and there are rotten apples. The votes of resentful rotten apples have brought Trump to power. He has promised to restore them to their former pristine and shiny boy-scout glow and vigour -- yet without any effort at all on their part. But what will happen to democratic 'America' when Trump waves his magic wand and *nothing at all* happens? God Save America indeed, because Donald J. Trump the opportunist hasn't a snowball's chance of preventing a new French Revolution. Trump's bad apples snooze in dreamland: what will happen when they suddenly see that he can't deliver? And what will be the collateral damage inflicted on the rest of the world? So: one and a half cheers for democracy.

comment_text: The dilema for me in this forthcoming election is akin to the expression of cutting off one's nose to spite your face. This whole campaign has been marketing orientated: sell the sizzle and not the stake. None of the three political leaders have expresed any unique and personal ideas on how to resolve the problems of this province in a prudent fiscal, socially responsible manner without putting the burden and fiscal belt tightning on one specific sector of the population. Both Hudak and Wynn should have dusted off the Drummond Report and used that report as a roadmap to resolving the economic problems of Ontario. Instead Hudak goes and looks for advice from some radical neo-conservatives such as David Frum and Benjamin Zycher of the American Enterprise Institute. This is the infamous David Frum, former Canadian ,present American and possibly an Internationalist; a rich , Harvard educated boy who has probably not worked a week in doing any manual work in his life, a true propergandist and a proponent of the concept of the 'Axis of Evil' speech of the superstatesman George W. Bush. The problem with our present day system of Democracy is how such people at both the provincial and Federal level are allowed to direct or destroy the lives of those that voted them into power. Look at the educational and working background of most politicians and you have to ask yourself how we permit and assign them so much power to run our lives. These dotards , when in power, turn to the consultants and lobbysts for advice. Worse still is the fact that a political leader and party can wreck economic havoc during a term in office and not be responsible or accountable to its citizens for the maladministration while in office. At least in the Roman Republic any magistrate or public individual could be brought to trial and prosecuted had acted improper during his tenure of office. I like the Globe editorial board have the same doubts, skepticism, cynicism towards all three provincial leaders. It is irrelevant who becomes leader of this province after the election. What is important is that we do not vote for a majority government. Just look to what Harper and McGuinty government have done with a majority government. Keep these guys on a short leash so we can control them until which time we may find a skillful Moses to lead us out this provincial quagmire.

comment_text: An entertaining article but I think missing an essential component to the (rather simplistic) question of 'is it better to be single or married?' question. When singles say that they are nervous about giving up their freedoms, they are referring to their relatively happy and stable states of being. The question is really more 'if I trade my currently satisfactory life for one shared with someone else, will I be happier or not?' I've seen and lived through relationships which were extraordinarily miserable. Single people - single women - increasingly have a choice of being married or single, and what they are choosing is to control their lives. Such was not the case even 60 years ago when the choice was largely to marry or to remain at home. I think a major factor in the increase of numbers of people living alone is the unwillingness to trade something pretty good for something worse.

comment_text: I guess I have lived longer than this column writer--or I have benefited more from my long experience. There is no one-size-fits-all 'best' life. I have been everything on the map from single (before married), married, single (after divorce), married, single (after widowhood). The most difficult time was when my first relationship eroded away. We were both lonely. Being single gave us the incentive and opportunity to find a partner to which we were better suited, but the interim of single-hood allowed us to grow up--something we each badly needed to do. That was one of the most fruitful periods of my life--artistically and personally. When my next relationship came along, I had more to offer than my neuroses and needs. Being in a relationship was nice but NOT perfect. Nothing ever is. When he died, I was gutted. Now I'm single again--and yes it can be lonely. But life is what you make of it. If you stop focusing on yourself, there are many ways to reach out so that you are not left feeling lonely and abandoned on the tracks of life. I get impatient with articles that extol any particular life-style choice (or circumstance) at the expense of any other. Some have no choice about how their pairings and relationships turn out. When they compare, some feel bitter, some feel superior. I figure, stop comparing. Get out there, live your life--whatever that may be. If you're not satisfied, do what you can to change it.

comment_text: Living in a transracial family teaches me a lot about white privilege and about model minorities and about the hierarchy of race that shifts through time here in Canada. The comments in response to this article make the case for more education and discussion about 'white fragility' and racism. The highest scoring comment champions white racial superiority and jokingly reduces racialized immigrants to 'the great hordes' - thou doth protest too much. Call it 'implicit bias' or 'racism' but we know that individual attitudes are shaped by social forces that are sometimes not even apparent to you. Recent articles on hiring where the manager talks about how (s)he has to go through a conscious effort to not go with the 'common sense' assessment of candidates that can tend to simply validate the status quo and reaffirm prejudices. And then there is last night's baldfaced racism of Donald Trump whose response to questions reduced and framed African Americans as 'inner city' - a bit ironic when we consider who the sitting President is. Or when he replied to a question about Islamophobia with advice that Muslims should be reporting. This last comment provoked a twitter storm of protest that American Muslims existed solely as secret agents in a terrorist plot. That's the US Presidential Debate wrestling with a gorilla. But we here in Canada are as we know too well capable of terrible racism. The latest polls on attitudes towards immigration are chilling in that too many Canadians want to erase difference. There is lots to think about in how Canada works at this point in time. We don't have the internment camps for the Japanese or the Chinese Head Tax today but we do have lots of documentation and testimonies about the mistreatment of racialized peoples. Our long colonial history is mapped out in the Idle No More Movement, and the US initiated #BlackLivesMatter movement is too relevant here. And the ongoing current of Islamophobia post 9-11 in Canada makes Muslims here to conscious of being under suspicion. All of this points to how 'race' is a social rather than a biological category. And it reminds us that the 'white fragility' phenomenon is something those of us passing for 'white' need to address.

comment_text: I am very pleased to see that this issue is now gaining national attention, and that the Globe has written a superbly accurate editorial on this bizarre boondoggle. We already have a memorial to recognize the 114, 000 Canadians who did not return home. It’s called the National War Memorial, and it’s in Ottawa, the nation’s capital. Where it belongs. It’s been there since 1939. It was built by the people of Canada after a year-long world-wide competition for a suitable, dignified design. Seems like the “Never Forgotten” gang have forgotten this. They also seem to have forgotten the nearly 7000 memorials we already have across this country. May I ask these proponents, what is wrong with the current cenotaph in Ingonish, CB? Or the one down the road in Neil’s Harbour? Or the ones in pretty well every community in Canada? Are they not big enough? Do they not have enough corporate sponsors? Or perhaps they are unsuitable because they don’t have gift shops attached? Does a memorial have to be 30 metres tall in order to prove how much we thank the sacrifices of our veterans and previous generations? I think our previous generations, and our current and future ones, have done and will continue to do a commendable job of never forgetting. We don’t need a gigantic hunk of Disney-fied schlock in Green Cove to prove that. We need to keep our national parks as our forebears intended them to be; Canada’s greatest natural places where protection of their ecological integrity is paramount.

Consumption did go up again after prohibition, but legalization created a context in which consumption could be reduced through education. www.med.uottawa.ca/sim/data/Alcohol_e.htm...which shows deaths from cirrhosis of the liver dropping by half, the last 40 years. Cannabis was sold to us as being right up there with heroin, back in the 1930's; if that was a lie, the whole legal structure is a house of cards.

comment_text: Judges have been making law for somewhat more than 800 years. The entire corpus of the Common Law has been made up by, interpreted by and amended by judges time and again. They have made law not because they can--but because it is their job. Over the last eight centuries the delicate balance between Crown, Parliament and Bench has evolved. It has absorbed the development of parliamentary democracy. It has absorbed the transfer of the Crown's power from the King to a Prime Minister. And it has absorbed the transformative nature of the Charter. Why did we need the Charter? Because the 1960 Bill of Rights demonstrated the true mockery that Parliamentary supremacy makes of any attempt to protect individual rights through legislation. To suggest that Parliament is the only proper law making body is to demonstrate a gross ignorance of what the law is. Individuals make law every single day by making contracts. Lawyers make law every day when they give opinions and advice and clients decide to guide themselves accordingly. Public servants make law every day when they administer the statute created by Parliament, by Legislatures or by Councils. The idea of judges making law is neither offensive nor retrograde. The entire law of negligence was created, whole cloth, by judges. The time may come when a Prime Minister feels compelled to invoke section 33. And there, ultimately, is the check upon the authority of the Bench. That Prime Ministers have--to date--exercised forbearance serves as a demonstration that the system is not broken.

comment_text: Shrill climate science denial is all too common in the 21st Century, as if one could simply handwave all the science, the thousands of peer-reviewed papers, and make it go away. Newsflash: that's not going to make any difference to reality. You ignore this science at your children's peril, friends. Not yours, of course - none of us will be alive to fully appreciate the reality of today's decisions regarding climate change. You might as well deny the link between cancer and cigarettes while you're at it - the science is very clear there as well, and millions of people die from the consequences. We're a little like the proverbial frog in the slowly heating water. Early on it can deny that it is in any danger:'You're in trouble''Ahhhh Shaaddaaaaap!''Our calculations show that, at this rate of warming, you will eventually be cooked. By tomorrow morning the temperature will boil you alive''Ahhhhh Shaaddaaaaaaap! Your model is off by .00001 degrees. I'll be fine!'The rest, as they say, will be history. And once we've waited long enough, we won't be able to reverse much of the damage done to other species we share the planet with. When I say 'we', I don't mean you and me, I mean our descendants, who will probably shake their heads and say 'They had plenty of warning, just like the Easter Islanders, but they just didn't listen. This could have been avoided. New York and New Orleans would still be habitable etc'There will be no pleasure in being correct. Quite the opposite in fact. It is truly tragic how foolish humans can be, and how pervasive the cavalier anti-science movement is.

comment_text: Over the years, I have heard and read these same doctor-bashing articles time and again. Time and again I have enumerated the fiscal realities of becoming a doctor and practicing medicine in Canada. No one cares. We all seem to expect that doctors should take the holy orders and work for “more noble goals than money”. Well it’s easy to do if you don’t have to worry about paying off your student loans, paying your office overhead, saving for your retirement, and trying to raise a family and purchase a home or have all of these major life expenditures behind you (as I presume Seraph1 does). If you compare opportunity cost and overall net compensation, doctors are not that well paid as compared to other professionals, healthcare bureaucrats or business executives. The six-figure salaried - indexed pension healthcare bureaucrat is still being paid when he/she travels on business - and his or her office overhead and travel expenses are being paid. The doctor isn't earning any income when travelling to attend required CME meetings but still has to cover his or her office overhead AND he or she has to pay for his or her travel expenses. What is the value of an indexed pension? HUGE!. If you are a government employee who retires at age 65 and has a pension indexed to the cost of living increase (~2%/year in Canada) and your first year pension pays you $95,000 and the pension goes for 25 years (to age 90), the cumulative value of that pension is $3,042,878.47. If you had to save yourself to generate that same retirement benefit (like a doctor has to), you would have to be able to contribute $55,000 per year earning 4% per year into tax-free vehicles such as an RRSP for 30 years starting at age 35!Two-thirds of doctors in BC have gross billings of less than $200,000 per year. Subtract $80,000 (40%) for overhead and you have a pretax income of $120,000. If you want to generate the same retirement benefit as the $95,000/year government employee, you will need to find a way to set aside $55,000 into tax sheltered vehicles (not likely under RRSP contribution limits) leaving you with $65,000 per year to live on. Sorry, you aren’t going to be buying a house in either Vancouver or Toronto - maybe a condo. So what is the answer? I suggest two options: 1) Close the medical schools and let the other members of the healthcare team take over. But wait, who is going to take the calls in the middle of the night and assume the overall medical-legal liability? You see the problem here. Everyone on the team wants to have a “say” in the delivery of care but they all want someone else to take midnight calls and overall responsibility: and 2) put the doctors on salary. The problem with this one is that while I’m sure the majority would take it, they would demand the same salary and benefits (including the multi-million dollar indexed pension) and working hours as the healthcare bureaucrats - time and a half or double time for overtime too.

comment_text: So flossing turns out to be another big fat medical fraud. No wonder folks say 'Diseases don't kill people, people kill people'.When billions of dollars are at stake even the most well-meaning physician cannot be trusted. For the last 40 or more years, there's been a huge campaign to scare folks about various shadowy things that might be lurkling, like terrorists, in our mouths. From the marketing aimed at children's cavities to the really serious adult stuff like bad breath, plaque, gingivitis, tartar, calculus, and gum disease. Thus the multibillion dollar business of mouth washes, dental floss, and other dental paraphenalia. And thus the warnings from dentists and hygienists to have 'regular' teeth cleanings. 'Teeth cleanings' are the worst and most costly part of the fraud. Scaring patients they will lose their teeth if they do not submit to 'debridement' and scaling of the gums, picking, poking, probing and reaming gums, supposedly to remove plaque. What they don't tell you is that regular sessions of that gum probing with needle-sharp instruments will eventually poke holes in the gums. Then problems arise with food particles putrifying in the mouth, 'requiring' further 'teeth cleanings' and other serious dental problems. If this goes on, the gums can incur deep 'pockets' that eventually abscess, resulting in permanent pain and discomfort, the inability to eat properly. These holes can only be fixed with extremely expensive and painful surgery. To say the entire 'teeth cleaning' scare is a lucrative racket is like saying Al Capone was not a nice guy. It's an unsurprising part of the fraudulent pattern to realize flossing is a waste of time. But on the sunny side, always use an electric tooth brush. They remove most of the plaque when you brush the gums, they prevent gums from bleeding, and one three minute brushing is effective as at least 10 brushings with a manual tooth brush.

comment_text: The first past the post system works fine in a two party model like the US. However, most democratic countries are multi-party. Our system has five parties plus independents meaning the winning party will likely never have a true majority (>50%) of the votes. Further, we only have a participation rate in the 50% area so, if a party wins with, say, 40% of the vote, they only represent 20% of the electorate or, put another way, 80% don't prefer that party. This is not an unfair comparison since too many people don't vote because they cannot support any of the choices that are likely to win and don't make the effort to vote because any other choice would just be wasted. A compulsory voting system, like Australia and other countries use would, at least, give a more defensible mandate to the winner. In my view, a preferential voting system would better reflect the electorates mood on a riding by riding basis without some of the negatives of a proportional system.

comment_text: Parliamentary Rights of Private Members. As someone who served in three Parliaments, I firmly believe that you're wrong, Margaret. My comment is made as someone who was very active as a Private Member during my terms in Parliament. Our tradition is that the business of the House is partitioned into 'government business' and 'Private Members business'. The former are subject to strict protocols of party discipline and the latter are not. Every MP has the right (and the responsibility) to press his / her personal views or the views of his / her constituents in Private Members business for discussion. The Private Member does not, of course, have the right to ensure that any such proposal is voted upon and approved in the House. While I understand that some outside the House would prefer that some topics never be debated in the House, doing so risks the rights and responsibilities the underlie our Parliamentary democracy. Canadian Parliamentary democracy is fundamentally different from the way the US Congress operates. There, the party leaders can ensure that a bill or a motion to limit the size of gun magazines never comes to the floor. Same for a bill to impose background checks. Those restrictions might sound fine if you oppose such legislation; but what if you support the measures? On balance, however uncomfortable having such measures discussed on the floor might be, I feel our traditional Parliamentary democracy is superior in serving the Canadian public.

comment_text: Lysiane Gagnon here mirrors a line of reasoning that, arguably, underlay in large part Canadian foreign policy under both the Chrétien/Martin and Harper lead Governments concerning matters relating to the former Yugoslavia, Afghanistan, the Middle East and North Africa. Simply put Canada’s operating assumptions when crises arose in these regions were that: 1. Canada had no direct national interest there beyond a general desire that the global peace and stability be restored and maintained, that basic human rights not be systematically violated and that the established international agencies for collectively addressing such crises be strengthened in the process, 2. Canada could best foster the aims under point 1 by encouraging collective international action through established international agencies such as the UN, NATO, etc., 3. Canada’s role was to follow the lead of the US in consultation with other NATO partners, but, in doing so, to stress the need for the international community in general, and the West in particular, to act in a manner consistent with points 1 and 2, and4. Canada could gain influence and credibility, especially with the US, by acting on the basis of these assumptions. There is nothing inherently wrong with these assumptions. However, they are incomplete insofar this leads to Canada subordinating and abstracting the actual circumstances in the countries in crisis and refocusing Canadian response away from the actual circumstances of the crisis at hand to concentration, instead, upon simply coordinating with US plans. At its worst, this promotes cynical fitting in with the decisions of our senior allies (regardless of the impact in the crisis area) in the hope that Canada, thereby, will have added good will in these quarters when bilateral trade and other issues of direct importance to Canada are later at stake. In the context of the current Iraq/Syria crisis, this leads to us valuing duplicating in miniature the US response (i.e. they focus much of their efforts on air strikes; therefore it’s important that we have our token air strike response.). We choose to do this despite the limitations evident in the effectiveness of the coalition air strike policy (i.e. It in isolation is not defeating ISIL and may, in some ways be aiding their cause) or the utility of Canadian air strike participation instead of other more efficient and effective military and humanitarian aid. In other words, a mindless application of these assumptions means that Canada values keeping in lockstep with the US above all else in this crisis regardless of the impact upon the crisis itself. Arguably, the policy now adopted by the new Government is more in keeping with an intelligent application (i.e. stress points 1 and 2, downplay points 3 and 4) of the assumptions set out above.

comment_text: Thank you for the article Margaret and Globeandmail, intriguing and thought-provoking as always! As a medical graduate and aspiring dietician, i argue that neither saturated fats, non-saturated fats or sugars make us fat. Calories make us fat. Weight loss is based on a calorie deficit, or burning more calories than you consume daily. What you eat doesn't really matter. If your body burns 2250kcal/day, you can eat 8 slices of pizza at 2000kcal and lose weight, correct? The reason why me are so worried about fat is because fat has 9calories/gram, while carbs have 4calories/gram. Its easier to get fat with fat, but if you cant calories it doesn't matter. Maintaining a good weight and BMI to reduce morbidity and mortality is a lifestyle choice that we can all make. My suggestion for those who are struggling to lose weight is to count calories and make sure you are in a calorie deficit daily, and find a good diet. Do research and read some excellent diet reviews (http://goo.gl/mbPVrT) and pick one that suits you, keeping in mind any diet will work as long as there is a calorie deficit. A high protein diet, frequent meals and high-carb cheat days help maintain metabolism so you can keep the weight you lose off :). Its becoming more and more easy to blame WHAT we eat for our weight problems, but i believe the answer lies in how MUCH we eat. Good luck everyone. Thank you for the great article Globeandmail.

comment_text: The labour market has lost sight of what a university is and is supposed to be.Universities were intended to produce two things: liberal arts graduates and researchers. During the twentieth century, however, they began to acquire a monopoly on professional instruction. The doctors, lawyers, nurses, accountants and engineers who used to learn their professions through a combination of apprenticeship and professsional instruction, became cohorts of university graduates. Then soon followed pretty much every white collar job in the marketplace. Next, the colleges, which had for decades successfully trained technicians, technologists and bookkeepers by the thousands decided that they, too, should get into the business of awarding post-nominal letters. The Liberal Arts are inherently valuable. Successful graduates of sound liberal arts programs have the capacity to learn and the capacity to apply their skills in the widest range of fields of endeavour. No, we don't need more BAs--but not because a BA isn't valuable. Rather, because the post-secondary degree industry has turned a university degree into a prerequisite for white collar employment--a completely artificial standard.

In quoting the Bill of Rights, the author capitalizes the word 'people.' The author argues uses this capitalization to support his argument that the Founding Fathers clearly meant the Second Amendment rights to apply collectively. In the original text of the Bill of Rights, 'people' is not capitalized. Also, the Fourth Amendment refers the to the right of 'the people' (uncapitalized) against unreasonable search and seizure of property. The Fourth Amendment clearly applies to individuals and not just state-level agencies against the federal government. How is it possible that the Bill of Rights treats the definition of 'the people' differently in two separate amendments? None of this means gun control laws should not be tightened in the United States. However, deception and misdirection does not help forward those goals of gun control supporters.

comment_text: A city-centre-to-airport rail link opened last year in Helsinki is configured as a loop. Roughly equivalent to a line running west out of Union to Mississauga or Oakville, then north and east through Brampton, to Pearson, then on through Vaughn, Richmond Hill, to Ajax and returning to Union. Trains run clockwise and counter clockwise. Travellers can access the airport to/from any point on the loop, or travel between any other set of points (example, Vaughn to Pickering). Fare is zonal but cost ~$5 from Helsinki train station to Vantaa airport.

comment_text: Wente raises an interesting point but disappoints with a failed analysis. Public sector unions, in the true sense of the union concept are obsolete. By that I mean, unions exist to balance the power of a corporation. Demands and negotiations are constrained by an economic version of MAD - Mutual Assured Destruction. If a union strikes too long, demands too much or the business demands too much and extends a strike, the business fails. Investors lose their money and the union members lose their jobs. However, in the public sector, that MAD dynamic does not exist (although many, including myself would argue another version of MAD, simple 'madness' exists, but that's another story....).When it comes to salary and benefits negotiations, public sector unions should have consultative role but in the end, their ability to strike based on these outcomes should be limited or removed. The public does not have a choice in where we can take our 'business', giving the public sector a monopoly. In those cases, regulation or more specifically, direct government oversight reigns. To balance government mismanagement (abuse of this power), you will see an exodus of teachers, public servants, etc if governments go too far. We've seen this with nursing shortages and also see it in the federal public sector (middle and senior management roles) where people have left to seek better opportunities. The government continues to struggle to recruit and retain good mid/senior level managers. Public sector unions are necessary to protect and represent their members in all other areas - discipline, promotions, general management. Given the past history of government (mis)management, that would be the best and most useful application of union oversight.

comment_text: This article troubles me greatly. I would just like to begin by saying, that discovery learning is employed in classrooms to help students see the connections between the concepts they are learning and the real world! Rather than have students passively memorize times tables like robots, we give them situations to work through have involve the skill of multiplication. This allows students to work creatively, critically, and collaboratively - all skills that are needed to succeed in today's society. Many of today's great thinkers, and great business people did not become who they are by regurgitating facts, but by thinking outside of the box. This is what we are trying to teach our students to become... creative, unique individuals. In reality, our children are already creative individuals. By teaching them in this method, we are fostering their creativity rather than killing it with rote memorization. Rather than tell them, 'This is the way we do math and their is no other way.' This type of learning community is not one that is created overnight. It takes a lot of hard work and dedication from teachers to foster and facilitate this process. By allowing students to come up with their own process, teachers must meticulously examine their work, conference with them individually or in small groups, and then assess where the student is at in terms of their Understanding, Thinking, and Application of concepts. Throughout this process, teachers provide students with written and oral feedback in terms of next steps, how the student can go back and improve their solution, or how the student can extend their thinking. These are higher order thinking skills. When looking at Bloom's Taxonomy of thinking skills, remembering and understanding are on of low end of the spectrum. We no longer merely expect our students to remember and understand. We expect that they create their own solution, and evaluate their own work and the work of their peers to see which solution to the problem is most effective. Coincidentally, creating and evaluating are on the highest end of the spectrum. Discovery learning ENGAGES children. It gets them interested and excited about mathematics (as well as other subjects). No longer do students question, 'Why do I have to learn this?' Now students see the connection between their world and the domain of learning. As a new teacher, I 100% agree the notion of discovery learning. This environment fosters each individual in the classroom and helps them to succeed. In this climate, we create multiple avenues for success, rather than one. With this method, students are valued as individuals, creators, and innovators. I am extremely proud and honoured to be entering the teaching profession at this time. For a different perspective on today's education system, please view the following video by Sir Ken Robinson - world-renowned education and creativity expert. http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zDZFcDGpL4U

Coincidentally , creating and evaluating are on the highest end of the spectrum . Discovery learning ENGAGES children . This environment fosters each individual in the classroom and helps them to succeed . In this climate , we create multiple avenues for success , rather than one . With this method , students are valued as individuals , creators , and innovators . I am extremely proud and honoured to be entering the teaching profession at this time . comment_text: The back-to-the-basics education argument rears its head periodically as though the basics (however that is defined) have been replaced by something insubstantial or nefarious. Project based learning, critical thinking, leadership skills hands-on learning ARE NOT the cause for poor math performance nor do they replace Basic Skills or Understandings in any subject area. Project based learning, for example, is a WAY of teaching, not a SUBJECT. Critical thinking is a WAY of ensuring language arts and social studies curriculum in particular involve thoughtful student analysis, something required for an informed citizenry. In fact many of the things cited in this article as negatives are exactly what schools are working to implement. Critics need to ask themselves what it means to be an educated person in the 21st century, surely it has to defined differently than the 19th century. Science classrooms where students in pairs design, execute experimentation and research outcomes are basic science but orchestrated by the teacher in a more challenging format than just a traditional lecture. Importantly, science scores (as well as interest in science) actually go up through this hands-on, project based methodology. They are in fact the cause of more intelligent, thoughtful and high performing students. The real issue for our public schools is that math and science university graduates infrequently choose education as their career pathway. In part this is because of lower wages, the sometimes long pathway to entering the profession, and what is seen as a less rewarding opportunity to use their skills. If we want teachers who are passionate about teaching math and science, we need to find ways to attract them into our classrooms--what about university debt load forgiveness? what about sabbaticals every 7 years like university profs to explore original research in their field? what about salary differentials? Criticizing our teachers for implementing approaches to learning that are based on research and provide good outcomes is not the way to address a math/science deficit in our school systems.

comment_text: Yes, we saw the problem early on and steered our kids away from approaches that downplay fundamentals. The fundamentals require intuition as to proportion and relations and a precise sense of quantification. So we had our young daughter in gymnastics. With this, i taught her the concept of negative integers in a minute. what are negative numbers? it is the same as the distance when you dip below the beam; think of the beam as zero. oh, i get it. She also learned the times table early on. We used a sheet that went up step wise, column 1 was 1x1=__, 1x2=__, etc., column 2 was 2x1=__, etc. up through column 12. The ordering is important because it allowed her to solve either by multiplication of fast addition--the two became seamless, so she internalized the relation with precise quantification. Each time she did the sheet we timed it and wrote the time and kept the sheet in a binder. For each best time she earned a loonie. Remarkable progress. She started at over 14 minutes and after not long was under 5. This served her well as she did extremely well in math, coming first among girls in one national math contest and always coming in the top 2 percent of all test writers in national Amercian math society contests. Best, with a foundation of intuition fornrelation and quantification as implicit knowledge embedded in skill, she easily grasped new mathematical relations and contests. (Explicit knowledge does not provide the intuition to grasp higher concepts. even Guass practised calculation tables through the end of his career.) We reinforced this foundation by enrolling her in the Spirit of Math program, which emphsaizes skills acquisition and well-ordered introduction of concepts. During her AP calculus course, during which she was a TA at Spirit of Math teaching lower grades, she observed that she now understood why various fundamentals were introduced when they were. Things she learned in elementary grade math helped her understand concepts in higher math. Hail to the wisdom of ages. Math is much like martial arts. Learn from the ways of masters, with methods developed over generations. Through high school she read books on the history of calculus and math generally as leisure reading. The importance of math intuition through skills acquisition for all precise thinking has been recognized since the time of Pythagoras, Euclid, Plato and Aristotle. Pity fashionable new trends that overlook the necessity for implicit knowledge are depriving a new generation of students of his advantage.

comment_text: I'm surprised to see this opinion coming from Jeffrey Simpson, an opinion which to me seems strangely oblivious to the hundred-years-plus history of Western (Britain, France, and the US) military and colonial intervention in that part of the world. And to the fact that it was the latest US & British military adventure - the spectacularly ill-advised and possible even criminal invasion of Iraq - that led directly to the horror that is ISIS. And yet it is now they who will not forget our actions? Yes, ISIS is a horror and, yes, we share the same democratic values (and vulnerabilities) as our above-mentioned allies. We also have tremendous empathy for the situation they are in, and we have real and valid concerns about our own security as well. But joining those allies in the military sequel to Iraq is neither militarily necessary nor consistent with our somewhat unique values. Nor does it make logical sense at this point. We can better help our allies and the people of the region by direct aid, including training if necessary, while demonstrating that not all Western nations follow the military and economic policies of the historically 'imperial' powers of the West. The long-term solution to the problems of the Middle East are not military. Canada is well placed to consider this point, and to aggressively explore political solutions while presenting itself as a nation with strongly Western political values but one without imperial baggage or proclivities. This is not a 'free pass' for Canada, but rather a call for us to craft a foreign policy in the Middle East that actually helps in solving the problems rather than becoming just another (and very minor) military player in a theatre of ongoing animosity and hatreds. This will take careful and creative thought, and possibly courageous action on occasion. But what better effort to be engaged in?

And, if Canadians and Albertans are prudent and smart, they will take any editorial from the Globe and Mail, telling them who to vote for, with the same grain of salt conservatives extend to issues like health, education, pensions, childcare, and the well-being of children, veterans and seniors.

comment_text: I am puzzled as to the point of this column. Mr. Simpson would apparently have the prime Minister stress that global warming is happening, and that it will have profound effects on the North. Oh yes, and by the way, all the people there already know this. But since there is an army of scientists, activists and bureaucrats who dedicate themselves full time to spreading the news about warming and its effects, the Prime Minister would not be accomplishing anything, especially since there is nothing he can do about it until an international treaty is signed that commits each country (and all countries) to specific reductions. When such a treaty is signed, and regardless of who is in power, Canada will be a party to it. Until that happens, no purpose is served by Prime Ministerial grandstanding. The Prime Minister is behaving quite reasonably in speaking only about those things he can do right now to help the people of the North. As for global warming, if there is any region that might possibly benefit, it is the Canadian Arctic. No one dares suggest this, though the real possibility is obvious. Of course there can be disagreement about whether benefits to one region should even be contemplated at the likely expense of great damage in others, but since the PM's purpose is only to promote the immediate possibilities of growth and increased prosperity in the North, raising the issue of global warming could only obscure and even contradict his message.

Michael Harris is a hack and he's writing this merely to make a living, rehashing old allegations and accusation, none with any substance. Lots of room for libel suits, no doubt, which could follow Harper's tenure as PM. Because fair comment isn't when the animus is so obvious. Trudeau glowingly said last week that he had written his new book. But now we find that was a lie. He had a whole group involved, including a National Post editor. He was group-interviewed, taped, comments edited and re-arranged, written together, edited, then re-written by Trudeau and re-edited. That isn't 'writing' a book. Things which can't be fact-checked -- his personal life and memories -- dominate, while his vision, his political acumen, his decisive take on the challenges facing the country and Canadians over the coming years and decades ? -- crickets. He was against free trade. But when the Donald MacDonald Royal Commission reported to him and recommended it, he listened and took the recommendation. comment_text: Sadly, Jeffrey Simpson conflates three issues into a single one. Having presumed that all discussion about this is no longer necessary, he concentrates all his fire on the political problem, i.e. where is the action? He has done this for years now. But the questions remain valid: Is there global warming? How much of it is due to human activity? How effective are the renewable energy initiatives in delaying or stopping this? The answers are anything but clear or settled: Yes, there is global warming, has been for the last 150 years since some reliable measurements were first taken. But the rate of increase over those 150 or so years is well within the known parameters going back some 2000 years. Yes, humans are causing some of the observed warming, but other factors are clearly involved as well. Quantifying these is very difficult and we are far from being able to do so.The renewable energy initiatives are the easiest to evaluate, given their 20-year history in Germany and Denmark. They contribute virtually nothing to reduce the production of CO2, they are so costly as to sap the energy out of the economy, and they use up precious financial resources that might be better used to mitigate the consequences of a potential return to earlier rates of warming. ( They have stopped for the last 16 or 17 years ).Mr. Simpson should stop presuming that he knows everything he needs to know about this subject.

comment_text: One can disagree with the usage of the term 'barbaric' in cases such as this without recourse to ethical relativism, something this editorial fails to consider. I object to employing terms like 'barbaric' and 'uncivilised' as generic pejoratives because it's a false comparison. Historically it has been civilised societies that have perpetrated the greatest crimes, which should surprise no one as such societies have greater destructive power. No so-called primitive culture has - or even could - carry out something like the holocaust, for example. This may sound like semantic hair-splitting but I think it's morally significant that we can't seem to be honest about the fact that the acquisition of knowledge does not purge us of our darker impulses. Similarly humans often describe our own evil acts as 'animalistic' despite the fact that these actions are often uniquely human (i.e. killing for pleasure) and that attributing a moral dimension to animals is an obvious category error in the first place. That said, I'm making a philosophical and not a political point; I broadly agree with the government's policy here.

comment_text: How could the Democratic Party lose to such a deeply flawed candidate? Perhaps Ms Kendizor needs to reflect on her own scurrilous columns on Bernie Sanders and reflect on the behaviour of the Democratic National Committee and reflect on the actual record of Mrs Clinton in office and reflect on the history of sleaze around the Clintons. She could ask her children whether it is OK to give one student the questions before the exam, but not others, and then to promote the woman who does it. That's, after all, what happened to Donna Brazile, who was promoted to head the DNC after forwarding debate questions to Mrs Clinton, but not Bernie Sanders. She could also ask why Chelsea Clinton herself seems to have had questions about how the Clinton Foundation was run and its easy slippage between private and public business. President Obama himself said that Mrs Clinton was the most qualified presidential candidate ever---a claim repeated by many in the media. Mrs Clinton's record of success seems pretty trivial by comparison. The answer to my opening question is: by running a deeply flawed candidate themselves. I am not suggesting moral equivalence here or that Mrs Clinton deserved to lose. However, some fault must lie with the Democratic Party itself and its party luminaries who were so blinkered beforehand that they failed to find and encourage a wide range of candidates, including women, to present Americans with a fresher and less flawed candidate.

comment_text: As a happy Globe subscriber, I find that this article is one of few that make me question the quality of journalism that sometimes finds its way to print. Wente points her accusatory finger at Klein and apparently, all the activists trying to make change with regards to the climate problem, suggesting that they basically have no idea what they're talking about. In writing that 'the activists should do themselves a favour, and grow up' she is using far too broad a storke here. If Wente is going to be cut down so many people with her accusatory tone, you'd think that she had better trumpet her answer to this problem as loudly and clearly as she criticizes everyone else. But this is not the case, as she instead opts to provide a few little blurbs where she says the real problem is the developing world. Okay, that's fine, but then, that's it - her line of thought simply stops there. If Wente is correct, and she might be, in suggesting that the focus needs to be on developing nations, what becomes immediately clear is that this 'complex and fiendishly hard problem' is probably going to need to be solved by the Developed nations - the only ones who have the power of innovation, because how else are we going to provide power and feed the world's population? Not being a specialist on the subject myself, I would assert that the solving of this problem brings us right back to the developed world - the countries that are currently fighting the ideological battles that Wente appears to undervalue. If David Suzuki & Leo DiCaprio are right (yes, they are activists) one of the main solutions is technologies and innovations that actually help an economy while fixing the problem. Such technologies, innovations, and ideas are most likely to come out of the developed nations where the ideological battle is being fought. In the end, the 'self-centred morality tale' of activists fighting evil corporations and absent politicians has a very important role in the developed world, and it is this view that Wente seems to blindly discredit the most.

comment_text: Donald Trump's frustrated fans keep asking why so many in society and in media (and even in his own party) are so emphatically opposed to his candidacy; some see a huge conspiracy, as they tend to do. It might be because in a general way decent people in this part of the world had thought -- or at least dared to hope, whatever else -- that we had begun to move beyond the racial/ethnic/sexual divisions that have plagued us in the past. This is after all the 21st century, not the 1950s. But now Trump and his mob come along to crudely remind us that those resentments still fester in a large segment of the public. Of course the economic issues are there. The American Dream of social mobility and material security is less convincing now to many citizens whose experience tells them otherwise. Still, the insecurity that allegedly explains the fury and fear in Trump supporters has plagued the population throughout the decades -- does anyone think that voters didn't have anxiety during the years of the Great Depression, or WWII, or the war in Vietnam, etc. -- but they never coalesced on such a scale behind a huckster like The Donald, and made themselves look so foolish. There are reasons for their anger but no excuse for their choice.

comment_text: Struggling to figure out any possible rationale for the Globe & Mail's bizarre editorial (Oct 18), I went back & re-read it, in case I'd misunderstood its intent. But no, it's there in black and white.'But choose, voters must.' So this is intended to be advice for the choice we face, not some exploration of an alternative reality.'His party deserves to be re-elected'. 'But, after October 19th he should quickly resign'. The inanity of this as advice in casting a ballot Is staggering beyond belief. It totally ignores the fact the modern 'Conservative' party is entirely Harper's creation. Without him it is nothing. After him, profound, fundamental, change and total rebuilding will be required. Jeffrey Simpson, in the Globe (Oct 17) has written clearly about the hollow shell the party has become. So a vote for the 'Conservative' party is a vote for a totally unknown quantity. A pity your Editorialist didn't read it.[I put 'Conservative' in quotes as a case can be made that the Harper party is not in fact Conservative in anything other than its knee jerk favoring of business and low taxes; but that is another topic. ]Such rebuilding is supposed to be done on the opposition benches. The time to vote for or against the results is obviously after it is complete. As the Globe Editorialist knows, or should, Harper is under no obligation to resign unless he loses the confidence of the house. True, he has made statements indicating he may voluntarily resign at some point. But there is absolutely no guarantee of that. His lust for power at any price is well established, as is his proclivity to go back on his word when it suits him (government accountability for example). So I would not hold my breath on that. It is ironic, to reach for a polite term, that Mr Black whose sympathies are assuredly conservative, writing in the Post, is able to see clearly where the Globe cannot. After praising several of the governments achievements he gives a trenchant analysis of their trampling over the role of parliament and assaults on civil liberties and accountable government, concluding that Mr Trudeau '.... has earned his chance. We really cannot have another four years of government by a sadistic Victorian schoolmaster.' (Personally I think sociopathic is nearer the mark than sadistic, but never mind). He understands, as the Globe Editorialist does not, that voters must choose from the parties actually running in the election. This is not Rotisserie politics. We expect better from the Globe & Mail.

comment_text: I rarely read G&M editorials anymore, and this is a prime example of why. 'From that time in 1965 when the Liberals painted our national flag the same colour as their logo...'?. Whoever wrote that completely ignored key facts. After unsuccessful efforts by different prime ministers to create a new flag, a 1958 extensive poll found 80% of Canadians wanted a flag completely different from any other country's flag (so no Union Jack, Red Ensign or fleur-de-lys) and 60% wanted it to feature the maple leaf (which happens to be red, in nature). Pearson favoured a spray of 3 leaves on a white ground with two blue borders invoking Canada's motto 'from sea to sea' but referred the issue to an all-party Parliamentary Committee (7 Liberals, 5 Conservatives, 3 from other parties). The Conservatives tried an end-run that resulted in a ditching of the version with blue borders and a majority vote for a single maple leaf, white ground and red borders (see Wikipedia). The writer also appears not to have travelled much. In many different countries over the years, I have only ever heard (probably, in all, hundreds of individual) Canadians identify their nationality when asked where they are from or 'Are you American?' No claiming or implying of 'greatness'.Further, Mr. Harper is the only PM I have ever heard -- in my six decades -- publicly label fellow citizens 'unCanadian', simply for their daring to disagree with him. He also repeatedly presumed to know and baldly state -- while showing no interest in hearing from anyone outside his own tent or hodling other world views/values than his -- what Canadians, collectively, want/feel/believe on far too many occasions. My spouse frequently attends international conferences, where many delegates from other countries have spontaneusly offered, 'I'm glad Canada's back'. I personally have had nmerous non-Canadians, as soon as we each happened to identify our nationalities by way of polite chit-chat, and without the subject of politics having been raised, spontaneously express their congratulations on Canada's new national government. I wish Ken Thompson would fire the entire board and bring on a group with better research skills and broader life experience. But I know he doesn't, on principle, interfere with any aspect of daily operations. So back to the other option of just skipping the editorials, I guess.

comment_text: @Vernunft1'The death knell for any defense of religion' is rather a stretch for evolution. There are many religions and many variants of individual religions and of those there are quite a few who have no problem at all with Darwin or evolution. It's true that Darwin exploded the belief in a literal six day creation, but literalists were already losing ground in Christian circles before Darwin. Evangelicals and Fundamentalists resist, but their attempts to make the poetic factual is doomed to failure. I'd recommend the Great Code by Northrup Frye or The Battle for God by Karen Armstrong to gain an understanding of how religion informs our lives. I find your Right/Left dichotomy outmoded. It's true that some people can reassess their religious beliefs, even when that's Marxist materialism, and come to a new World View. However, I've noticed that certain zealous people merely change the names of their idols and carry on in the same way. There's a cartoon by Gahan Wilson which shows 'NOTHING is sacred'. It's funny how some nihilists get that way. I'm not sure what your views on Climate Change are. Surely the science has shown human activity to be the major cause and I don't see it as Leftist of me to say so. Modern industrial exploitation of the planet is done by Wall St corporations or Communist Chinese Five-Year-Plans. There's not much difference. Ah, so you don't really know what goes on at the Patent Office, do you? May I recommend James Gleick's NYTimes essay Patently Absurd. I'd also recommend Skloot's book on Henrietta Lacks. I have no contempt for modern science. I do, however, find Big Pharma and the corporate giants of technology and agri-business to be claiming ownership of things which they really don't have any right to. And much of this began when the Patent Office in the USA became a for-profit government division. I don't see why you should engage in ad hominem attacks on me by suggesting I'm similar to a Jehovah's Witness or Christian Scientist. Prayer may have some placebo effect, but I trust my doctor to do what's right. I don't pray myself. I do, however, meditate. (Cogito, ergo sum.)And where are these false gods? Isn't that the problem? You want to name Jesus Christ and Yahweh and Allah. What about the Almighty Dollar or Communism or Private Property? Are they false gods? And who decides? Isn't that why we have a Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the US has the Bill of Rights? I certainly don't want you deciding who's IN and who's OUT. The Danish newspaper cartoons were printed to incite hatred. The reason it became front page news is because the Danish government mishandled the entire affair, giving the impression it was endorsing the bigoted cartoons. Contempt and disrespect should never be championed. And, as they say in Law, silence is consent. Sadly, it was men like Ezra Levant who wanted to reprint the cartoons. And we all know Ezra to be fair-minded, right? Unless you're a Roma.

comment_text: I'm a little bit curious about how the Globe can see that Donald Trump is not fit for public office, and yet - four times in a row - the Globe could not see that Stephen Harper was not fit to hold public office. Donald Trump is only the latest illustration of a larger problem that has been building in Western democracies for a long time. It is a very complicated problem, certainly. There is no doubt about that. It is an incredibly dangerous problem, no doubt about that, either. It is what prevents us from doing anything about climate change. It is what prevent anything done about transit/congestionIt is what prevents us from matching tax revenues to the actual costs of public sector goods and services. It is what prevents us from dealing with growing problems in international affairs - by far the worst being the inability to prevent Russia from sliding back into totalitarianism, and now taking other countries e.g., Turkey, Hungary, maybe Poland, with it.The solutions to the problem are not simple, either. They involve things as disparate as(a) restructuring our school systems - the rise of Harper, Ford, and Trump is surely the cost of graduating two generations of students who have virtually no knowledge of history, geography or literature(b) getting a true grasp on political campaign financing(c) getting a true grasp on the dangers of agency capture(d) understanding the urgency of electoral reform - and above all the urgency in Canada, the US and the UK of abolishing First-Past-the-Post which, of all electoral systems is the most pathetically vulnerable to manipulation and abuse. It may be worse in the US than Canada, but the same patterns are easily discerned.-----The well-spring of our prosperity for almost 200+ years has been the strength and openness of our democratic institutions. Over that time, those institutions have evolved and become steadily more democratic. In recent times, however, they have come under sustained attack. For two generations we have done an abysmally bad job of protecting the integrity and viability of out institutions of democracy. Harper, Ford, Brexit, Trump. These (and many others) are the symptoms of that problem coming home to roost. The first step to solving it is getting rid of First-Past-the-Post, as soon as possible.

comment_text: The problem with climate change activism for Canada is twofold. First, our economy is now heavily dependent on exporting the oil, gas, and coal that we have in abundance. Quite possibly other industries could replace this activity within a half century or more, but if we try to shut down the extraction industries too quickly, it will mean condemning a couple of generations of Canadians to a significantly lower standard of living. That doesn't mean we shouldn't cut back on our own consumption, but it does mean that no Canadian politician, of any party, can afford to choke off the supply of Canadian energy to countries that need and want it.The second difficulty is even more perturbing. Climate change would clearly be a huge problem for many parts of the world. But it is not clear that the disadvantages of warming to Canada, measured in economic terms, would be greater than the benefits. Our new immigrants may be different, but they are every bit as decent and worthwhile as those before them that led the way into this country. Our attitudes will eventually become their attitudes, and theirs will become ours. The varied tapestry of everyone's cultural assets should be cherished. But, if we teach bigotry, intolerance, and racism, and we will fall apart as a society. Ultimately, the power of positive thinking and inclusiveness in this society will prevail.

comment_text: I know very little about homeopathy, but I know denial when I see it. Deniers of homeopathy never acknowledge its safety. Homeopathic medicines are harmless compared even to the OTC medicines you commonly take such as acetaminophen, or even the vitamins you buy at the health food store. Homeopathic medicines are even more safe compared to prescription drugs. That's an important point, because the toxicity of any drug is equally important as any benefit it provides. For example, a medicine that eliminates headaches in a split-second is useless if it induces blood clots a day later. Unlike conventional medicine, homeopathy stays close to the Hippocratic ideal. One of the Hippocratic oaths is: 'Nor shall any man's entreaty prevail upon me to administer poison to anyone.' In other words, first do no harm. Now recall that conventional medicine is the first to swear that even if you drank 20 liters of a homeopathic medicine and then bathed in it afterwards, it wouldn’t do a thing. Therefore, because it can’t hurt your health, homeopathy already has a leg up on any conventional medicine. The moment you put anything in your mouth you’re laying a bet. You’re wagering that your life will be better, or longer, for taking the medicine(or food!) than if you don’t. At the same time wagers are placed against you: namely, the statistical risks associated with what you just put in your mouth. According to modern science, the ingredients in homeopathic medicines are so dilute that they could never have any effect on you whatsoever, let alone harm you. So their risk is essentially zero compared to any drug that conventional medicine might offer. The short story is, short, medium and long term controlled trials testing the efficacy of homeopathy would be a very good idea.

comment_text: The fact that Ford still has support points to serious problems with the mega city form of government. While some of Ford's support comes from people who are so ideological they would support any excess committed by a fellow true believer, without any exercise of their limited brain power, some support him because of a striking divergence between the perceived interests of the suburbs vs those of the core. In Vancouver, from where I get to watch this Toronto gong show, I can take some comfort that the regional approach here still allows a great deal of municipal independence. Vancouver can ultimately call its own shots and not be dictated to by the suburbs on important decisions. If that were not so we would probably have a freeway cutting all the way into the downtown because that would be more convenient from the perspective of those coming into town from the South and the East. Fortunately, those folks don't get to pick a mayor and counselors who make the decisions for Vancouver. Vancouverites do that and residents of other municipalities pick their own mayor and council. Bigger ain't necessarily better. Maybe that's why we have a real person for a mayor who exhibits the normal qualities one hopes to find in elected officials, such as a moral compass. Watching it all from here it sure seems it would be better for the whole Toronto region if Ford were only mayor of Etobicoke.

comment_text: Back during World War II, when the German army over ran Denmark, the Nazis forced Danish Jews to wear the Star of David, to identify themselves as Jews. So this Globe editorial, in a very real way, restates the Islamist objections as to depicting their prophet Mohammed. This Globe editorial -- a very important editorial -- essentially it tells its readership this the Islamonazis who murdered Charlie Hebdo do indeed have a point. comment_text: Empires fall slowly but they do go. In many ways Brexit is the last whimpering squeak of the failed British Empire, the realisation that 'Land of Hope and Glory' is just a song, not a state of being. Imperialism, divide and conquer, subjugate and intimidate, can no longer be the operating system of Victoria's England, that long moment in the sun has moved into dark shadow. How galling to discover that you were not monarch of all you survey, but a victim of failure, forced by circumstances beyond your control, to take to your bosom peoples you had once held under your thumb. Old beliefs die very hard, helped along by almost half a century of wars, dissolution of a way of life, attrition of values and the weaknesses of an ailing State. The jump to internationalism, mentioned often here, is a leap driven forward by trade, commercialism, corporate empire building, not about social integration and cultural understanding, those fusions take hundreds of years, not several decades to achieve. The human world, God help every other species, is flailing about, performing the mythical bird trick, living the fast life in ever increasing confusion, reaching almost to the point that anything we do is to the detriment of all around us.Maybe we should look on Brexit as a brake vigorously applied, a frantic effort to recover balance, not the old time-worn status quo.

comment_text: The argument put forth by Ms. Lang is a classical capitalism argument. Ms. Lang accurately describes how things work. Investors/shareholders and those who work on their behalf seek to maximize shareholder/owner/investor value by driving down costs and maximizing returns. My question is where does this logically lead. Jobs (all kinds, including high skill jobs) are moving to parts of the globe where the cost of doing that job is lower than doing that job in Canada (or other so called 'developed' economies- whether in North America, Europe etc.). Standards of living in the developed economies for those who are unlucky to be in these job sectors are dropping (real incomes adjusted for inflation have not increased appreciably since the mid 70s) while the standards of living for those in the emerging economies working in these fields (whether manufacturing and now increasingly in high value services) is rising. It seems that what we are in a transition period where western economies overall are getting relatively poorer (slower annual growth of gdp in the range of 2 - 4 %) and emerging or developing economies are getting relatively richer (higher annual growths of GDP 5 - 10 %) . From a global welfare point of view this is not a bad thing, most people are not against poorer countries doing better. However, when it happens at my expense or the expense of the well being of my children just starting out , the thinking changes as we all become a lot more parochial. The question for economies like Canada is what labour adjustment policies are needed in this time of transition and equalization. The current government appears to be signalling that in their view if you are unemployed it is your fault, you are lazy and indolent and you should not be catered to. In reality the situation is very complex with many types of unemployment and underemployment with all of our governments (provincial and federal) sticking their heads in the sand hoping it will go away.

If it weren't for the IPCC's self-imposed consensus mandate then a secondary and alternative minority report would have come out. comment_text: I firmly believe that democracy is very poorly served, in every regard, by any election system that fails to achieve reasonably accurate representation by population. Each elected representative should, in all fairness as a necessary condition of democracy being effected, represent very closely the same number of citizens. Each should have essentially the same workload as to representation, in terms of the number of people in their riding. Each should be elected by a majority of voters from a total number of voters where the total number per riding is essentially as similar as possible. In that way each elected member is better assured of a standing that is essentially similar to all others in terms of political power and responsibilities. The latter balance cannot be achieved unless you have representation by population. Otherwise you have immense disparity as to individual member influence, power, prestige, and intensity of responsibilities, as to work load. Disparities as to work load need to be resolved, as do issues as to member status within parliament that are based on disparities as to whom, in terms of demographic numbers, a member actually represents. Every member of parliament needs to have the very same status in a true democracy, as a member, and each should have approximately the same work load in relation to having the same pay and benefits. Once that is properly resolved then, and only then, can a government, such as Canada's national government, begin to effectively and meaningfully deal with other problems of disparity that increasingly plague the country.

comment_text: Saying that most people voted for parties that want electoral reform is disingenuous; the various parties have quite different reforms in mind. I commend your attention to RangeVoting. org; it's American but it has wealth of information on various systems. A simple ranked ballot, which appears to be Justin Trudeau's preference, is strongly preferential to centrist parties and in the long run deadly to small parties. The NDP, Greens and other small parties would prefer proportional representation, but that tends to constantly changing coalitions and too much bargaining power for fringe elements. There are plenty of bad examples of how that works. STV and Approval with Delegation are two ideas intended to produce more representative government with least regret. The two have different ways of allocating the votes on the second and subsequent rounds that have interesting implications. Anyway, we need a proper discussion on this, not the usual partisan carping. The Liberals do not have a mandate to impose their preferred solution; there is enormous moral hazard in that.

comment_text: I come from Northern Ontario and have since moved to Norway. It took be a long time to understand social capital. I thought all the bad decisions I was surrounded by were due to alcohol and poor economy. When I moved to Norway, I saw the same bad decisions being played out in dive bars across the city. This was strange. Norway is a social democracy with generous benefits. Everyone lives well above the poverty line - is there a poverty line in a social democracy? So why would people, with enough money and good jobs, make these same bad decisions that are rampant in my small Northern Ontario town? Social capital. Even still, we all have choices. I did not graduate high school. I attempted suicide when studying for a biology test at 16 years old. A few months later I moved to Toronto and lived through a string of bad relationships. I was always smart, winning awards, captain of sports teams, but at some point, my lack of social capital caught up to me. Now I live in Norway and will defend my PhD in Medicine in early April. We all have choices. We all have free will. We can choose to suffer or work our butts off for a better life. We can build our own social capital, one book at a time.

comment_text: I think Mr. Cameron's big mistake was focusing on Muslim women only when he made his language comments. I believe a nation that accepts immigrants has every right to expect the immigrant to make as much effort as possible to become fluent in the language, with help from the host country of course. This shows the proper respect for the country which has granted them the privilege to stay, and through the language, communicates the values of the society they've come to live in. In the end, the immigrant has a chance to really prosper in their new country. The host nation should make every effort to support immigrants in learning a language, because only successful integration makes an immigration program work. All pretty simple and basic really, and it's surprising that nations do not take this common sense approach - and immigrants feel such a sense of entitlement that they feel victimized by the host nation expecting them to speak the language of their new country.

comment_text: Couldn't agree more and I am a former CBC news employee and someone who believes in true 'public' broadcasting - which sadly the CBC does not engage in.
