Then have the federal government fund what would be a true 'public' broadcast entity.

comment_text: This article reads as a shotgun blast---it goes everywhere without hitting the exact target. The only accurate point made was that language proficiency is largely contingent on usage, and even that is debatable. Some view language proficiency as a skill that needs daily practice. I'll admit that I was fluent in German as a grad student, only because I read it every day for research. Suffice it to say, I've become somewhat rusty with it. I was even decent with Russian for the same reason, but that, too, has diminished over the years. Even so, I also found that part of learning a foreign language was understanding the underlying logic. From experience, I found German and Russian easier to learn than French or Spanish. I've even dabbled in Latin, and actually found it easier than French or Spanish because I was already acquainted with cases and inflections from studying German and Russian. Even then, not all languages use case the same. Indeed, I found that Latin uses the ablative and Russian the genitive in ways that are strange, whereas German was more properly balanced in how it used case---yet this is only my opinion. If the author asserts that those who struggle with French are likely to struggle with English, this is true in one important sense: English and French, while having similar vocabulary, are grammatically dissimilar. If you wish to better understand English grammar, study German, or better yet, Dutch or a mainland Scandinavian tongue. Finally, part of why official bilingualism hasn't taken off big time in Canada is cultural. Let's be honest, the British and French have a terrible reputation with learning foreign languages, reflecting xenophobia perhaps. Even in Europe, few Brits and French are bilingual. Given this, I don't know if official bilingualism will ever prove successful here.

comment_text: Political commentary aside (and it's millenia, not milleniums, G&M editors), Ms. Wente's experience of being in Israel is very similar to mine when I went a couple of years ago. She captures the behaviour and attitude of the local Israelis very well. Also, having traveled a little bit in the Middle East, it is also perhaps the one country in which a Western woman can move about freely. I particularly appreciated that at the time, because I was travelling solo. She didn't say whether she met any Arab Israelis as well as Jewish ones, which you will, especially if you are in Jerusalem. It is here that the society bifurcates - the Jewish Israelis feel that they have been supportive and helpful and have given the Arab Israelis the tools to succeed. The latter of course feel discriminated against (not wholly unjustified because some Israeli companies will not hire them, claiming fear of terrorism).The political history there is very complicated, but there's no question that since 1948, the Israelis have created a jewel in the midst of the desert, and preserved the sanctity of the holy places that serve three religions. On the other hand, there is also no question that they are so heavily supported by the United States, that it's hard to say how much of all that development is really to their credit (and this is a big part of the problem for their neighbours). In the days of the cold war, when Israel was one of the U.S.'s few allies in that area, the support made some strategic sense. 20+ years after the end of that cold war, much less so.

comment_text: Another thing is lower turnout doesn't necessarily mean parties right of centre cannot win. It does however mean they will have to have a broader appeal and certainly the Harper based Conservatives likely won't do this. In Australia, they've had plenty of conservative governments and they have mandatory voting. But since the Liberals (who are really conservative in Australia) rarely get over 50% on the first ballot, they have to appeal to people's second choices. In Germany and France, turnout usually exceeds 80% yet the CDU/CSU in Germany and UMP in France have a better winning record than the Conservatives in Canada. The difference is in Germany, usually it involves forming coalition so they have to be willing to cooperate with others while in France it goes to run off so much like Australia they have to appeal as second choice of others. Heck here in Canada, turnout is usually over 70% in the Maritimes where PC party often wins or in the last Saskatchewan election it was 70% where the Saskatchewan Party led by Brad Wall won a record 64% (note Harper's support in Saskatchewan has ranged for a low of 42% in 2004 to a high of 56% in 2011).The difference is the PCs in Atlantic Canada are mostly Red Tories who appeal to a larger segment and likewise Brad Wall maybe centre-right, but he is not a divisive type who hates anyone who disagrees with him like Harper. Its true in the US, the GOP benefits from lower turnout, but that's because their policies are to the right of many and since the demographics most likely to vote GOP are more likely to show up, they figure a lower turnout benefits them. This is the path the Conservatives seem to want to follow and is a bad choice in my view. They should find ways to appeal to a broader demographic not suppress turnout on the basis their base is more likely to show up than other party's.

comment_text: Seniors get blamed for too many societal ills through broad generalizations. I am a senior, relatively new to it as well. Here are a few ideas to ponder before generalizing. Health Care: I don't know about Canada but statistics I have read from another developed country, Australia, indicate that seniors can only be blamed for something like 4% of the rising costs of health care. You might consider rising rates of obesity and lack of fitness in young people as a cause of rising health care costs too. Drug overdoses, alcohol poisoning, stabbings and shootings, car collisions as a result of speeding and texting must play a part too. And then there is the corporate greed of pharmaceutical companies and all the other suppliers of medical equipment. Jobs: I worked hard to complete an education too. I enjoyed my job and the ability to earn a living. Youth can wait their turn as I did. Wealth: I am not rich. I do not have the latest flat screen TV (there are better ones discarded at our local dump). I do not have a smart phone. My car has 250 000 km on it and is good for much more. I do not eat out at the drop of a hat - cook everything from scratch because I enjoy doing so. Did so when my kids were growing up and I worked. Guess who does have all those things plus debt of course. We saved for our retirement. Both our kids own their homes because we gave them part of their inheritance when they actually needed it. (Also they paid their own way for most of their university educations). We are not greedy. We pay for the grandchildren's RESP. We buy the snow suits boots and shoes. We pay for a summer cottage rental for a week. We pay for lessons for the grandchildren. We babysit for one week at a time because our daughter has to travel for work. We donate to the Salvation Army, United Way, and a free lunch programme. Our satisfaction from life comes from being able to share. We don't need stuff - most people don't need as much stuff as they accumulate. It's just shopping therapy. All ages need to look at what is important in life - it's not at Walmart. Then you can save for your future. I am sure that there are young people who are well educated and unemployed. I've known a few. They didn't whine. They changed expectations, used initiative and creativity to forge a new way of earning a living.

comment_text: Banked sick time is not a problem. Indeed, it's an indicator the person doesn't take sick days. It's when an employee has been on the job for several years and has no banked sick days, that questions should be asked. Does this person suffer from Monday/Friday-itis, using up all sick days each year? That is a greater concern, not only because of the abuse of the sick leave provision, but also because there won't be any sick days available when there is a real illness. Banked sick days are purely an insurance policy, more likely to be used in later years than earlier ones, just as older people tend to need medical care more than younger people do.I have seen the occasional use of banked sick days at the end of a career, when a fully healthy person got a doctor's certificate to allow that. I find that morally objectionable and indefensible. But I also saw that management didn't challenge the certificate, thereby aiding and abetting the abuse. For myself, I retired with over 200 banked sick days. That was an indication I had almost no days off due to illness throughout my career. Given that the sick days were in effect an insurance policy, I couldn't cash them in, any more than I can cash in my house insurance policy because I've never had a fire. I'm glad we had banked sick days, which in fact cost the government nothing. I'm even more glad I remained well throughout my career and didn't have to make use of them.

comment_text: Mr. Wright provided personal funds to Mr. Duffy, a legislator. This was not a loan but an outright gift. Mr. Duffy belongs to what is, nominally, an independent legislative body. This creates the impression that Mr. Wright was buying favours - either in the present or the future. To determine whether he was buying favours in the present requires further investigation. Mr. Wright argues that he was simply helping Duffy to pay back what he owed taxpayers. This is probably true, bearing in mind that Duffy claims he did not break any rules and that he may be right. But the appearance that Wright was buying a Senator's loyalty -and possibly silence -through the use of money is undeniable. Was this a crime? That remains to be seen. But it merits further investigation and it underlines a potential source of enormous corruption in Canadian politics and it is certainly unethical. Legislators have to be held to a different standard of conduct than the general public, especially when it comes to their finances, for exactly this reason. Obviously, we cannot have a situation develop wherein wealthy individuals can simply provide gifts to legislators to help them with their personal finances. This is why we have such things as restrictions on campaign fund donations and the need for full disclosure of personal finances with elected officials. The Senate is an unelected body that still plays a crucial role in the governing of Canada. Its members cannot be accepting cash from private citizens, without any disclosure or oversight.

comment_text: I think sometimes the purpose behind articles like these isn't to inform readers, it's to get them to think about a public issue in a very specific way. The author wants us to think that Donald Trump is rising because of something he calls 'national racism'. That's fine, but it doesn't really explain the simultaneous rise of Bernie Sanders. The only factor they both have in common is that they represent a growing public distrust and anger at both the Republican and Democratic parties. In a way that cuts across the traditional political divide. Yes, some of that anger is being expressed in racist terms, but some of it isn't. Some of it is being expressed as anger targeting corporations, and not groups of people. Either way, the anger is quite real. And trying to come up with reasons that neatly avoiding addressing the reasons for that anger isn't doing the general public any favours.

comment_text: Ms. Wente is precisely wrong in her focus. The issue is not about the political views of the graduates of TWU's faculty of law; the issue is about who gets admitted to TWU's faculty of law. Law school places are few and far between, heavily oversubscribed by undergraduates who wish to pursue a career in law. And the 18 Common Law faculties across Canada are the exclusive route of entry into that profession. And this is where TWU falls afoul of the law. Because law school isn't just a private course of academic study leading to a degree; law school is the only means by which a citizen or permanent resident may become a participant in the fundamental pillar of one of the three branches of government. None but a law school graduate may become an officer of the court; none but a law school graduate may be summoned to the bench; none but a law school graduate may earn a living providing counselling others in the law. A gay student taking up a place at TWU is exposed to a culture in which that student's sexuality is fundamentally undermined and denigrated. And that gives socially conservative christian students a leg up--because they will have a certain number of law school places available to them and to no one else. To say that gay students will have equal access to TWU's Law Faculty is nothing short of mendacious. Ms. Wente should be ashamed that she has put herself in the position of being exposed as a liar.

comment_text: Who did Canadians put on their list of most-admired people? Well, that’s the thing. No one. The list of names weren’t chosen by Canadians. They were chosen by someone named Shachi Kurl. She’s not a pollster. She’s a former journalist who went into PR. She came up with the list of names. And then she asked Canadians whether or not they liked the names on her list. Canadians weren’t allowed to choose their own names. They had to choose from Shachi’s list. The three federal party leaders were on the list; fair enough. But there were two senators, too: Pamela Wallin and Mike Duffy. Why on earth would two lightning rods like them be put on a list of most admired Canadians? It’s obvious: To pad the list with names that Canadians would obviously not choose. To push people to the names Shachi wanted them to choose. Shachi put two former politicians on the list: Belinda Stronach, who hasn’t been an MP for five years, who served in the Liberal cabinet for just nine months, whose sole claim to fame was inheriting a job at her father’s auto company. Why was she on the list? Or Stephen Lewis, the Ontario NDP leader in the 1970s? Do you see a pattern? Shachi’s scandalous names were all Conservatives, though Liberal senators such as Mac Harb and Colin Kenny are embroiled in scandals, too. And Shachi’s list of saintly retired politicians are left-wingers — no Preston Mannings or Deborah Greys. Shachi chose three journalists. But all of them were from the CBC. Why not the great Lloyd Robertson of CTV? (I asked Shachi if the CBC paid for the survey, but she didn’t answer.)Why no real heroes, non-political people, like Chris Hadfield, the astronaut? Why no sports heroes like Sidney Crosby or even Wayne Gretzky? There was one “sports” name on the list: John Furlong. Sixty-three percent of survey respondents had no clue who he was. He was the bureaucrat who ran the 2010 Vancouver Olympic committee. And just last month he was sued for the third time, facing unproven allegations of being a child molester. Shachi put him on the list. Let’s recap: A PR hack with no training as a pollster, chooses a personal list of friends and enemies. She calls it a survey of Canadians, but Canadians aren’t allowed to select their own names. They’re forced to choose from her list, that’s padded with obvious stinkers — that pushes people to choose her friends at the CBC or left-wing politicians. That’s not a poll. That’s a CBC-David Suzuki press release. Suzuki is a fake. And this survey is a fake.

comment_text: What followed was a series of emails and moves to get Duffy out of the audit. The RCMP allege that Wright asked Gerstein to get in touch with a contact at Deloitte — a partner named Michael Runia — to see what was happening with the audit. By March 8, Wright had decided to pay the Duffy expenses himself and told his assistant, Chris Woodcock, about his decision. “….For you only: I am personally covering Duffy’s $90K…” he emailed Woodcock. The RCMP say Wright didn’t tell Harper about the “minutiae” of Duffy’s repayment, but that Harper was kept apprised of problems with Duffy’s expenses as the controversy increasingly became a political headache. At one point in the documents, the RCMP quote from a May 14 email from Wright where he says: “The PM knows, in broad terms only, that I personally assisted Duffy when I was getting him to agree to the expenses.” It isn’t clear from the documents what “personally assisted” means in this specific context. The documents says the 2,600 emails the investigative team has reviewed suggest “the Prime Minister was informed by his staff that they were working on a plan to have Senator Duffy repay expenses,” a plan contingent on Duffy not losing his Senate seat.

comment_text: 'When introducing the legislation, Harper stated that 'fixed election dates prevent governments from calling snap elections for short-term political advantage. They level the playing field for all parties and the rules are clear for everybody.' [7] However, despite the new legislation, the prime minister is still free to request an election at any time. As the Bill C-16 amendments to the Canada Elections Act clearly states 'Nothing in this section affects the powers of the Governor General, including the power to dissolve Parliament at the Governor General's discretion', the change effectively altered only the maximum duration of a parliament by ensuring that it ends no later than October of the fourth calendar year after its commencement, while leaving the possibility of an earlier end unaffected.[4]This situation was illustrated by the dissolution of parliament at Harper's request on September 7, 2008. This led Democracy Watch to initiate proceedings in federal court against the Crown-in-Council, the Prime Minister of Canada, and the Governor General of Canada, challenging the decision to call an election prior to the fixed election date. Judge Michel M.J. Shore dismissed the matter, saying the applicants who launched the suit 'do not demonstrate a proper understanding of the separation of powers,' since '[t]he remedy for the applicant's contention is not for the Federal Court to decide, but rather one of the count of the ballot box'.[8] The court effectively found that the fixed election dates were not binding on the prime minister or legally enforceable by the courts. With elections being held in October 2008 (after an early election call) and May 2011 (after a vote of non-confidence), no parliament has yet reached its maximum life. The election of a majority government in the May 2, 2011, general election makes it probable that the date of the next general election will be determined by the fixed-date section of the Canada Elections Act.[9][10][11] This would cause the next election to be on October 19, 2015.'-Wiki++++++++++++++++++++++++++++ Understand now, kids?

comment_text: Correct me if I am wrong, but it would appear that Margaret is arguing that we should keep the current system that we have, one where we have public and Catholic school boards (with parallel boards for French instruction which she is not discussing but also exist). If this is the case her conclusion is logically flawed. Margaret's premise is that we should have Catholic schools because their student outcomes are superior to the public board (a feeling that many on these comment sections seem to agree with). To explain why this is so, she presents 2 reasons (or at least in quoting a CD Howe study she does) and leaves one reason to be implied. None of these reasons supports her contention that we maintain the current system. The first is that Catholic schools are selective (“Maybe they’re more selective' quoted from the author of the CD Howe report). If you can control the inputs you have a better chance of improving the outcomes. However, the purpose of public funding of education is to educate all, not just those we select. If society feels that it is better to be selective then we should be looking at the abolishment of public funding for education and replacing it with a bursary or grant system. We shouldn't be looking at maintaining the current system. Secondly (and this is the one Margaret spends most of her time on) is the idea that competition makes the Catholic schools better. Left unsaid is why this same competition doesn't make the public schools better, but I'll leave that inconsistency aside for now. If that is the case, why is 2 the ideal number for competition? Wouldn't it make sense to completely do away with the two boards we currently have and go the charter school route? Then you would have real competition which would improve education even more dramatically. (By the way I am totally opposed to this, but I'm working within the constraints of Margaret's argument.)The third reason is implied. If Catholic schools are better it must have something to do with their catholic nature. Either Catholic values, Catholic culture, religious education, or something. If that is true then we are purposefully preventing 75% of our kids from getting a quality education by continuing to fund public schools. Margaret should not be arguing for maintaining the status quo, she should be arguing for abolishing the public boards. So, in conclusion, Margaret's argument is seriously flawed. By her logic we should be debating: 1) the existence of publicly funded school boards completely, 2)the abolishment of public and Catholic boards completely to be replaced with charter schools, or 3) the abolishment of the public board so that all kids could be taught by the superior Catholic board. Of course that would imply that there has ever been logic in Margaret's arguments.

comment_text: There is a widespread (and mistaken) belief that the top 1% of income earners are all 'wealthy', even though nothing could be further from the truth. It's not at all unusual for high income earners to have little to no net worth, thanks to their high debt loads. Also, most of these high income earners derive most of their income from salaries and do not have enough invested wealth to be able to retire in comfort. And even among those who own businesses and are among the highest 1% of income earners, most could not afford to play golf for the rest of their lives. In fact, there aren't that many people in this country who can be classified as truly 'wealthy' - ie. at least $5 million in invested wealth, although many would set the threshold much higher than that these days. Unfortunately, most of our Liberal and NDP politicians are more interested in pandering to the lowest common denominator than seeking to govern based on facts and common sense.

Arguably it is necessary to retain the PMO because of the modern need to have a central focus for the oversight of the political operations of the Federal Government (i.e. The fact that the PM alone, aided only by a Principal Secretary and one or two other staff, could perform this function fairly adequately until the 1960s no longer applies given the many diverse demands upon the PM’s time current scope of government and the 24 hour news cycle). Further, the fact that Jean Chrétien and now likely Stephen Harper have been brought down by the excesses of the PMO activities that each was responsible for to both Parliament and the public is evidence that accountability exists (but not that it operates in a timely and adequate fashion).The problem, in other words, is that Parliament and the public allow matters related to PMO excess to metastasize and fester too long before the PM in question (and therefore the Party that PM leads) at the time is called upon to account politically. This is a problem that can be rectified by an alert public, press and media if only we disabuse ourselves of the notion that ‘it’s only politics’ or, if our Party is in power, by partisan motivated excuses (such as that the other guys did the same or worse).The fact that PMO related scandals were instrumental in bringing down (and darkening the reputations) of one (and probably two) very recent PMs and their Governments should be a serious caution to the next Government (and encourage the media and Opposition MPs to challenge be on the lookout for signs of future excesses before the balloon to Adscam or Duffygate proportions). There is, however, no procedural fix that will automatically keep a PMO contained within its proper scope and conduct; That is the role of a vibrant and vigilant democracy.

Lebanon has been combating ISIS forces on the ground near its border to prevent them from spreading southward from Syria. By any civilized measure, ISIS has committed crimes against humanity and war crimes. Mass executions of prisoners, genocide of people who have other religious or ethnic backgrounds, brutal beheadings of people who were no threat to them and capturing women and girls as slaves – does none of this move the NDP’s sense of justice and social responsibility? Given the history of what they oppose, what they support and what they fail to speak out on; it stands to reason the NDP is opposed to stronger anti-terrorism measures. His latest excuse to do nothing; striking ISIS in Syria will only assist Assad, misses priority number one defeating the far more dangerous enemy and they have to be attacked where they are. It is time Canadians start to ask hard questions about exactly what the NDP and Liberals stand for.

comment_text: In April 2011, during the previous federal election campaign, StatCan announced a spectacular increase in the CPI inflation rate from 2.2% in February to 3.3% in March. Much of this increase was a one-shot boost due to the exit effect of hotel prices coming down in Vancouver in March 2010, the month following the Winter Olympics. This was incompetently explained at best in the CPI release. It was worse because unlike every other country in the Anglo-Saxon world, from Ireland to the United States, Canada does not publish component contributions to change for consumer price series, so no journalist could have gleaned from published tables how Vancouver hotel prices falling back to normal levels a year ago would have affected the inflation rate. Jack Layton immediately started attacking the Conservatives for letting inflation get out of control in his stump speeches. Whether this was due to malevolence or simple incompetence on the part of StatCan is unclear. However, at least the appearance of anti-Conservative bias in our civil service and the lack of transparency with which it operates could keep the Liberals in power for years if not decades to come. Canada is at best a one-and-a-half party state that may be on its way to becoming a one-party state.

comment_text: Both of our son's were enrolled in early french immersion programs in Toronto. Both returned to the english stream. One in grade 2, the other in grade 9. Both, still in high school, struggle with reading and writing in english. We were the classic naive parents, thinking we were doing what was best for our sons. In hindsight, it was a mistake that many of today's parents are certain to repeat. We found the teachers in the English stream, as a group, superior to the French Immersion teachers. French Immersion teachers are difficult to find in Toronto. A large number were students themselves in French Immersion. French is not their first language and it effects their ability to teach. I would not recommend that parent's today enroll their child in French Immersion unless French is spoken as the language of choice in the home. In this way the child truly is immeresed in the language.

comment_text: I taught in junior, middle and high schools in Canada and the UK for 35 years. Good, bad or indifferent, every student who arrived at my door got the same degree of attention from me, or at least that was my intention. In fact 'problem' students got more of it,the kids with learning, behaviour or language problems. Sometimes, as a parent myself, I kind of resented the situation. I was paying the same education tax dollars so why should my own kids get short-changed just by being in an unstreamed class? But that's just the way it is when there are no gate-keepers. So I think both side of Ms Wente's argument are valid for parents. A true bilingual education I see as an asset for any student in any country. European travellers are often amazed at the widespread use of English in every country, even France. But there is no doubt that FI also acts as a streaming device. That being said, you would get the same effect were you to initiate an Arts school, or a math or science school. I did teach in a 'public school'in Britain for a brief period where the streaming devices were primarily money and dialect. No real problem students and super field trips and interesting parent interviews, but really no better test results. Oh yes, much easier on the teachers too!

comment_text: Dear Mr. Simpson, thank you for paying some attention to this problem! It is indeed not a very 'sexy' issue, certainly not for politicians trying to get elected. Taking the long view, the decades-long view, pays very little reward in the near future. And yet, this is arguably the central task of government: to spend public money responsibly within the bounds imposed by the limits of its income, taxation. This or that particular minor policy excepted, at the end of the day it's how governments spend money that counts, that enables (or not) all other policy. If we had limitless funds, we could afford limitless green energy, limitless infrastructure, limitless social policies. But we don't, so we have to make choices. When a government like the Liberals chooses to spend far beyond the income it has, this is a form of cheating. With situations like war or national emergencies excepted, spending more than one takes in is stealing money away from future generations. (Spending billions to gain the votes of a particular group, and millions in campaign advertising, in this case that of the public sector unions, is even worse: corruption.) And not just future, the Liberals' actions over the last ten years already cost us huge, huge sums of money in interest on debt: $165 billion new debt * 4% (typical long-term bond yield) = $6.6 billion/year. Imagine what we could do with an additional $6.6 billion per year! To reiterate (all figures can be found on the Ontario Ministry of Finance website: 2003-2004 - $139 billion debt2013-2014 - $304.4 billion debtTotal new Liberal debt: $165.4 billion, an increase of 119%.

comment_text: I am and have always been opposed to big wind. But I find much of the commentary against wind extraordinarily hypocritical and uninformed about the effects of alternative sources of generation. It is as though for the first time, Ontarians are beginning to realize that energy consumption has environmental impacts! Go and read an impact statement for a typical large-scale hydro project, and you will see how raptor nests are regularly relocated and how high quality habitat is regularly flooded. Go and visit Kentucky to see the effects of strip coal mining, or visit the boreal forests to see the effects of acid rain and methylmercury deposition due to coal burning. Go visit northeastern BC to see what (un)natural gas really does to the landscape and particularly to the populations of predators like raptors. It seems all that southern Ontarians want is energy with no impacts, which really means no impacts that we have to deal with.

comment_text: Great to see such a column and great to see the comments here. I think that we should remember that at the core of conservative thought is a valid idea: there ARE some things that it is tough for government to accomplish. It IS very hard for government to solve economic, financial, and commercial problems. The flaw in conservative thinking is to take that acknowledged fact and extrapolate it into nonsense: 'So, government should stay out of everything. It shouldn't intervene in anything, in any way. The major actors outside of government should be left alone in every respect, to do what they want in the way that they want.' This eager laissez-faire impulse arises in certain minds, the psychological centres of which are oriented toward ego, and selfishness, and self-centredness. Some people are just like that. All of us have a little of it in us sometimes. But it is this hardness that has taken over conservative ideology. Moderate conservatives recognized that government has some limitations while accepting that thinking fairly, broadly, and collectively was still necessary in many things. The range of rational political thought plays between what needs to be done by government and what needs to left alone with the goal of the best life for every single person. In other words, the range of opinion that excludes complete state control of everything, as an ideal, and no state intervention at all as the ideal at the other end. In modern Western world politics, socialists have generally learned the lessons of moderation of views away from absolutism. Conservatives have not. And it is in the nature of their emotional impulse that they never will. At bottom, the two are driven in different ways: The socialist thinks 'What's good for you is good for me.' The reactionary conservative thinks, 'What's good for me is good for everyone.'

What distinguishes the welfare state from a Ponzi scheme is the idea that, unlike suckers, there will always be a next generation. I for one don't look forward to being propped up for a couple of years at the end enjoying only one bath a week. comment_text: Harper is a fanatic who represents relatively few Canadians. Canada is a solidly centre-left country. But there are too many centre-left parties and, given the nature of Canadian democracy, they are splitting the vote too many ways, making it possible for Harper to win. In the last election, the late surge by the NDP siphoned away enough support from the Liberals to make it possible for Harper to win a majority - something that no one expected and which was probably a real aberration. In the next election, the people on the centre-left have to start voting strategically. If we want to save Canada from the corruption and abuse that Harper and his cronies have heaped upon it, voters have to vote smartly, not with ideology. Vote for the candidate in your riding who has the best chance of defeating the Conservative. Period. If Canada had a proportional representation system, we would never have been saddled with a Conservative government at all and Harper would have stayed in the basement, along with the ideological fringe that he represents. Bringing in such a system should be a major consideration of any future parliament. Unfortunately, the Liberals (in particular) believe that they can win by the present system and are averse to modifying a system that has served them well in the past. I hope that they do not have to lose another election to bring them to their senses. Harper is far too dangerous and destructive to continue in power. The level of sheer corruption and abuse of power we are seeing from him today is unprecedented. We can only imagine how much worse it will get if he and his PMO are given more time. BTW, Mr. Simpon's characterization of Harper as a control freak only underlines why it is so implausible that he did not know anything about the Duffy scandal. If he did not know, it is because he chose not to know. That is the only reasonable explanation, given the kind of person Harper has clearly established he is.

comment_text: Wente's first sentence: 'I actually feel a little sorry for the Royal Bank of Canada.' is already her first mistake. comment_text: I keep seeing this tired old argument... 'If you want the cheapest priced goods, you have to expect jobs to be exported overseas.'First of all, real earning power has stagnated for the last 20 years. In fact, many people actually earn less, when you take inflation into account, than they did 20 years ago. So those goods probably cost as much as or more than, in terms of percentage of income, than the same goods of 20 years ago did. Second, many of us are quite willing to pay more for quality, but we just can't find it any more. Things like appliances and stereos actually used to last a long time (I still use a stereo that I bought in 1983) so the cost per year of use was actually less than the cost of a modern cheap unit. Ever wonder why there's such a market for vintage things on eBay? Because people are fed up with the cheap crap that breaks down after just a year. We don't all want the cheapest bargain, but the retailers don't offer anything else.

comment_text: This is the most superficial and poorly considered bit of writing on the subject of 'self-censorship' that I have read--in the last several days, constituting our examination of the Charlie Hebdo events. No, you should not self-censor out of fear. But, yes, there is a social expectation that individuals will not make a pastime or a profit of abuse of others' sensibilities. That's the formula that lets us get along. It has been in operation for the two hundred thousand years of existence of homo sapiens sapiens and, arguably, longer still, if we imagine the societies of ancestor ape species. It happens, but it is never endorsed as acceptable by a society. All of that is why Charlie Hebdo was allowed to publish the things that they published, but also why normal people filter what they say in order not to discomfit others unnecessarily. I may disagree with people on matters of belief (I disagree with virtually everyone on matters of belief), but I like being able to talk with them, enjoy a coffee together ... whatever. There is a funny-bone element to our individual psyches that predisposes almost all of us, in varying degrees, to laugh at the misfortune of others. It reinforces hierarchy and structure by accentuating general differences in levels of different kinds of competence. There is a similar tendency to laugh at difference; this one reinforces tribal strength and power development. A properly socialized person recognizes those tendencies and reins them in. That is done, not out of fear, but it is done to help the society operate. For better or worse, our 'society' is a global one. Much humour operates, therefor, by putting down those who CAN BE put down. Much satire has the effect of making its targets look like less and by fomenting collective ridicule and denigration of the targets. It is NEVER wrong to say, 'I don't support Islamic (or Catholic, or Jewish) ideas because ...' If there is something that you find wrong ... say it. But to make a cheap joke to put someone down and to profit from that ... it's wrong. All individuals and all media entities have the legal right (in Western democracies) to do just that. They almost never do. Both of those things are as they should be. If rights are abridged, we don't get to see what people call 'normal' and we can't understand what's going on around us. But it is definitely right and appropriate for an individual or a newspaper to say, 'No, we're not going to show that; it's unnecessarily inflammatory; how does it help rational public discourse?'In my view, bridling at the whole idea of 'self-censure' reflects an unhealthy degree of insecurity and lack of maturity and judgement. It's adolescent. We have to allow every bit of press freedom and general freedom of expression as we can. But responsible people and news media have to think very hard about abusing the right. Where we impose very strong limits on expression, we can't examine our society and our efforts to improve it.

comment_text: Clifford Orwin provides a fallacious argument. Two points. First, the requirement to show one's face in the citizenship ceremony is not an attack on religious freedom, and, second, Orwin's argument that Harper is appealing to collectivistic jingoism by requiring inductees into Canadian citizenship to show their faces is false. On the first point, we need to recognize that inherent in the norms of a liberal democracy is the valuation of the individual and of the identity of the individual. People become citizens as individuals, not as members of specific named groups. The niqab sublimates the identity of the individual into that of the religious group, which subsumes her identity. In a liberal democracy, such a thing is generally unacceptable, especially in a citizenship swearing-in ceremony. On the second point, which is anyhow related to the first, the requirement to show one's face forces a recognition of the primacy of the individual as the holder of citizenship. It has nothing to do with jingoism, or collectivist fantasies, or whatever, despite the loaded terms that Orwin uses here. comment_text: I feel ambivalently about Wente's column. On one hand, I've seen plenty of slackers in government union shops. However, I also see a lot of dedicated workers who bring their best to the workplace every day. A lot of the absenteeism can certainly be ascribed to the slackers. However, there is a distinct lack of morale in many government offices because they are often seen as the easy pickings for their cash strapped employers, even though the same employers are willing to spend obscene amounts of money on their pet projects (F35 jet fighters, gas generating plant closures, wind energy subsidies, etc.). Also, the politicians themselves have by far the richest gold-plated pension plans in the world, far surpassing anything the public service has. Granted, the defined benefit pension plan is probably dead. The unfunded liabilities ensuing from such plans have effectively bankrupted a few municipalities in the US. Nonetheless, perhaps the politicians themselves could take a leadership role with regard to their own perks and maybe they can look at ways to reduce the waste that their little politcal pet projects represent.

comment_text: Yes I am a medical student and yes this article bothers me. I agree with many of the comments issued by Hintobean. In terms of having real-life experiences and failures of our own, many of us have many. Some of us have few. To offer my own anecdotes: I have experienced being so broke I could not afford food; being estranged from family (you can use your imagination to come up with why that might be the case); having to leave school part-way through my undergraduate degree due to a serious illness; multiple deaths of friends my age and younger. I actually did carefully think through my decision to go to medical school, prior to applying. Being a doctor is an immense privilege--you are granted trust and respect by virtue of your position, and patients will grant you access to some of the most vulnerable parts of their bodies and minds, so you can do what's possible to ease their suffering. Medical school is certainly not for everybody, but for me, I can't think of a more valuable and rewarding life path.

If a woman would like to be a Canadian and also desires to honor her religion by wearing a niqab, it is reasonable to expect her to demonstrate some flexibility and compromise (another Canadian value). It is reasonable to ask that niqab's be removed when engaging with the government and particularly for services such as a Citizenship swearing in.

comment_text: Its possible that Trump's success has nothing to do with his policies or his temperament. It could be that people are fed up with the ever increasing size of government. We know Trump won't be able to implement some or all of his supposed policies. (or even decipher them) But they don't mind. Some people don't want government to increase its continual encroachment into the sphere of our personal lives. For the past decade(s) government has appeared to get larger in the US. The ever increasing debt is proof of that. Perhaps we also don't want government to champion issues and concepts which historically were 'personal' issues only discussed in our personal lives. The rise of 'identity' politics, 'equality' politics and increasing levels of politically correct 'group think' championed by governments which make many intelligent and educated people wonder (quietly to themselves) if we are actually watching the closing of the 'north American' mind. We can't debate issues or even 'unpack' them anymore for fear that we will be labelled some sort of unpleasant 'deplorable'. We apparently can't even debate the use or misuse of pronouns anymore without fear that government sponsored agencies will get involved in an effort to somehow correct and re-educate any departure from the 'approved script'. Trump isn't an ideologue. He isn't going to tell us what to think. Most of us are able to do that ourselves. He doesn't care about progressive or regressive politics. He doesn't likely care what 'the church' thinks, or what planned parenthood thinks. In the Trump world, those are private issues. Do what you want but pay for it yourself. The public might be fedup with government appearing to lead us by 'taking sides' and subtly promoting agendas with public funds. The uneducated masses may actually be rejecting the government led ideologies. They want to go back to a time when government actually debated issues of substance and worked out an affordable compromise. A Trump presidency will certainly give rise to heated debates and it probably offers the subtle promise of less intrusion in our lives.

comment_text: As a father of a 13 year old boy I would like to recommend to any parent enrolling your kids in the Canadian Forces Cadets program. My son was initially nervous but we forced him to sign up. (Sometimes kids have to be pushed out of their comfort zone for their own good... it's called parenting.). The cadets even get paid a small amount to attend so they can earn some money. Camps are offered in a variety of specializations with opportunities for overseas travel to Europe and Australia for senior cadets. They age out of the program at 19 but can start as early as 12. I'd rather have my son learning valuable life skills and making life long friendships than wasting his youth playing video games. Might be worth mentioning that the males / female ratio seems to be about 50/50 and girls are actively promoted into leadership roles along with boys based on numbers of years in the program. He is even taking school academics more seriously now. I can't recommend the program enough.

comment_text: While much of Ron Paul's platform was incredibly simplistic, his arguments that there is a limit to US 'force projection' in the world were absolutely spot on. The late CIA analyst and author Chalmers Johnson argued much the same thing in his book 'Blowback'.However, Mr. Simpson is entirely correct in his argument that every government faces the same reality: inertia followed by soft corruption and 'troughing' leading to eventual dumping. It's important to note just how wrong pre-election polls have been lately, in Alberta, in Quebec, in the US and even in Israel's recent election. Each featured a last-week shift that went against the perceived notion. Wildrose was denied despite being far ahead; The PQ was denied a majority despite clear fatigue with Charest's Liberals; Obama prevailed despite lacklustre support and anaemic approval ratings, and Netanyahu was completely denied the clear victory that was supposed to be a sure thing. Anyone who thinks Harper is safe due to perceived vote-splitting or Liberal weakness is 'whistling past the graveyard'. The new normal for voters may well be 'when in doubt, throw them out.'

comment_text: This topic is certainly worthy of further discussion. Wente raises some valid points that have been raised by many in the past. I certainly think this is a situation where some 'outside the box' thinking might work wonders. As a former police officer who bailed for the private sector after eight years, I certainly saw waste, inefficiency and over-staffing. However, at times, I also found myself as the only available patrol car in the south half of a city of over a million. One thing to consider. I have travelled extensively, and police corruption is common throughout the world. Where I'm living now, the police, all three levels, are rife with corruption. I am a victim at least twice a year. In Calgary, not only did I not witness corruption in my eight years on the job, I never even heard rumour of it. I have no doubt if someone in my district was shaking down citizens, he would have been arrested by his or her partner if found out. Heck, our district inspector was even arrested for impaired driving by a junior constable from his own district following an accident. Therefore, I assume that, just like judges, one of the reasons Canada has a fairly above board justice system is due, in part, to the high pay.

comment_text: I am married to a Belgian and I have spent a lot of time there both for pleasure and for work. I can say without question the place is one of the most racist countries I have come across. Because someone is a socialist, it doesn't make them benign or liberal for that matter. Unlike Canada or the UK where I lived along time or Hong Kong where I currently live, you rarely come across someone who is Flemish or Wallon that has a friend who is not from their own community. It is a very very provocial place which is partly explaied by the fact that everyone is still living in the same village of their ancestors. When my wife's uncle did the family tree, he traced it back to the 16th century and everyone (with the exception of one Dutchman) was from 4 or 5 villages all within walking distance of each other (albeit it could be an hour or two by foot). That is the norm. It also means that people speak radically different dialects within 5 minutes car ride from each other. My wife's family is from the east and they can barely understand the people from the west of the country which is a little over an hour car drive away. The place is very fragmented which contributes to the lack of national identity (which is mostly caused by the French and Dutch divide). But it's kept that way as unlike most countries where the march to the cities drove a national identity by stamping out regional differences or at least muting them, Belgian is so small that people just stay in their villages and commute to work in Brussels or Antwerp or frankly pretty much anywhere from there. It's great in a way as you keep your family and friends but it also means you are not willing to make new ones. So Margaret's article is complete rubbish. Belgian is completely about exclusion and isolation. It is not a mosaic or melting pot of different nationalities. It's a fragmented country of tiny communities all speaking different dialects and very distrusting of each other, no matter foreigners.

comment_text: I agree with Prof. Bliss. However it is with considerable reservations. The House of Commons can be controlled by a plurality of voters (typically 40%) who can elect a majority for one party. The Prime Minister holds inordinate authority over the MPs in his party. This concentration of power has and will continue to lead to abuses of power. The Senate, provided that it is reformed in a way that limits the Prime Minister's ability to appoint his political allies to it, can act as a counterweight to the Prime Minister. If Canada adopts a system of proportional representation so that no party can have a majority thereby forcing the Prime Minister to share power with other parties, I can heartily agree with abolishing the Senate.

comment_text: I buy the Bliss' argument that an elected Senate wouldn't work, but his argument for why developing a better appointment process wouldn't work is weak. It's not clear why we couldn't arrive at a more intelligent selection process. Several worthwhile ones have already been proposed. Conrad Black's suggested framework is enticing. Senators appointed from 3 equal groups: 1) federally as is, 2) provincially, 3) a commission that would seek the 50 or 60 most distinguished Canadians of all serious occupations. Appointees from the third group, if not the second, would certainly command the legitimacy that appointed judges maintain. The legitimacy and prestige of the last two groups would likely drive up that of the first. The ensuing lift in character of discussion and increased quality of appointment would isolate and discourage the partisan silliness we see today. And to suggest Mike Duffy was ever considered a 'high-quality appointment at the time' is delusional. That appointment was lambasted for its terrible judgment at the time and has proven out so. There was some positive reaction to Pamela Wallin's appointment at the time, but just as much mixed reviews about the appropriateness of the appointment, and there were not insignificant rumblings about her excessive expenses at previous posts that should have given pause.

comment_text: The defence did not ask for an independent psychiatric evaluation? The defence lawyer himself asked for 50 years without parole? I find it almost impossible to conclude that the interests of justice have been served in this case. Given the inexplicable nature and gravity of the crime; the defendant's unusual behavior in the year prior to committing the offence; and the precedent-setting sentence that was meted out, I believe that an injustice has occurred. This is true whether Mr. Bourque himself did not want an independent psychiatric evaluation, and instructed his lawyer accordingly. Scenario: you're an ordinary Canadian. For reasons unknown you have a psychotic episode and commit a grave crime. After the psychotic episode is over, you're horrified by what you perpetrated. Feeling deep remorse and guilt, you resist efforts to find out why things went wrong and accept whatever onerous sentence is handed out. Consider the case of Quebec cardiologist Guy Turcotte. Following the break-up of his marriage in 2009, Dr. Turcotte murdered his children in a horrific manner. The jury at his trial rendered a verdict of 'not criminally responsible due to mental disorder (adjustment disorder with anxiety and depressive moods.)' Dr. Turcotte's legal problems aren't over, but as of today he's a free man. The psychological episode that induced him to kill his children has passed, and he is no longer deemed a danger to the public. I invite you to compare Dr. Turcotte's situation with that of Justin Bourque. As a man of means, and of previously sound reputation, Dr. Turcotte was able to convince the justice system that he wasn't guilty of first degree murder. In Justin Bourque's case, neither his lawyer nor the trial judge seriously explored the possibility that a mental disorder precipitated or contributed to the crime. Justin Bourque received a sentence so severe it has no precedent in the Canadian legal system. For that to happen without every conceivable effort being exerted to ensure no miscarriage of justice has occurred, is no justice at all. Guy Turcotte and Justin Bourque- two very different faces of the Canadian justice system. Would someone like to explain?

Then again, maybe that's the Conservatives' real plan all along: to disgust so many voters with these deflection tactics to the point we'll refuse to take part, leaving their core group of petty, angry, frightened supporters free to tell the rest of us how we're going to do things their way because hey, 'the people have spoken.' Well, it's not going to work. I'm still coming out to vote. And I hope everyone else does, too.

comment_text: But Margaret absenteeism is up everywhere. Thats due to a number of factors - aging parents, more women in the workforce with family responsibilities, more stress at work. You make it sound like Public Servants (in the Federal Public Sector they number almost 300, 000) are out of work lolling about eating bon bons. How many of those people are really ill? Or have to take time off to deal with family issues? I am a retired Public Servant who had hundreds of days banked when I retired. Thats because I was rarely off. Before going into the Public Service I had worked in the private sector - with no sick leave. So when I was off, I lost my pay. I was a single mother with no other income but what I earned. So when my kids were ill - which was also rare (thank goodness) or I had to take them to their annual physical or go to my own annual I lost pay. And you think this is a good thing? I had over 150 staff in my last Public Service job and I can honestly say that I did not see any abuses. If they had a real reason for being off we assumed they should be off. They were treated as adults not like someone trying to game the system. I dunno why public servants are always assumed to be slackers who get too much for too little. I can tell you that I worked my tail off for what I made. As did my colleagues. We earned what we made and the some. In the senior ranks the midnight oil burns nightly. We were the first to arrive in the early hours and stay late into the evening. Thats just part of the job. There has been low morale for some time and as the government/Minister/Deputy Minister of the day changes so change the rules under which we work. Its a job in constant transition at the whim of whomever is 'running the show'. We are under constant pressure to meet the demands of that Minister and his/her office at a moment's notice. Sometimes with unrealistic expectations to a deadline that would make anyone 'sick'.A Conservative government has traditionally loathed Public Servants as they assume most are closet Liberals. So they go about the business of playing to their own base by cutting jobs and imposing tougher and tougher sanctions. All designed to show their public how they've taken on those Ottawa fat cats. Funny thing is - many of those same Public Sector jobs are held by Conservatives in their own ridings. Many of whom entered Government 'service' because they believe in the work and love what they do. Too bad we rarely get the opportunity to express that and instead have to read articles like this one about how we are sucking off the public 'teat'. Nothing could be further from the truth.

comment_text: Interesting to read the majority of the comments criticizing this article. Reading through it, as a recent medical residency graduate, I thought that almost every single sentence hit the nail on the head for what my experience with medicine has been like. I don't even remember what answer I gave when asked why I wanted to go to medical school, but that fear and wanting job and financial security was a major factor. That, and the overall sense that, having been on top of the academic food-chain, the default option was to aspire to something prestigious like medicine without ever truly asking myself WHY. It was what I thought I SHOULD want. I'd like to, at some point, find a non-clinical career use for my MD. Money is not a factor for me, as long as I can pay off my loans and live comfortably, but as the author mentioned the debt and time investment make it nigh impossible to get out clinical medicine should you find yourself discovering that it isn't for you. I'm not bad at my job by any means. In fact, my feedback has all been that I'm quite good at it. I like (most of) my patients, I always try to be friendly and empathetic, but the overall job has left me cold. Having entered this profession for 'wrong' reasons (or mostly, just without really thinking it through) I'm quite burnt out and would love do something else, but feel trapped. For anyone thinking about medicine, you really have to love patient care, and be ok with your career being high-stress, high-debt, long hours and generally taking up the majority of your free time. Know what you're signing up for.

comment_text: Being a professor in health sciences working in a hospital, I've written quite a few reference letters for students applying for medical school and I think the article touches on some good points. Namely the desire to go that route out of prestige and fear of not knowing what else to do. The medical profession is a 'white-collar trade' because once you're in medical school your career path is set. It provides a comfort of knowing that you won't have to search for a career and it is a career at the top of the food chain. Is this wrong to aspire to that? Maybe not as I'm sure most of us would have wished to avoid the years after graduating searching for a career. I don't see many students going in it for the money, but that desire for more money comes into play once doctors start practicing given the fee-for-service way doctors are paid. In reality, a senior nurse in a hospital, adding in all the benefits, can make more than a community family physician who has to pay for an office assistant and clinic overhead. The one thing that I don't think prospective medical students understand is that once you start practicing as a doctor, that is what you will be doing for the rest of your career. Day one on the job isn't much different than the last day on the job. For most doctors there is no advancement, no reward for doing a good job and no lateral moves in career path like other jobs. Again this suits many people just fine but a number of doctors leave the field because of this to move on to other careers.

comment_text: Mr. Trudeau's paid speaking engagements will not merit a mention in historical accounts of the evolution of our democratic institutions. Neither will the conduct of Miss Wallin, Mr. Duffy, Mr. Brazeau, Mr. Harb or Mr. Wright. What will be noted is the destruction by Mr. Harper of one of the cornerstones of our democracy, the daily question period. From the initial parliament to the beginning of the current one, question period has been a short daily allotment of parliamentary time, to the opposition, to allow questioning of the government on the most important issues of the day and to hold the government to account for its conduct of public business. Ministers and parliamentary secretaries are not permitted to ask questions and the speaker rarely recognizes government backbenchers who rise during question period. Commonly questions from those backbenchers are a staged opportunity for a minister to make a statement and the sham is quickly ruled out of order by the speaker. Historically speakers have not allowed prime ministers or ministers to encroach on opposition time by straying off the subject of a question or by giving overly long but evasive answers. Unfortunately the current speaker since Mr. Harper has had a majority has allowed him to make question period more deplorably partisan than ever before in our history. Lately the prime minister and his ministers have been permitted to attach to unresponsive answers gratuitous attacks on Mr. Mulcair and Mr. Trudeau which no previous speaker would have allowed. Many people no longer expect Mr. Harper. his ministers or his speaker to act in accordance with decent principles. But what is disconcerting is the haste with which the press pounces on others but fails to condemn Mr. Harper and his minions for damage they are doing to our democratic institutions. Shame on Mr. Harper. Shame on Mr. Speaker. And shame on the Globe and Mail

comment_text: Margaret Wente’s article seems to show a lack of understanding of the topic she is writing about. 1- She implies that firefighters works part-time because they only work 1 out every 4 days. What that works out to is a 42 hour week which is more hours than the average Canadian worker works. Assuming the same standard applies to all Canadians is she implying that most Canadians work part time? 2- She does not seem to understand the 24 hour shift as it is more of an advantage to the city than the firefighter. While the advantage to the firefighter seems obvious the advantage to the city is not mentioned. The 24 hour shift cuts to on overtime paid out at shift changes as it cuts the number of shift changes in half. It also discourages booking off on sick time as a firefighter now losses 24 hours from is/her sick bank if they book off instead of an average of 12 on other schedules. It also cuts administration costs connected to shift changes in half. 3- Yes the number of fire calls are down but she does not factor other areas firefighters respond to such as, medical calls, hazardous material, water rescue, ice rescue …etc. In some cities such as Montreal the amount of overall calls has actually increased in the last ten years. 4- The comparison to a nurse is unfair as a firefighter’s job is physically harder and they operate in dangerous environments which the average person does not. Even when not at a fire the job is physically demanding, just try walking up 10 flights of stairs in turnout gear carrying high rise packs in the middle of summer. 5- What also has to factor in is the increase of the insurance FUS rating that would come with a cut back in firefighters. Whereas the city would save expenses in cutting firefighters the actual citizen would see an increase in insurance premiums. A tax payer on a tight budget just barely making ends meet may not be able to afford this increase and may have to cut the coverage.

comment_text: 'Income-splitting is supposed to help “hard-working taxpayers,”Wrong! This tax measure was never designed to benefit anyone, rather it was designed to balance an inequitable tax equation. The argument is that income splitting will only benefit wealthy families. How is a dual income family with two income earners each making $50,000 any different than a single income family with an income of $100,000? Hopefully you said the $100,000 single income family has less take-home pay. While both families (and let's say they both have 4 kids to keep things even) earn $100,000 per year, the fact is that the $100,000 single income is taxed at a higher marginal rate than $50,000. Stripping all credits out other than the basic amount to which everyone is entitled, the tax paid by the dual income family will be roughly $16,000 whilst the tax paid by the single income family will be closer to $24,000 (that factors in the basic credit for the spouse). Even if the maximum credit for the income splitting was achieved for the single income family, they would still be on the hook for $22,000 in tax. All income splitting was ever designed to do is try an balance the equation... and rightly so too.

comment_text: There is much deeper set of issues than simply one of teachers' unions protecting their own members, particularly when they feel under siege because of declining enrolments, rising parent dis-satisfaction, and constrained budgets. All unions do this, it is why they exist. First, the notion of 'professionalism' is twofold - first, a commitment to doing good work, and second, a body of knowledge and proven experience that defines the 'profession'. Teachers, most of them, do the first well, they profess a desire for excellence. Teachers as a profession do not easily fit the traditional definitions of what is a 'profession'. Hence, there is always a tension, a need to prove' one's worth. Second, too often teachers' professional bodies and their unions are one organization. There is no balance between demonstrating and furthering the 'profession' and 'professional' with acting in solidarity with members, and protecting negotiated rights, often cumbersome. Third, teachers are 'socialized' (i.e. they select themselves, and are professionally trained) to see the classroom as their 'private castle', where they hold all power, without being (overly) constrained by the outside (i.e. parents, school boards, and ministries of education). There are lots of examples of this such as resistance to cross province testing, recommendations for compulsory continuing education, reviews by principals).Until teachers decide that: (i) it is the school as a whole and the partnerships with parents, not just their classroom and themselves, that matter in children's learning, nothing much will change. and (ii) professional development and self regulation need to be kept separate from employee rights and union solidarity, nothing much will change.

comment_text: Quite correct that unions and government make it next to impossible to fire incompetent teachers. However, how does the Alberta proposal for periodic recertification (i.e. putting in place additional administrative hoops requiring pieces of paper that are meaningless to job competency), or metrics tied to standardized testing (favours not the best teachers, but rather those who can most effctively teach to the test, as well as schools who can manipulate results trending over time) in any way address this issue? It's not just teachers in the US who are rebelling against standardized tests, it's parents (i.e. customers), typically after they read some of the actual questions they ask on those tests. In business, if you want to weed out incompetency, you don't put all employees (good and bad alike) through non-value added recertification or metrics exercises (costly and time consuming!), you get rid of the bad ones and reward the best ones, based on subjective management assessments. How is the Alberta proposal doing anything of the sort? In a way, the Alberta teachers are right - the government plan is designed to simply make their lives more unpleasant, and create more paper that an administrator can point to and say 'aha' when they want to build a case to get rid of someone. What they don't realize is that this is what management will do when union and administrative bureaucracies make it next to impossible to weed out poor performers and reward good ones. I'd be interested to know how easy it is to fire or discipline unionized workers in the private sector (e.g. General Motors) versus teachers. Not very much, I'd predict. The main difference is that companies don't bother with crap like certification and metrics, they simply move their operations offshore and lay the workers off. Another thing to keep in mind is, who then makes the decision about hiring and firing, the Principal? At my kid's school, there are some loser teachers for sure, but the worst of the bunch is the principal. The office doesn't even know how to send out a permission slip.

comment_text: The Titanic we call publicly funded health care hit an iceberg some years ago, and government after government rearranges the deck chairs as the ship lists and sinks deeper and deeper. This article, like many things written about health care, is superficial and unhelpful. Wasted opportunity and the Globe should be embarrassed. I expected more. As long as health care remains completely 'private' (other than the private system- drugs, health care for athletes and politicians, insurance health care, etc), the ship will eventually completely sink. It's simply not sustainable with such a gaping hole in it. But most people ignore it, until they get involved in the system, as a patient, and discover how horrendous things are (with a few exceptions). But then the patient gets better, and moves on. There are so many simple fixes, such as having physicians provide patients with bills, which would help stop physician overbilling and show people that health care is NOT free; linking up physicians and giving access to patients' records to avoid patient (and doctor) abuses (doctor/clinic shopping); and then, truly making health care a partnership by holding people accountable. And if you want physicians to play a role, keep the public system but allow the private side to grow also. It's so offensive that it is unlawful for a person to buy private care for OHIP services (and in my view, a much more egregious breach of my Charter rights than what the courts have supported). Unfortunately, I won't see change in my lifetime, as we lurch from election cycle to election cycle, with politicians hoping the ship doesn't completely sink on their watch Long term thinking is dead, and no one has the vision or guts to fix health care. I congratulate the doctors for sending the message to the politicians, and the OMA, that this is just not acceptable. The OMA executive has to step down and allow others to try to move the ball forward. However, the government will just ignore this, and impose its will on doctors, who are many of our smartest and talented people. And they will just take it (perhaps regretting they didn't go into investment banking, or throw a baseball, which is what society truly needs). It's time for all of us to stand up, face the mess we're in, and find solutions, not blame. Given that health is the most important thing we have.

comment_text: Doctor bashing is a popular sport in which journalists with no real ideas or knowledge can always engage. The real issue is the concept of 'free' health care where any demand for service is considered valid, and without limit. This is not supportable and year by year the taxes will be raised, the availability of service will be lowered, until finally the system is so broke it will have to be abandoned. Until such time journalists will complain about doctors, doctors will complain about administrators and governments, federal and provincial, will blame everyone but themselves. Ultimately what is required is a system of 'user pay' linked to capacity to pay for service received -- necessary health care should be readily available to everyone, but it is not 'free' and restricting its availability to control cost defeats the original intent of a health service.

comment_text: Besides your bit on Khan academy, did you do any research at all, or are you just spouting nonsense based on the emotions created by yesterday? One would have to be an idiot to be a teacher and not have union protection. Teachers are falsely accused of wrongdoing by students and parents all of the time. For every true miscreant jerk that abuses a child there are multiple cases of teachers accused of wrongdoing for no greater reason than a student didn't want to admit something to parents at home, so he makes something up about the teacher. Happens all of the time. Parents run directly to the Children's Aid Society and one in entangled in months long investigations. Having union legal, and emotional, help on your side is invaluable. You state that politicians are happy to comply with wage demands. How could this be since their ability to balance a budget has a significant impact on their reelection chances? You state that my work hours are strictly regulated. This is a lie. My work hours end at a variable time each evening when my work for the day is done. Specific tasks, such as daily instructional and supervision minutes are regulated, but certainly not the maximum amount of time it takes to finish my work for the day. In theory it could be 24 hours. Frankly teachers are not fully professionals, nor are they just hourly workers. It is an unusual arrangement. You say nobody gets fired, well that is not on the union. There is a process of notification and opportunity for improvement. If improvement does not occur, teachers can be fired. The union just insures that each member gets due process and is allowed the opportunity for improvement. If incompetent teachers, who refuse offers to improve, are not fired that is not on the union. No union member wants to work next door to an incompetent teacher. No union wants incompetent teachers teaching. Where you really fall apart is your insinuation that every child is treated the same. Did you interview any teacher, school board official, ministry representative? comment_text: From the article: 'They’ve vastly overstated what the science “says,” and treated anybody who is the least bit doubtful as the enemy.'=================This line, I think, sums things up quite well and I suspect that a lot of scientists (real scientists, not politicians pretending to be scientists) would tend to agree. The politicizing of this whole debate is hampering their ability to perform legitimate work. Many probably struggle to get funding unless their conclusions are expected to match some per-conceived notion of those providing funding want. In at least a few cases the raw data that so many scientists might use and normal assume is from a trusted source has ended up being tampered with which just leads to more skepticism and doubt, regardless of the findings. A pretty basic principle of science is 'garbage in, garbage out', if the raw data can't be trusted 100% then everything that comes afterwards is suspect. Unfortunately I don't see much of a solution to this. Most of the scientists out there will continue plugging away and doing their due diligence to try and come up with the very best information and understanding we are capable of, but the discussion will likely inevitably be dominated by political groups of one stripe or another. Maybe this is something that the U.N. (inevitably a political group in and of itself) should never have become involved with in the first place? Maybe governments should place limits on how corporate donations (particularly from interested parties like coal mining and power plants) to Universities are handled (presumably the Universities themselves have some code of ethics in place here, but is it enough?). Maybe politicians should never say 'the science is settle' because that is *NEVER* true for any real science, which is always evolving and growing. Or maybe we should all just step back for a second, take a deep breath and ignore all the hype from all parties involved.

comment_text: The main problem with Wade's book, and one that Ms. Wente overlooks, is that although there are genetic differences between people, none of those genetic differences correlate unambiguously with any racial group. So either you redefine race based on genetic differences, which means that race no longer means what people typically think it is, or the argument is wrong. The other problem is, of course, that the kind of subtle genetic variation that underlies complex traits takes much, much longer to cause significant changes in populations than the kinds of cultural characteristics about which Wade writes. So the two main points of the book are fatally flawed. It would be nice if people writing about the book knew enough to consider the fatal weaknesses in the thesis with a cogent discussion. Sigh.......

comment_text: Another typical Wente drive-by. She goes on about 'abortion absolutism,' then, except for a few crumbs here and there, solely blasts the pro-choice side. Here's the thing, Ms. Wente - I believe the vast, vast majority of pro-choicers are fine with defined limits on later-term abortions. I know I am. You don't hear of a bunch of feminists demanding the right to abort an eight and a half old fetus. The problem is that as soon as you even raise the possibility of changing the laws, the anti-abortion side of the coin will start pressing for their version of absolutism. I don't get a lot of sense that the anti-abortion side waves those signs and holds those demonstrations to get laws on late-term abortions - they want the practice outlawed, period (look at the US, where there are restrictions, and conservatives are constantly introducing new and creative laws to restrict it more). Given that possibility, a lot of people have concluded that the imperfect status quo is better than the possibility of heavy restrictions. I hope we can move beyond this in the not-too-distant future and legislate some limits, but it probably won't happen soon. No party wants to invest valuable political capital on such a divisive debate. If it becomes less divisive, maybe. And Trudeau should *not* have placed that restriction on Liberal candidates - he needed only say that party policy is pro-choice.
