comment_text: The Ian Leslie article was in response to the discovery of suppressed data in the Minnesota Coronary Experiment from the early 1970s. This study was not the run-of-the-mill observation study that looked for correlations in low-quality diet surveys to theory-based “risk factors” for heart disease, which are essentially Rorschach ink-blot tests for confirmation bias of the current theory. This study was very well designed randomized intervention trial based on objective cardiovascular outcomes (such as death from heart attack--the ultimate risk factor) that was expected to demonstrate conclusively that saturated fats (butter) were harmful and substituting them with polyunsaturated fats (margarine) would both reduce serum cholesterol and objective heart outcomes. In fact, it showed the opposite. Heart outcomes were a little worse and all-cause mortality was significantly worse. The results, however, were buried. Publishing them in 1973 would have been career suicide for the researchers. And this was not the only “gold standard” study that was buried. The Sydney Diet Heart study found the same result, and was buried. So we have a mountain of question-begging observational studies that do not show causation and we have gold standard intervention studies that disprove that polyunsaturated fats are healthier than saturated fats. Both gold standard studies showed that lowering serum cholesterol did not improve heart disease outcomes and, in fact, increased all-cause mortality. This comes hand-in-hand with the recent cancellation of the CETP-inhibiting drug phase 3 trial two weeks ago. The drug was supposed to be a miracle (under the cholesterol hypothesis for heart disease) because it both lowered LDL “bad” cholesterol by 37% and increased HDL “good” cholesterol by a whopping 126%--more than double. The result was … no change in heart outcomes. Yet again, lowering cholesterol had no cardiovascular benefit. But what of statins? The data indicate statins are only effective where there is already inflammation in the artery walls. The JUPITER study indicates that the only statin types that are effective are those that are anti-inflammatory. The ones that just lower cholesterol have no benefit. The inescapable conclusion is that serum cholesterol simply does not have a causal role in heart disease. Dr. Malcom Kendrick’s interpretation of the evidence has been right all along. The cholesterol hypothesis is finished. We are witnessing perhaps the largest seismic Kuhnian paradigm shift in the history of medicine.

For that reason, they often are not best positioned either to render judgment or to guard confidentiality. The fact that it is difficult to set up a fair process is not a reason to continue to avoid setting up such a process today.

comment_text: AESOP'S FABLE PCed: The ant works hard In the withering heat and the rain all summer long, building his house and laying up supplies for the winter. The grasshopper thinks the ant Is a fool and laughs and dances and plays the summer away. Come winter, the shivering grasshopper calls a press conference and demands to know why the ant should be allowed to be warm and well fed while he is cold and starving. CBS, NBC, PBS, CNN, and ABC show up to provide pictures of the shivering grasshopper next to a video of the ant in his comfortable home with a table filled with food. America is stunned by the sharp contrast. How can this be, that in a country of such wealth, this poor grasshopper is allowed to suffer so?Kermit the Frog appears as support on Oprah with the grasshopper and everybody cries when they sing, 'It's Not Easy Being Green...' ACORN stages a demonstration in front of the ant's house where the news stations film the SEIU group singing, We shall overcome. Then Rev. Jeremiah Wright has the group kneel down to prayfor the grasshopper's sake, while he damns the ants. President Obama condems the ant and blames President Bush 43, President Bush 41, President Reagan, Christopher Columbus, and the Pope for the grasshopper's plight. Nancy Pelosi & Harry Reid exclaim in an interview with Larry King that the ant has gotten rich off the back of the Grasshopper, and both call for an immediate tax hike on the ant to make him pay his fair share. Finally, the EEOC drafts The Economic Equity & Anti-Grasshopper Act Retroactive to the beginning of the summer. The ant is fined for failing to hire a proportionate number of green bugs and, having nothing left to pay his retroactive taxes, his home is confiscated by the Government Green Czar and given to the grasshopper. The story ends as we see the grasshopper and his free-loading friends finishing up the last bits of the ant's food while the government house he is in, which, as you recall, just happens to be the ant's old house, crumbles around them because the grasshopper doesn't maintain it. The ant has disappeared in the snow, never to be seen again. The grasshopper is found dead in a drug related incident, and the house, now abandoned, is taken over by a gang of spiders who terrorize the ramshackle, once prosperous and peaceful, neighborhood. The entire Nation collapses bringing the rest of the free world with it.

comment_text: first, this story doesn't speak in everyone Canadian's name. second, the whole fear/uncertainty is way overblown. This is about a group of people who don't identify with the political decisions from a central government that doesn't represent them anymore. It's not about NATO, it's not about the euro, the pound or whatever else. It's about making their own decisions. And the solution is to bring decisions closer to home. On this subject, Obama said 'if it ain't broken don't fix it'. Well, that explains the deadlock with Congress. Sure, it might not be 'broken' but it can certainly be 'improved'. If they vote YES (and it's up to them, not from anyone here who pretends to speak for everyone in Canada), then everyone will have the best interest to come up with a solution that is the least disruptive. Sure, people can act like kids and create more FUD. But I have a sense that if Scots don't want to go to Iraq, they want to make that decision. Their population gets to decide if they send their kids or not. Not some government far far away who has their own agenda. I don't believe in breaking up countries but when you're just not represented well enough and you don't get to control what is most important to you, you have to take that power back. And it doesn't mean ALL power. It just means that you have to redraw what decisions get to be taken where. And if London wants to act like a kid, then sure, borders will go up and they will lose even more. This won't happen. Just like, in Canada, there are things we share and things we decided to put at the provincial level; it makes no sense to force the postal workers in some rural town in Alberta town to speak French (perfect example of things that could be improved). So far, yes, we've done a great job at distributing power in Canada and I'd argue that the ROC should start to pull more power out of Ottawa and into their provinces but that's up to each province to do so. I'd think that together we are always stronger. But I don't believe in too much power in some central far-away central government. It makes sense to have a central food inspection lab, postal service and that kind of thing. But some decisions need to stay local... It's up to them to determine how to get that power back and how it should be shared going forward.

comment_text: If Canadian society truly cared about protecting children from abuse, we would go about things in a very different way than we are now. For instance, a pro-active approach would be the following. On the first day of school an accredited public health nurse would visit the classrooms of every child in the nation. And in that disarming and friendly way that PHNs are well-known for, they would explain to every child that no adult may ever intentionally cause them physical, emotional or sexual harm. That information would be explained in as much detail as necessary to get the message across to kids. And it would likewise be explained that society will protect every child from adults who try to hurt them in any of those ways- no matter who that adult may be. Even if it's their parents, a relative, a teacher, a priest or a total stranger. That procedure would apply to every single child in the nation, as a mandatory part of every schooling curriculum. Children who are home-schooled would have to meet with a PHN to receive the same information. That's what we'd do if we were really interested in protecting children. We wouldn't just sit back and punish the perpetrators of abuse after the fact. We would be pro-active in our approach, by providing children with sufficient knowledge and skills so that they can avoid or lessen the harm that some adults are willing to inflict on them. Do you really want to protect children? Or do you just want to stand back and rant about the perpetrators? So far, Canadian society chooses the latter.

comment_text: No, I do not believe this is as good as it gets. I believe it got 'as good as it was going to get' about twenty years ago, over all. At best, however, I believe there are limits to the SPEED of economic growth (we are seeing this now) and in the future, we will regard economic growth as a fabled concept while the world's economic indicators continue to diminish, year after year, rendering today's debate over 'growth' moot. I believe the reversal of growth--with its many immediate (mostly negative) effects--will be incremental. This will be a slow process rather than an overnight apocalyptic event. Two trends are converging: technology and its creation, Big Data, which effects people's lives in ways we can barely comprehend (yesterday, on the factory floor, today and tomorrow, inside every floor in every downtown steel-and-glass tower.) and our continued estrangement from the natural world, through plunder, poisoning and benign neglect. The result: natural calamity, food shortages and human displacement beyond our imaginings. Does this usher in, eventually, a slower-paced, bucolic society in which (western-world) people, having lost their zeal and rationale for forming technology's 'future frontiers' stop and smell the roses, instead? Don't believe so. Most people didn't stop too long to smell many roses 120 years ago, as the 1800s became the 1900s (what many consider to be the start of the truly 'modern' technological era.) Many were too busy trying to survive. Our grandchildren may be preoccupied in a similar way.

comment_text: For a change of pace... the phrase is 'beckon call', not 'beck and call'. Now that that's out of the way, here is a view from an economist: From statistics, picture a bell-shaped curve. This distribution captures considerable casual observations (some made in these comments). At the far right of the distribution, there are a few very healthy people. At the far left, there are a few very unhealthy people. Everyone else is in relatively good/bad health. Overlay the distributions of the US and Canada and you will see the Canadian average is higher than that of the US but its distribution also is more tightly packed. The Canadian distribution doesn't extend as far to the left or right as the US's distribution. The reasons for this are many but they include government healthcare programs. The Canadian system keeps its distribution from going too far to the left but also (may) keep it from extending further to the right. Ultimately, the average Canadian is healthier than the average person in the US. A US system (pre ACA) spreads the distribution but also lowers the average. The ACA is an attempt to reduce the spread in the US distribution. Time will tell if the US average also rises.

comment_text: Liberal Canadians would do well to ask themselves why Canada hasn't see the populist discontent that toppled establishment governments in the UK and USA. The key is to look at the demographics: It was mainly less educated rural voters who championed Brexit and Trump after suffering a decade of economic decline or stagnation. So why haven't Canadians of that same demographic revolted? Because Canada recovered from 2008 far better than the UK or the USA, and many of those blue-collar, rural or suburban voters still had good jobs. What jobs? Well, mainly the energy industry. Canada's counterparts to the discontented Northern UK or American Rust Belt workers moved to to the West to work in the oil patch or in mining, and earned a good wage doing it. Things have been far better for a welder or a truck driver in Canada because of those high paying energy industry jobs and the trickle-down effect they had on the job market. Well, the party's over. Those workers have gone back home to New Brunswick or Ontario. Families and rural communities who relied on those high-paying jobs are in distress. And discontent will rise. So I guess the lesson is those who don't want to see a Brexit or Trump uprising in Canada might reconsider the agenda to curtail or shut down Canada's oil industry. Deny those citizens who would work in the oilsands or build pipelines a livelihood and we could very well see our own populist tidal wave.

comment_text: For those who spend their hours reading junk science who like to quote papers they haven't even read, such as The Lancet, here's reality for ya:From The Lancet:'In their Review, Grandjean and Landrigan claim that fluoride might cause neurodevelopmental harm, a claim based on only one paper, of which Grandjean is a coauthor. The study methodology contains several flaws that undermine its credibility and calls into question its applicability to the community water fluoridation programme in the USA. The study is a meta-analysis of 27 cross-sectional studies done in poor, rural communities in China, Mongolia, and Iran, countries where the drinking water contains high levels of naturally occurring fluoride. The 27 original studies did not adequately control for a variety of intervening and confounding variables that could have affected intelligence quotient (IQ) scores, such as parents' education and socioeconomic status and air and water pollution. It is unfortunate that Grandjean and Landrigan did not mention these limitations. Additionally, they did not clearly state that the reference groups in their article use water fluoridated at about the recommended level. Thus, another interpretation of their analysis could be that communities fluoridated at the recommended level have a higher IQ.No credible scientific studies show a relation between fluoride consumption and IQ levels; however, several have shown that fluoride ingested at recommended levels is not harmful. Grandjean and Landrigan did not acknowledge the animal study that showed no evidence of a neurotoxic effect of fluoride, even at levels up to 230 times the recommended concentration; an earlier study showing that fluoride causes no harm to children; two formal reviews that delineate weaknesses in the Chinese fluoride and IQ studies; and the conclusion by one of these sets of investigators that biological plausibility for a link between fluoridated water and IQ has not been established. Unfortunately, Grandjean and Landrigan's Review has been aggressively and improperly used by antifluoridationists to frighten the public about the effects of fluoridation, a well-established public health measure that has been shown to be cost-effective and safe. As a result, the public's oral health, especially that of the most vulnerable people, is put in jeopardy.'

comment_text: If Dwight Newman is right, these meetings wouldn't be taking place. Dwight Newman is wrong, which is to say, he makes correct but selective observations that cover part of the story, while ignoring other issues that are equally as important. If you want to build a pipeline across the country, you need all the ducks in a roll. Having some/most of the ducks in a row, isn't good enough. *** Dwight Newman is right. That's the law. The C.A. 1867 creates the federal government and gives it certain powers. Again, the Court has made it clear: undertakings between provinces, specifically pipelines, are within the federal powers, not the provincial powers. Wynne/Couillard are within their rights to set dialogue along the lines of: 'We have serious and legitimate concerns because this pipeline will run through our provinces and we want those concerns heard and addressed.' What they do not have the legal right to do is to set conditions for 'approval.' That's like say for example, if you're in Canada and over the age of 18, your parents deciding whether you can marry someone. Depending on your culture, they may have more or less of a say in it, but in legal terms, they don't have the legal right to make that decision. There is no argument to the contrary.

comment_text: While I agree with much of the sentiments expressed, the recent uproar about TFW has morew to do with businesses rather than single 'employer' nanny situations. The stories in the news the past 4-6 weeks echo my experience in several smaller communities in eastern Canada, where Filipinos were hired wholesale to replace local workers. Yes, hiring local kids and lower educated adults can be a problem for the employer. But I've seen the experience of the TFW being paid higher wages with housing subsidised by the employer, and, when they arrive in sufficient numbers, the scheduling favours their own at the cost of even less time for local and lower paid workers. The towns I have experience in are industry-based towns with a tier of high union/technical wages underpinned by barely minimum wage jobs. This leaves little opportunity for younger people to work locally while housing and support costs are driven higher and higher. The main culprits (but not all) are the franchises: McDo's, Timmy, U-name-it Chicken place where the local prices are dictated by head office, leaving the local franchisee little option but to bring in foreign labour. It's hard to know all the details and one wants to be fair. But -- my policy has become: when I enter a restaurant or store with a majority of foreign workers, I leave. And if my experience continues in any one chain, then I don't bother to enter, tantalised as I am by the burgers, doughnuts, etc. The benefit has been a few notches off the belt!

comment_text: People always want to say this time is different than last time, but for those willing to see the big picture, thousands of years of history show the same patterns and lessons emerging repeatedly. The USA approach has usually been to think of brute force as courageous or a clever long term strategy. This conclusion has mostly failed, as even a cursory review of America's conflicts demonstrates. Canada has mostly seen humanitarian assistance, negotiation and a peacekeeping role as more effective both in the short term and the long run. I submit this has been equally courageous (given the temperament of our neighbours and partners) and much more effective, both in terms of doing actual good and of cultivating good relations in a world that sorely needs someone to provide leadership in the realm of civilized behaviour. It is when we have provided this leadership that I have been proud to be a Canadian.

comment_text: I fully believe n the need to investigate all questions openly and fairly. The question of whether or not 'racial differences' matter or are real is certainly one of them. However, the problem with the kind of argument made by Mr. Wade is that nothing is so simple. Are there genetic differences between people? Certainly. But the argument that the cultural differences matter far more is far more persuasive. Why are the Jews so successful? Well, it may have a lot to do with their need to preserve their culture through literacy, a rare and highly advantageous trait in the emerging European world. The fact that Jews were most numerous in Europe and the early Islamic world also meant they were in the right place at the right time to benefit from that advantage. Does this have a genetic component, after a few centuries? Possibly. But, if so, it's a combination of environment and genetics that cannot be separated. But then let's look at your other question: why are Chinese so successful? It wasn't that long ago that Europeans were looking down on Chinese (and all other non-white peoples) as clear examples of racially and culturally inferior people because they were so easily dominated and lacked whatever amorphous European qualities that had made the Europeans so successful. Now, you are holding up the Chinese as examples of racial superiority. Interesting how that can change, and so quickly too. Maybe this kind of discussion has a social context? Moreover, why not make the same argument about all Asian peoples? Sure, it wasn't that long ago that all of Asia was controlled by the 'superior West.' But today, Asia is on the rise and Asian children (from almost every Asian group) excel in Western schools. In all likelihood, in North America, we are seeing the emergence of an Asian social and economic elite that will easily displace the WASPs and the Jews. What happens to the racial argument then? But none of that needs to be explained using genetics; most of it can be explained by cultural values and norms. And then there is Africa. There are strong reasons to think that Africa will be the next site of major economic development. What happens to these racialist theories then? And one last point: to associate non-violence with Western society seems utterly bizarre. The worst wars in human history were strongly rooted in the West. Western colonialism, which has defined the history of the planet, was a massive exercise in violence. The point is this: genetics may be part of why human societies are different. But, in an incredibly complex world, it is, at best, likely a very small contributing factor when considered in comparison to economic, cultural and geographical considerations. Finally, there is another point: what do you do with this knowledge/belief? How is this information used? What kind of policies follow? Science, especially science that deals with society, is never neutral.

comment_text: Ultimately, we might be able to find out if Wade is right using similar analysis to that outlined here:'Genetic Inference: ... Europeans differ systematically in their height, and these differences correlate with latitude. The average Italian is 171cm, whereas the average Swede is a full 4cm taller. Are these differences genetic? Have they been under evolutionary selection in recent human history? Michael Turchin gave some pretty convincing answers to these questions, using genetic data from the 129 thousand individuals in the GIANT consortium. He compared the frequencies of alleles that are known to increase height, and found that they are more common in Northern Europe. Interestingly, he found the same relationship for alleles that have weaker evidence for height association, showing that there are still a large number of common height variants hiding in the genome, which are also more frequent in Northern Europe. Height differences are thus heritable, but have they been under evolutionary selection? Or are these differences merely down to genetic drift? This can also be tested using the GIANT data, which shows significant statistical evidence of selection on height variants in recent history. On top of that, the magnitude of the selection is correlated with the effect size of the height variant, providing strong evidence that these variants are being selected specifically for their impact on height. This is a textbook example of how an evolutionary study should be done; you show a phenotypic difference exists, that it is heritable, and that it is under selection. This opens the question as to why height has been selected in Northern Europe (or shortness in Southern Europe). Could the same data be used to test specific hypotheses there?'

comment_text: Indians in the Idle No More movement say the Canadian federal government (the big Crown) should respect First Nations sovereignty and abide by the treaties the Crown has with Indians. The British Crown made many different treaties with various groups of Indian bands and in the treaties the Indians agreed to become subjects of the Crown and obey the laws of the Crown so they can't claim sovereignty. Furthermore, the Crown didn't promise in any treaty with Indians to provide, pay for and maintain infrastructure like roads, bridges, houses, treatment plants, old age homes, Indian healing centres, community centres, bingo halls, playgrounds, hockey rinks, band offices and equipment, etc. or to pay for services like policing or fire protection or to pay for social programs for Indians on Indian reserves. Nevertheless, the Canadian federal government (the big Crown) now sends about $11 billion from taxpayers each year to pay for and maintain infrastructure like roads, bridges, houses, treatment plants, old age homes, Indian healing centres, community centres, bingo halls, playgrounds, hockey rinks, band offices and equipment, etc. and to pay for services like policing and fire protection and to pay for social programs on reserves the Crown did not promise in treaties for Indians on reserves. In addition, the provincial governments (the little Crowns) are providing millions of dollars from taxpayers each year to pay for projects on Indian reserves even though Section 91 part 24 of the Canadian Constitution says the Canadian government is responsible for 'Indians, and Lands reserved for the Indians'.And mining and other companies that are setting up on Crown land outside of Indian reserves are now also sending millions of dollars to Indian reserves even though those companies pay taxes to the Crown and it sends some of that tax money from those companies to Indian reserves. With all of that money, the Crown is sharing with Indians and is providing far more money than is required according to treaties to pay for infrastructure, services and social programs for Indians the Crown did not even promise in treaties for Indians on reserves. But do we hear a thank you? No, we only hear demands for more. Maybe, when PM Harper meets with Indian chiefs in Ottawa on January 11, 2103, he should tell the chiefs the Harper government will abide strictly by treaties; will stop paying more that is required in the treaties and will stop paying for infrastructure, services and social programs the Crown did not promise in treaties for Indians on Indian reserves. If the Indians want the Crown to live up to the treaties, maybe the Crown should live up to the treaties.

comment_text: Dear Mr. Simpson, My name is Sadie Clark and I am a 14-year-old student in the ninth grade at the Calgary Science School. I am responding to the editorial 'To Many First Nations Live in a Dream Place' published in The Globe and Mail news article on January 5th 2013. In this article you say that, 'The obvious conflict between reality and dream pulls some aboriginals to warrior societies; others to a rejection of dealing with the 'Crown' at all; others to fight for the restoration of 'rights' that, even if defined, would make little tangible difference in the lives of aboriginal people; and still others, such as Attawapiskat Chief Theresa Spence, to go on a hunger strike.' Although your article was brilliantly written, and I do agree with the majority of what is being conveyed, this one sentence is borderline racist, and is not being very respectful to the culture and beliefs of the Aboriginal peoples. comment_text: Good article, as usual. Not all social aggressors are men. By social aggressors I am not talking about sex; just the day to day things like space on the subway or standing in line. i reminded of the time i was in a long line, a few people from the front, waiting for a theatre to open. After being there for 20 minutes or more, with the line getting longer two older women arrived and slowly headed for the door, where they took over the first place in line. Nobody said a word. I waited a bit and then simply said in a loud voice 'ladies the end of the line is down the stairs'. The offenders quietly went to the back of the line. We have to individually take responsibility for our role in these interactions. It is not constructive to rant about an alleged group who are blamed for a non criminal lack of civility in life. It is also not useful to constantly whine about the usual problems in life such as hogging a seat in the subway or running a red light. On the subject of Dalhousie I appreciate the clarity that Ms. Wendt has brought to the discussion. Frankly I am not sure what I would do if I was close to the situation way out there in the Maritimes. I have done activist work. The best general strategy is to 'hold their feet to the fire''. I believe that is what Ms. Wendt is advocating. Get the issue moved up the food chain if nothing useful is done and get it in the press. However, it is not useful to make sweeping generalizations and/or unfounded charges. In addition I would bet that most women close to that situation don't fear for their safety because of some loose cannon, horrible and very stupid comments by a few guys. If safety was compromised by every crazy thing that someone said in private then we would be in constant fear and lockdown. I do believe that women have to use common sense about being in places where they need to keep a look out for sexual predators. However as a man I also do keep my radar on in situations where I could be vulnerable to mugging. I don't naively go just anywhere without assessing that potential. In isolated public washrooms I scan the cubicles so I know if someone is there, however harmless. Late at night in any city I would keep a watch as I passed dark alleys where there was no one around. I also would not verbally admonish someone who looks like a wacko with dangerous tendencies. Leave well enough alone. I believe it would help any woman to take a short course in a martial art or boxing at an early age so they can have confidence that in close quarters they can hurt an aggressor if needed. It is not about the act of hurting someone it is about the confidence of knowing you could. Please, please let us take more individual responsibility for our part in society and stop witch hunting any group, men or women, dentists or not.

comment_text: You wouldn't know this article was a book review about the psychological difficulties of communicating the realities of climate science, if you just read the comment section at face value... Although there are plenty of case studies on display!!! But I want to discuss specifically Ms. Renzetti's preamble to the book review itself. She details the overwhelming (near-unanimous) scientific consensus on climate science amongst scientific practioners... and then the closer to 50/50 split on the issue amongst the lay public in the English-speaking, western democracies. She then bridges onto her review with Marshall, which seems to want to explain why this 'consensus deficit' exists - i.e. why the public at large does not understand and accept to the same degree what the scientific community does. But this is a bit backwards, and is a key misunderstanding that the book's author, George Marshall, makes (in an otherwise intriguing and insightful book for those involved in climate communications.)In fact, a large reason the broad public does not hold the same degree of acceptance of the underlying science is that they are largely unaware that such an overwhelming consensus exists amongst scientists. When asked what percentage of scientists agree on the fundamentals (that greenhouse gases drive warming, that the warming is occurring, that we are driving the greenhouse gases, etc.) they again - incorrectly - get closer to the 50/50 guess, rather than the ~97% reality. Further, studies show that understanding that such a consensus exists tends to be a 'gateway' belief - i.e. if you are exposed to the fact that such a consensus exists, you are much more likely to accept the science, and also to support action. They've run experiments where individuals are first informed of the consensus, and then asked the poll question as to whether they personally accept the mainstream science. In those experiments, a vast majority of the respondents did accept the science. So simply being exposed to the existence of the scientific consensus *DOES* change personal acceptance of that science. comment_text: Don't have any answers to much of this. Sometimes we don't have answers, just questions. Martin has some. Good. However, he also makes some arguable statements. Allow me to argue a bit. 'But it’s a joke to think a healthy democracy can be restored given the continuing depletion of the one industry that holds business and government to account.'Based on numbers who went to the polls last year, Canadian democracy doesn't yet need restoring. Newspaper amalgamation and closures are hardly a new phenomenon. Sometimes its not lack of classifieds. Sometimes it's been union wage demands. and its not just newspapers: back in 2009, Canwest closed down a TV outlet in a provincial Capital--Victoria B.C. Staff bought it and it continues to operate; in the 1980s, small town radio took a hit when satellite radio first appeared. Who'd listen to Fort St. John radio when you could hear New York radio? Now there are more, not fewer, small-town stations. Not EXACTLY as they used to be--especially around ownership and technology--but more efficient than ever.'Newspapers being reduced to digital edition...' Why is the death of hard-copy bad? Why is a digital edition seen as something less? On-line comment pages serve many times the readers than restricted 'letters to the editor' space ever could. Journalists theoretically now have no space limitations. They keep writing, I keep scrolling. Oh, wait, I get it: lost jobs. Dislocation isn't new, either. The energetic, imaginative, sometimes, the merely desperate change, grow and create--as Julian Assange did-- 'the next great thing.'Mr. Martin asks, 'How many important stories, controversies, scandals have gone uncovered and will go uncovered as a result [of job loss]?' I have another question that just recently occurred to me: 'Would the stories make a difference? HAVE the stories made a difference?'The 21st century's greatest threat to democracy, certainly the greatest abuse of power in any western nation, came directly from the White House in the guise of 'Counter-terrorism.' comment_text: I don't think things are any worse than they were in my grandmother's day. My sister and I were fascinated as children when she told us our fortunes by reading tea leaves. In those days no-one would walk under a ladder, or open an umbrella indoors. My mother never believed in evolution and was convinced that Adam and Eve existed and the universe was formed in six days exactly. Many of my relatives read the News of the World, with its stories about alien invaders and flying saucers, although my uncle would hide it under the seat-cushions if anyone came to tea. Ms Southey is correct. there is a huge market for this stuff, but it has always been there. The internet has simply lifted up the rock so that we can see the millions of things wriggling about underneath. We just weren't aware of them before. Now they are exposed from all corners of the world for all to see. The antidote, of course, is education. We live in the most scientific age in the history of our planet and the same technology that has lifted up the rock also gives us access to factual data. What we do with all this information, of course, doesn't necessarily lead us to 'truth'. It leads us to our particular version of the 'truth' depending on our own inherent biases and beliefs. The 'truth' according to Ms Southey would not be the 'truth' according to her colleague columnist Ms Wente. So it's not quite as cut-and-dried as listening to the established media as opposed to other sources. Interesting column though. Thank you.

comment_text: Generally-speaking, I enjoy Ms. Wente's column. As a journeyman curmudgeon myself, I have come to appreciate her masterful wit and insight. This column, however, reads like a dog whistle to climate change deniers and tax-slashing neo-cons.It's all well and good to be derisive about 'nanny states' making decisions on our behalf that well-reasoned people should be able to sort out on their own, but the fact is that they just plain don't. Indeed, some never do, which then places an unfair burden on those of goodwill who are trying to make a difference. Think of the Earth's atmosphere as being like a really (REALLY!) big pool that we are all swimming in - one in which the water never gets changed. Historically, when people had to 'go' they could just 'let it rip' into the water. The pool seemed so very big that no single act was going to make much difference. After centuries, however, the water has started to look rather grey. To a person, of Ms. Wente's vintage, perhaps this isn't a problem. She may be long gone before it is unsafe to swim in. To a millennial, however, who is trapped in the murk for another 70 or 80 years, the situation looks rather alarming. There is plenty to ridicule in the environmental movement - where good intentions often run well ahead of sound engineering and thoughtful economics. There have been plenty of mistakes made by governments trying to address the issue of global climate change. Perhaps, when one realizes that one's house is on fire, good decision-making is hard. This is exactly why the problem needs minds like Ms. Wente's to keep the debate focused on practical solutions. Mere ridicule, pretending that there is no problem, and hoisting the flag of 'No!' to all proposed solutions is a waste of her talent. With respect, Paul.

comment_text: As the article states, raising minimum wage sounds like a great idea if you are earning minimum wage but it doesn't sound so great if you are running a struggling business. Most small and medium sized businesses are not making huge profits, they are just getting by.Two other big problems. First, jobs that continue to pay minimum wage are jobs that require no skill. For jobs requiring skill, there are varying levels of ability available in the job pool. Businesses that want to do better than their competitors will want those higher skilled workers and will pay more to get them. I am not in favour of a legislated wage increase for people who make no attempt to improve their skills. Second, any increase in wages get passed on to the consumer in the form of higher prices. Most minimum wage jobs produce goods and services consumed by everyone and people at the low end of the wage scale pay a larger percentage of their income on those goods and services so their increased earnings do not improve their ability to spend or to save. They will be no further ahead with an increase and at the same time will have been put at higher risk of losing their jobs. This move is nothing more than a sop by an unelected premier who is attempting to look proactive when in fact she does not understand the labour market or she would never have introduced this now.

comment_text: Alberta is fundamentally different from other provinces owing to the fact that a great many people living, working, and voting in the province do not plan to be here in 15 years. From the 26-year-old making $130,000 welding on Fort Mac, to the accountant five years away from retiring back home to Manitoba, to the executive saving for a property on Vancouver Island, this province is full of people who's overriding concerns are how much money shows up on their paycheque, and how long until they can leave. This attitude has afflicted even those born and raised here. Among the 30 to 50 year olds, the citizens you would expect to be most concerned about a sustainable tax base and strong public services, venality and unrestrained materialism are the order of the day. Frugality is regarded as an eccentric personality quirk. Then you have the simply ignorant, who believe the provincial budget is 30 per cent MLA pay, 10 per cent each health care and education, and 50 per cent waste. Between those two constituencies, it's almost impossible for a political regime to promote and carry out rational, long-term planning. Peter Lougheed would have no chance of getting elected by the voting constituency in Alberta today. It's sad. I found Alberta a much more agreeable place in the 80s and early 90s, before people became blinded by dollar signs in their eyes and came to regard their community as nothing more than a big work camp with some nice malls and restaurants in it.

comment_text: Sewing ambivalence is Simpson's instruction for today. Related are previous tactical obfuscations like, 'They're [politicians or parties] all the same,' and 'It's too close to call---a three-way split,' which serve to foster ambivalence about voting at all, and to obscure which opposition rival might be a strategic vote-choice for getting rid of a given Con candidate. Today's approach is to suggest the election result won't really matter in terms of key issues, Harper policies for which , Simpson would have us believe, the opposition contestants have been forced to adopt because they're so widely accepted by voters. Con partisans, for example, would prefer that this was really so because, like the other propaganda tactics, it would imply that, again, there's no real point in voting if, as the 'logic' goes, there's no real policy difference between the parties. Really, that notion is ridiculous to anyone paying attention---but, there's the rub, isn't it?Cons know good and well it's easier to get voters to take a pass than it is to get them to take a position, and this sinisterly applied truth informs much of the Cons' campaign so far: their narrow, highly circumscribed and tightly focused message (shielded from Q & A) is all about galvanizing the converted and naught about attracting proselytes, and their machinations are all about electoral dirty-tricks like cheating on allowable campaign spending, intentionally misinforming voters, and spreading as much ambivalence as the marginally participatory electorate will tacitly accept. Posit that Harper has reduced this margin considerably, and he did it the old-fashioned way: he earned it.With a smallish democratic minority, the Cons' know they can only win (short of garnering support meritoriously) if the opposition's divided, and the best sauce for that recipe is to dissuade voters from voting at all, low turnout increasing the effect of vote-splitting. To match the passiveness of electoral ambivalence, Cons must actively discourage strategic voting. Simpson's attempts to portray SV as unlikely, inadvisable and impossible have been transparently weak, whereas ambivalence probably has more natural purchase among potential voters. He has failed, however, to show how another term of Harper would be a good thing for Canada. BTW, 'balancing budgets' is a distraction: it's how, not if, and the Opposition has certainly laid out how its means to this end would be better for Canada than Harper's.

comment_text: After reading some comments here, I must say that I'm quite alarmed by how many deem earning graduate degrees a waste. If you wish to hold the position that there are too many young people holding multiple degrees, bear in mind that this demonstrates more what is currently wrong with post secondary education than education itself. What I find disquieting about post secondary education today is that it's viewed as a means to an end, rather than an end in itself. Indeed, Bachelor's and even Master's degrees are viewed as job training above all else. While this may be somewhat appropriate at the former level, it certainly isn't at the latter; a Master's degree should be an introduction to academe, and if not, it should teach people to ask WHY they are doing something in a particular filed, instead of teaching them HOW to do something. Unfortunately, undergrad and some graduate programs have been watered down for considerations of meeting labor demands, As others have noted, many of today's graduates can't gain employment in their chosen fields largely because the business community has irresponsibly abandoned job training to universities. Even worse is how aforementioned community doesn't recognize the irony of what it has produced, and that business education in many instances is an oxymoron. Finally, Margaret has omitted another contributing factor: credentialing, created by baby boomers to protect them already 20 years or more ago from younger competition. If post secondary education today perpetuates adolescence, it's only because society has permitted it to do so.

That is as ineffective a getting rid of mandatory testing of big highway rigs and relying on self-regulation, which works just until ---actual case----some rig wipes out on the 401 and closing all lanes of traffic for 8 hours, only for it to be found out after the fact that the suspension was held together by bungee cords.

comment_text: The claim that we can readily convert to a 100% renewable energy system is false and irresponsible. The only form of renewable energy capable of providing dependable capacity on the scale required to displace all carbon sources is hydro. To displace the existing coal and gas resources and meet load growth from electrification of transportation would require about 60,000 MW of new large-scale dependable capacity, almost all of which would be hydro, even if we initiate geothermal projects. The Site C hydro project in BC that the David Suzuki foundation is opposing would be just the tip of the iceberg. The carbon fundamentalists, by proposing a 100% renewable electricity system, are basically declaring war on Canada's rivers and, ironically, the First Nations who depend on those waters.

comment_text: This is a welcome look at the flipside of the coin, which we've unfortunately seen very little of to this point. The complexity of the consequences of different approaches to prostitution illustrates the importance of this being resolved by Parliament, and not by the courts. I don't say that out of fury over the courts' illegitimacy; I say that because constitutional restrictions imposed by the Supreme Court are very nearly impossible to 'undo', or even modify in any significant way. The good news, I think, is that Parliament should still have options open to it to wiggle away from whatever the Supreme Court decides. The problem with the current laws stems from the fact that prostitution itself is technically legal, but then made dangerous by laws surrounding it (sort of like telling people they can drive cars, but they can't wear seatbelts). All Parliament has to do is make prostitution actually illegal, and the constitutional issues evaporate. I expect that the court will structure its decision in such a way as to leave the maximum amount of room for Parliamentary intervention possible, while still resolving the constitutional questions that's obligated to address. Then the ball will finally be firmly in the politicians' court, where it belongs.

comment_text: Doug Saunders is right in highlighting the temporariness of today's temporary migrants that distinguish them from his parents' generation of immigrants to Canada. But there are other features of the conditions placed on their authorization to work in Canada that differentiate most of the people taking up low-skilled jobs that have accounted for the larger part of the recent boom in temporary residents. Principal among these is their deportability, a vulnerability inscribed in the very architecture of the Temporary Foreign Worker Program through closed work permits that bind today's migrants to a single employer and secures their acquiescence to conditions that workers with the freedom to choose their employer would find unacceptable. Another fundamental difference Saunders doesn't highlight is that most migrants are legally and practically prevented from bringing their families with them to Canada, a feature that fashions them into ultra-flexible workers—willing to work long hours over weekends, week on end, in order to earn something before their visa expires, and as importantly, available for shifts that Canadians might (have to) refuse because during those hours they are active in the everyday act of caring for others. Canada needs to grow through more immigration, but will be much better off as a nation if people arriving in this country to work are given the same rights as Canadians and the same ability to practice them. Kerry Preibisch, Associate Professor, University of Guelph

comment_text: Interesting that the author portrays the debate as 'science vs religious dogma'.Of course, any enlightened person should be able to see the difference. It's almost come down to a 'church vs state' argument. Politicians have been left guessing which way the wind is blowing so the smart ones have been hedging their bets. Just look at the GHG reduction plans and agreements. Mostly talk with general non-binding agreement to meet future targets. Kyoto fizzled. The US-China agreement was hailed as a victory except that China 'would start capping emissions by 2030 and aim to get 20 per cent of its energy from zero-carbon sources by the same year'Wow- what a breakthrough.'According to U.S. government projections, China will add yet another U.S. worth of coal plants over the next 10 years, or the equivalent of a new 600-megawatt plant every 10 days for 10 years'And in Oct 2014'European leaders have struck a broad climate change pact obliging the EU as a whole to cut greenhouse gases by at least 40% by 2030. But key aspects of the deal that will form a bargaining position for global climate talks in Paris next year were left vague or voluntary, raising questions as to how the aims would be realised.'Not to mention that countries like Poland which depends on heavy coal use, refused to sign the deal unless they received heavy discounts and rebates'.And what of the countries that have taken direct action? Just ask Spain and good old Ontario of the economic havoc created by subsidized green programs.
